docs.title: IMPRESS
docs.text:
Integrated Machine-learning for PRotEin Structures at Scale

IMPRESS is an asynchronous framework for managing complex protein design pipelines with adaptive decision-making capabilities. It is built for deploying heterogeneous scientific workflows (mixed CPU/GPU and data sharing) in high-performance computing environments. Using a building-block approach to workflow design, IMPRESS enables high-throughput campaigns based on foundation models like ProteinMPNN, RFDiffusion3, and Boltz-2, or with custom models requiring runtime training and optimization.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Protein Design Pipelines: Example and custom workflows
  • Adaptive Execution: Dynamic pipeline spawning
  • HPC Optimized: High-performance async execution
  • Flexible Architecture: Standard and user-defined pipelines
  • Autonomous Campaigns: IMPRESS-A composes a new workflow each cycle

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

from radical.asyncflow import LocalExecutionBackend, WorkflowEngine

from impress import ImpressBasePipeline, ImpressManager

class MyPipeline(ImpressBasePipeline):
    def register_pipeline_tasks(self):
        @self.auto_register_task()
        async def analyze(*args, **kwargs):
            return "echo 'Analyzing sequences'"

    async def run(self):
        await self.analyze()

async def run_dummy_pipelines():
    backend = await LocalExecutionBackend(ThreadPoolExecutor())
    flow = await WorkflowEngine.create(backend=backend)
    manager = ImpressManager(flow)

    try:
        await manager.start(pipeline_setups=[{'name': 'p1', 'config': {},
                                              'type': MyPipeline},
                                             {'name': 'p2', 'config': {},
                                              'type': MyPipeline},
                                             {'name': 'p3', 'config': {},
                                              'type': MyPipeline}])
    finally:
        await flow.shutdown()

asyncio.run(run_dummy_pipelines())

The caller owns the WorkflowEngine: create it from an execution backend, hand it to ImpressManager, and shut it down when start() returns.

docs.title: Adaptive Pipeline Walkthrough
docs.text:
This documentation walks through the adaptive capabilities of the IMPRESS pipeline framework, focusing specifically on how pipelines can dynamically spawn child pipelines during execution. For a conceptual overview of the underlying protocol, see Architecture; for real-world adaptive workflows, see Examples.

To watch this mechanism run instead of reading about it — including what changing the spawn threshold does to the pipeline tree — see Run It In Colab.

docs.title: 1. Pipeline Configuration for Adaptivity
docs.text:
The DummyProteinPipeline class is configured to support adaptive behavior through several key attributes:

def __init__(self, name: str, flow: Any, generation: int = 1,
             parent_name: str = 'root', max_generations: int = 3, **kwargs):
    self.iter_seqs: str = 'MKFLVLACGT'
    self.generation: int = generation            # Track generation level
    self.parent_name: str = parent_name          # Track parent pipeline
    self.max_generations: int = max_generations  # Limit recursion depth
    super().__init__(name, flow, **kwargs)

ImpressManager builds each pipeline as type(name=..., flow=..., **config, **kwargs): the keys of a setup's config dict arrive as keyword arguments, so the constructor declares them as keywords. A configs: dict parameter would always be empty.

Key adaptive attributes: - generation: Tracks the current generation level of the pipeline - parent_name: Maintains lineage information - max_generations: Prevents infinite recursion by setting a maximum depth

docs.title: 2. Adaptive Execution Point
docs.text:
The adaptive behavior is triggered at a specific point in the pipeline execution:

async def run(self) -> None:
    # ... other pipeline steps ...

    await self.run_adaptive_step(wait=True)  # Critical adaptive execution point

    # ... remaining pipeline steps ...

run_adaptive_step(wait=True): - This method flags the pipeline for an adaptive step; it does not call the adaptive function itself. The manager sees the flag on its next poll and awaits the pipeline's declared adaptive_fn task. - wait=True blocks the pipeline until that task has finished; wait=False returns at once. - Child requests made by the adaptive function are picked up and submitted by the manager on a later poll, not at this call.

docs.title: 3. Adaptive Strategy Function
docs.text:
The core adaptive logic is implemented in the adaptive_optimization_strategy function:

async def adaptive_optimization_strategy(pipeline: DummyProteinPipeline) -> None:
    # Decision logic: stop if max generations reached OR random condition (50% chance)
    if pipeline.generation >= pipeline.max_generations or random.random() >= 0.5:
        return  # No child pipeline created

    # Generate unique name for child pipeline
    new_name = f"{pipeline.name}_g{pipeline.generation + 1}"

    # Configure child pipeline
    new_config = {
        'name': new_name,
        'type': type(pipeline),                    # Same pipeline class
        'config': {
            'generation': pipeline.generation + 1,  # Increment generation
            'parent_name': pipeline.name,           # Set parent reference
            'max_generations': pipeline.max_generations,
        },
        'adaptive_fn': adaptive_task  # the DECLARED task, not the bare function
    }

    # Submit child pipeline to manager
    pipeline.submit_child_pipeline_request(new_config)

Key adaptive mechanisms:

  1. Conditional spawning: Uses generation limits and random conditions to decide whether to create children
  2. Configuration inheritance: Child pipelines inherit configuration with incremented generation
  3. Recursive adaptivity: Child pipelines use the same adaptive function, enabling multi-generational spawning
  4. Pipeline submission: Uses submit_child_pipeline_request() to register new pipelines with the manager

docs.title: 4. Manager Setup with Adaptive Function
docs.text:
The pipeline manager is configured to support adaptive behavior:

async def run() -> None:
    global adaptive_task

    execution_backend = await LocalExecutionBackend(ThreadPoolExecutor())
    flow = await WorkflowEngine.create(backend=execution_backend)
    manager: ImpressManager = ImpressManager(flow)

    # Declare where the callback runs; the manager only awaits it.  This
    # engine's one backend is already a thread pool, so no name is needed.
    adaptive_task = flow.function_task(adaptive_optimization_strategy)

    pipeline_setups = [PipelineSetup(name=f'p{i}',
                                     type=DummyProteinPipeline,
                                     adaptive_fn=adaptive_task)  # a declared engine task
                       for i in range(1, 4)]

    try:
        await manager.start(pipeline_setups=pipeline_setups)
    finally:
        await flow.shutdown()

Critical setup elements: - adaptive_fn must be an engine task, declared by the caller with flow.function_task(...). The manager awaits it and chooses nothing; a bare function raises TypeError when the PipelineSetup is constructed, before any pipeline starts. The backend must be a thread pool, since the callback mutates the live pipeline object. - A child config must carry that same declared task, which is why adaptive_task is module-level here: the recursion passes the task on, not the raw coroutine. Passing adaptive_optimization_strategy instead of adaptive_task is refused by name — declaring a callback marks the bare function too, so the two are easy to confuse and worth checking for. - The manager handles the lifecycle of dynamically created child pipelines

docs.title: Adaptive Execution Flow
docs.text:
1. Initial pipelines (p1, p2, p3) start execution
  2. Each pipeline runs its tasks until reaching run_adaptive_step()
  3. Adaptive function evaluates conditions (generation limit, random chance)
  4. If conditions are met, child pipeline configuration is created
  5. Child pipeline is submitted to the manager via submit_child_pipeline_request()
  6. Manager spawns the child pipeline and adds it to the execution pool
  7. Child pipelines repeat the process, potentially creating their own children

docs.title: Key Adaptive Features
docs.text:
• Dynamic pipeline creation: Pipelines can spawn children during runtime
  • Configurable conditions: Adaptive logic can be based on any runtime state
  • Generation tracking: Built-in support for tracking pipeline lineage
  • Recursive adaptivity: Child pipelines can also be adaptive
  • Manager integration: Seamless integration with the IMPRESS execution manager

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: IMPRESS is built from four cooperating pieces: an ImpressManager that orchestrates execution, ImpressBasePipeline subclasses that define individual workflows, PipelineSetup objects that declare how a pipeline should be submitted, and a radical.asyncflow WorkflowEngine (bound to an execution backend) that actually runs each task. This page describes how they fit together. For a worked, line-by-line example, see Adaptive Execution; for full method-level detail, see the API Reference.

docs.title: ImpressManager
docs.text:
ImpressManager is the central orchestrator. It runs pipelines on a radical.asyncflow.WorkflowEngine that you create and pass in. The caller owns the engine: create it from an execution backend (a local thread/process pool for testing, or an HPC backend such as DragonExecutionBackend/RadicalExecutionBackend for production runs), hand it to the manager, and shut it down when done. The manager never creates or shuts down the flow.

flow = await WorkflowEngine.create(backend=my_backend)
manager = ImpressManager(flow)
try:
    await manager.start(pipeline_setups=[...])
finally:
    await flow.shutdown()

ImpressManager also accepts use_colors (console log coloring), telemetry_config (kwargs forwarded to flow.start_telemetry(), e.g. checkpoint_path, resource_poll_interval; None disables telemetry), and telemetry_subscribers (callables registered on the telemetry stream right after it starts). When telemetry is enabled, the handle is available as manager.telemetry.

start() is the only real entry point, and its lifecycle is a simple cooperative polling loop:

  1. (Optionally) start telemetry on the supplied engine.
  2. Submit every initial PipelineSetup as a running asyncio.Task.
  3. Poll all live pipelines on a tight loop (sleeping briefly when nothing changed):
  4. If a pipeline has flagged invoke_adaptive_step, launch its adaptive function as a background task.
  5. If a pipeline has a pending child-pipeline request, buffer it as a new PipelineSetup.
  6. If a pipeline has set kill_parent, cancel its task.
  7. Track which pipelines and adaptive tasks have finished. A pipeline whose run() raised is logged as failed (pipeline_failed, with the exception) rather than completed; the manager keeps running the rest.
  8. Submit any buffered child pipelines.
  9. Exit once there are no running pipeline tasks, no running adaptive tasks, and nothing buffered.

The important invariant here — confirmed by the test suite — is that start() does not return until both a pipeline's run() coroutine and any adaptive task it triggered have completed. A pipeline whose run() finishes quickly but whose adaptive function is still evaluating results will keep the manager alive until that adaptive function resolves.

docs.title: ImpressBasePipeline
docs.text:
Every workflow subclasses ImpressBasePipeline and implements two required methods, plus one optional one:

  • register_pipeline_tasks() — called once, synchronously, from __init__, before anything else runs. Use @self.auto_register_task() here to bind coroutines as callable task methods.
  • run() — the pipeline's control flow: call the registered task methods, and call await self.run_adaptive_step(...) at points where the pipeline should evaluate intermediate results.
  • finalize() (optional; default no-op) — cleanup/bookkeeping logic, typically invoked by a pipeline's own adaptive function after it spawns a child pipeline (for example, to remove migrated work items from the parent's tracking state).

auto_register_task(local_task=False, capture_stdio=True, **task_kwargs) decides how a task runs: by default it wraps the function via self.flow.executable_task(**task_kwargs), submitting it as an HPC-executable task through the workflow engine; with local_task=True the function runs as a plain in-process coroutine (used for lightweight local work like parsing a CSV or ranking sequences).

Defaults that every pipeline gets without asking:

  • stdio is captured. An executable task's stdout and stderr go to {task uid}.stdout / .stderr in the backend's work dir, which is {work_dir}/{engine uid} for the work_dir passed to WorkflowEngine.create(). The task's future then resolves to the stdout file path, not the text; pass capture_stdio=False to get the text. This applies to rhapsody's backends (Concurrent, Dragon). asyncflow's LocalExecutionBackend ignores capture_stdio: futures resolve to the text, and a failure's stderr is already in the exception.
  • failures explain themselves. When an executable task fails, the last lines of its captured stderr are logged and attached to the exception as a note (Python 3.11+), on backends that capture stdio. Without this, the error is only a file path or an exit code.
  • tasks are labelled. Each call is tagged {pipeline}:{stage} in telemetry unless the caller passes workflow_id=. Otherwise asyncflow names a task after its executable, which is usually just bash.
  • local tasks are traced. When telemetry is enabled, each call of a local_task=True stage emits one impress.LocalStage telemetry event (stage, pipeline, duration, status), since local tasks never reach the engine.

For a per-task log file next to a task's outputs, return self.logged_command(log_file, cmd) instead of cmd.

A pipeline's self.state dict is the conventional place to pass data between stages — task methods write intermediate results into it (file paths, scores, directories), and later stages or the adaptive function read them back out.

docs.title: The adaptive / branching protocol
docs.text:
"Adaptive" in IMPRESS means a pipeline can pause at a checkpoint, hand control to an external decision function, and optionally spawn new sibling pipelines based on what that function decides — without any of this being expressed as a static graph.

  1. Inside run(), the pipeline calls await self.run_adaptive_step(wait=True) (or wait=False to continue concurrently). This sets invoke_adaptive_step = True.
  2. On its next poll, ImpressManager notices the flag and awaits the pipeline's registered adaptive_fn(pipeline) as a background task. That callback is an engine task, so it runs off the event loop (see below).
  3. adaptive_fn inspects/mutates the pipeline's state and attributes (for example, comparing a current score against a previous one), and may call pipeline.submit_child_pipeline_request(new_config) to request that a new pipeline be launched.
  4. When adaptive_fn completes (or raises — exceptions are caught and logged, never propagated), the manager clears invoke_adaptive_step and unblocks anything waiting on run_adaptive_step(wait=True).
  5. Separately, on every poll tick, the manager calls pipeline.get_child_pipeline_request() on every live pipeline. If one returns a config, it's converted to a PipelineSetup and submitted as a new pipeline.
  6. A pipeline can set self.kill_parent = True at any point to have the manager cancel its own task on the next tick (self-termination).

An adaptive function is an engine task, declared by the caller. One event loop drives every pipeline's task dispatch, so an adaptive function that blocks it — even an async def that never awaits — stalls all pipelines while it runs. On an 8-node, 32-pipeline run this held the loop for 67% of wall clock and cut throughput to 37% of baseline.

The manager therefore does not run adaptive functions itself. A runner declares where the callback runs, the way asyncflow's own examples declare any task, and passes the result as adaptive_fn:

local = await ConcurrentExecutionBackend(
    ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n_pipelines), name="local")
flow = await WorkflowEngine.create(backend=[compute, local])

@flow.function_task(backend="local")
async def adaptive_decision(pipeline):
    ...

PipelineSetup(name="p1", type=MyPipeline, adaptive_fn=adaptive_decision)

The manager awaits that task and labels each call {pipeline}:adaptive in telemetry. Routing is declared, never discovered, so there is one execution path and no mode to infer:

  • The backend must be a thread pool. The callback mutates the live pipeline object, and a process pool would mutate a pickled copy.
  • The body must be async def. asyncflow rejects a sync function outright; it needs no await inside, which is the normal shape for a task body.
  • PipelineSetup raises TypeError for an adaptive_fn that is not a task, when the setup is constructed — so, for the setups passed to start(), before any pipeline starts, and without needing a manager. A child config is converted on the manager's poll after the request, so a bad child adaptive_fn raises out of manager.start() mid-run. The manager has no path of its own to fall back to, so this fails rather than silently running somewhere.
  • A child pipeline's config must carry the declared task, not the bare function. These are harder to tell apart than they look: asyncflow marks the function it decorates, not only the wrapper it returns, so the bare body carries __task_description__ too. PipelineSetup separates them by the wrapper being a plain function where the body is a coroutine function, and names that case in its error. Left unchecked it is near-silent — the call fails inside the adaptive task, where the manager catches and logs it, then releases the pipeline to continue as though a decision had been made.

Module-level caches an adaptive function shares across pipelines may be touched from several of the pool's threads at once. A reader reachable from a loop over accumulated history must be memoised — keyed on path, with negative results left uncached — or every decision costs one blocking read per prior entry, which is the O(entries²) half of the 37% collapse above. Size any lru_cache for (entries × pipelines), since one manager process serves them all.

Because child pipelines can themselves have an adaptive_fn that spawns further children, this protocol supports arbitrarily deep or wide trees of self-spawning pipelines, all drained by the same manager loop before start() returns. The example workflows under Examples each use this protocol differently — see each page's Adaptive Flow section for specifics. Three of them write adaptive_fn as a hand-written decision function; the fourth, Agentic Small Molecule Binding, replaces it with a model.

Taking that one step further is a different architecture rather than a different adaptive_fn: if the shape of the workflow is itself chosen each cycle rather than parameterised, the graph cannot be written down ahead of time. That is what IMPRESS-A does, as a separate package built on the classes described here.

docs.title: PipelineSetup
docs.text:
PipelineSetup is a Pydantic model describing one pipeline submission:

  • name — pipeline instance name.
  • type — the ImpressBasePipeline subclass to instantiate (validated to actually be one).
  • config — configuration dict merged into the pipeline's constructor kwargs.
  • adaptive_fn — optional adaptive_fn(pipeline) -> None. Must be an engine task the caller declared on a thread-pool backend; validated on construction, including for a child config going through from_dict().
  • kwargs — additional constructor kwargs.

PipelineSetup.from_dict()/.to_dict() let a plain dict (such as the config dict returned from get_child_pipeline_request(), which often carries arbitrary extra keys like parent_name or generation) round-trip cleanly into a PipelineSetup and back.

docs.title: ImpressLogger
docs.text: ImpressLogger is a small, hand-rolled colorized console logger used internally by both ImpressManager and ImpressBasePipeline (via self.logger) to report lifecycle events — pipeline start/completion, adaptive function start/completion/failure, child pipeline submission, and pipeline failures, and periodic activity summaries (at DEBUG level). All levels, including ERROR and CRITICAL, are written to the logger's output_stream (default sys.stdout); a min_level argument drops messages below a given LogLevel. Most users only interact with it indirectly, through the use_colors argument on ImpressManager, or by calling self.logger.pipeline_log(...) from within a pipeline's own run().

docs.title: Execution backends
docs.text:
The execution backend is any backend object supported by radical.asyncflow. For local development and testing, use LocalExecutionBackend (from radical.asyncflow) wrapping a ThreadPoolExecutor or ProcessPoolExecutor. For HPC production runs, use a backend from rhapsody (rhapsody.backends): DragonExecutionBackend, RadicalExecutionBackend (configured with resource requirements such as GPUs, cores, runtime, and target machine), or ConcurrentExecutionBackend.

IMPRESS itself is agnostic to which backend is used. You build the engine with WorkflowEngine.create(backend=...), pass it to ImpressManager, and every task registered with auto_register_task() is submitted through that engine.

docs.title: Agentic Small Molecule Binding
docs.text:
Location: examples/agentic_small_molecule_binding/

Experimental

This example has no production record. Use Small Molecule Binding for real campaigns.

The same small-molecule binder design toolkit as the reference example, with the state machine removed: an LLM is given the tools and calls them directly. The question it exists to answer is whether a model reasoning over the campaign's own metrics directs the search better than a hand-written router, at a cost the allocation can bear.

docs.title: How it relates to the reference
docs.text:
AgenticSMBPipeline subclasses SmallMoleculeBindingPipeline and overrides only run(). Every task, the shell script behind it, its thread cap, its GPU pinning and the local analysis steps are inherited unchanged, so both examples place identical demands on an allocation. The offline test asserts this directly, comparing each task's task_description between the two classes on both the Dragon and concurrent backends.

Execution is the reference's too: one WorkflowEngine over two named rhapsody backends, compute (Dragon) for every tool and local (a thread pool) for the decision step, with one GPU per pipeline and staggered starts.

docs.title: The tool surface
docs.text:
Tool Runs Resource design_backbone rfd3 + analysis_backbone GPU, 8 threads design_sequence mpnn + analysis_sequence GPU, 4 threads pack_minimize packmin + analysis_packmin CPU, 1 thread relax fastrelax + analysis_fastrelax CPU, 1 thread score_interface filter_shape + analysis_interface CPU, 1 thread fold_complex boltz + analysis_fold GPU, 8 threads inspect_ensemble campaign history, in process free finish ends the pipeline free

Each executable tool is paired with its analysis step because every analysis_* reads {taskcount}_<stage>/out, and taskcount advances with every executable task — the two cannot be separated.

docs.title: The decision layer
docs.text: Where the reference calls adaptive_decision() to pick the next state-machine step, this calls one turn of the model to pick the next tool. Both run as flow.function_task(backend="local") on a thread pool, for the same reason: the body is synchronous, and blocking it on the event loop stalls every pipeline at once — the defect that capped job 22534628 at 37% of baseline throughput.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Every model is reached through an OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint with tool calling, configured by a profile in models.yaml, so comparing models means changing --model-profile and nothing else. A scripted profile replays a fixed route with no model at all, and also serves as the degraded mode if an endpoint fails mid-run.

The rules-d profile is the comparison's control. It runs the loop from the reference example's own adaptive_decision() rather than a model, so the decision rules are held fixed while the execution path varies — which is what separates the harness's contribution from the decision-maker's. Every other arm changes both at once.

The -d names control model D, the deterministic arm of the four-model taxonomy documented under Control Models. The letter is the shared vocabulary, not a shared implementation: this profile runs the reference example's decision rules, where IMPRESS-A's own model D resolves a goal to a specification and picks tasks by output type.

Each pipeline writes llm_transcript.jsonl — every turn, tool call, result and token count — which is both the comparison data and what makes a run replayable.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
# offline: no GPU, no network, no key
PYTHONPATH=../../src python test_agentic_smb.py

# on Delta
export SBATCH_ACCOUNT=<project>-delta-gpu
export WORK_DIR=/work/nvme/<project>/$USER
export IMPRESS_MODEL_PROFILE=claude-opus
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
sbatch delta_gpu_run.sh

The launcher checks the profile, the key and endpoint reachability on the batch node before queueing anything.

See the example's README for the guards against a stalling or looping model, and for which figures to compare against the reference.

docs.title: Discontinuous Scaffolds
docs.text:
Location: examples/discontinuous_scaffolds/

A three-stage protein design campaign targeting the MCSA-41 benchmark enzyme active sites. The pipeline generates backbone structures with discontinuous binding-motif scaffolds, predicts sequences, and folds them — applying quality thresholds at each stage to route failing models into adaptive branch pipelines while passing models advance, including a geometry-aware hybrid-scaffold redesign loop when folds don't recapitulate the target motif.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: All arguments are passed as kwargs to DiscontinuousScaffoldsPipeline.

docs.title: Path arguments
docs.text: Argument Default Description base_path os.getcwd() Root directory for all task outputs scripts_path DEFAULT_SCRIPTS_PATH Directory containing the step shell scripts foundry_sif_path DEFAULT_FOUNDRY_SIF Apptainer/Singularity image containing RFDiffusion3 mpnn_dir DEFAULT_MPNN_DIR Path to the LigandMPNN installation

docs.title: Pipeline input arguments
docs.text: Argument Default Description rfd_input_filepath DEFAULT_RFD_INPUT RFDiffusion3 input JSON (per-model input, ligand, contig, select_fixed_atoms) lmpnn_pdb_multi_json / lmpnn_fixed_res_json auto-generated LigandMPNN batch JSONs; generated from rfd_input_filepath at pipeline init if not provided island_counts_csv None Reference CSV of residue-island counts, used in backbone/sequence analysis mcsa_pdb_dir None Directory of reference PDBs for RMSD comparison in the final analysis rmsd_threshold 1.5 RMSD threshold (Å) for Step 8 analysis and anchor-residue classification diffusion_batch_size 10 Structures per RFDiffusion3 batch lmpnn_num_batches 4 LigandMPNN sequence batches generated per model

docs.title: Threshold arguments
docs.text:
All threshold arguments are (lower, upper) tuples or None (either bound may be None for an open interval); None disables the threshold entirely.

Stage Argument CSV column Backbone backbone_rog_bounds radius_of_gyration Backbone backbone_ala_bounds alanine_content Backbone backbone_gly_bounds glycine_content Backbone backbone_helix_bounds helix_fraction Backbone backbone_sheet_bounds sheet_fraction Backbone backbone_lig_dist_bounds n_clashing.ligand_min_distance Sequence seq_ligand_conf_bounds ligand_confidence Sequence seq_overall_conf_bounds overall_confidence

Benchmark input files under scripts/: mcsa_41_rfd3.json (all 41 entries, produced from rfd3_benchmark/mcsa_41.json by reformat_mcsa41.py), mcsa_41_one.json (single-entry test file), and mcsa_mod8-{1..6}.json (8-entry chunks from generate_batch_inputs.py). The runner expects one file per protein, {SCRIPTS_PATH}/mcsa_41-{i}.json; these are not in the repository and must be split out of mcsa_41_rfd3.json before a run.

docs.title: Pipeline Stages
docs.text:
Step Name Tool Resource 1 backbone_gen RFDiffusion3 via apptainer exec GPU 2 backbone_post cif_to_pdb.py CPU 3 backbone_analysis analysis_backbone.py + plot_backbone_analysis.py CPU 4 seq_pred LigandMPNN run.py CPU 5 seq_post split_seqs.py CPU 6 seq_analysis analysis_sequence.py + plot_sequence_analysis.py CPU 7 fold_pred Chai-lab chai_batch.py GPU 8 pipeline_analysis analysis.py + plot_campaign.py CPU

These eight steps are grouped into three stages: backbone (1–3), sequence (4–6), fold (7–8).

docs.title: Adaptive Flow
docs.text:
BACKBONE STAGE (steps 1-3) --> check_backbone_results() --> adaptive_decision()
    passing models -----------------------------------------------> continue
    failing models --> spawn backbone-start branch
                          |
                    SEQUENCE STAGE (steps 4-6) --> check_seq_results() --> adaptive_decision()
                        passing models ------------------------------------> continue
                        failing models --> spawn sequence-start branch
                                              |
                                        FOLD STAGE (steps 7-8) --> check_fold_results() --> adaptive_decision()
                                            passing models -----------------------------------> done
                                            failing models --> spawn redesign-scaffold branch
                                            pipeline terminates (next_step = STEP_DONE)

A model passes a stage if at least one of its analysis-CSV rows satisfies all active thresholds simultaneously; it fails if no such row exists. If no thresholds are configured, every model passes and no branches are spawned (_identify_passing_models()).

docs.title: After the backbone / sequence stages
docs.text:
Condition Action All models fail next_step = STEP_DONE; pipeline terminates All models pass Continue to the next stage with the full input set Mixed pass/fail Filter the current pipeline's inputs to passing models; spawn a branch pipeline (start_step = the failed stage) for the failing models

Backbone branches receive an rfd_input_filepath filtered to the failing models (with relative "input" paths rewritten to absolute). Sequence branches receive filtered LigandMPNN JSONs and a symlinked directory of passing .fa files, plus initial_state={'pdb_dir': ...} to seed the state a skipped backbone stage would normally have produced.

docs.title: After the fold stage — redesign loop
docs.text:
The pipeline always terminates after the fold stage (next_step = STEP_DONE), but if any models fail rmsd_threshold, a redesign-scaffold branch may be spawned first. Two stopping conditions prevent runaway redesign loops — if either is true, no branch is spawned:

Constant Default Condition MAX_REDESIGN_DEPTH 3 This lineage has already been redesigned this many times MIN_RMSD_IMPROVEMENT 0.10 Å RMSD hasn't improved enough since the last redesign

If neither condition triggers, adaptive_decision() serializes the best fold per model, then runs scripts/create_redesign.py to build a hybrid scaffold: well-predicted anchor motif regions (Kabsch-aligned from the best Chai-1 output) are combined with poorly-predicted motif residues taken directly from the reference PDB (renumbered starting at 900); the contig string and fixed-atom spec are rewritten to match. A new backbone-start branch is then spawned from this redesign.json, carrying redesign_depth + 1 and the current best RMSD forward.

docs.title: Branch naming
docs.text: Branch type branch_id format Example Root pipeline {pipeline_name}_0 disco_p26_0 Backbone/sequence branch {pipeline_name}_{n} disco_p26_1 Fold redesign branch {pipeline_name}_R disco_p26_R Second redesign of a redesign {original_name}_R_R disco_p26_R_R

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
{base_path}/
  disco_p26_0/                     # root pipeline
    1_backbone_gen/out/
    2_backbone_post/out/
    3_backbone_analysis/out/
    filtered_lmpnn_pdb.json         # if a backbone branch was spawned
    4_seq_pred/out/
    5_seq_post/out/
    6_seq_analysis/out/
    filtered_seqs_split/            # if a sequence branch was spawned
    7_fold_pred/out/
    8_pipeline_analysis/out/
    best_fold.json                  # if a fold branch was spawned
  disco_p26_R/                     # redesign branch
    redesign.json
    M0024_1nzy/redesign_scaffold.cif
    1_backbone_gen/out/
    ...

The branch_id prefix isolates each branch's outputs from the root pipeline and from sibling branches.

docs.title: Running It
docs.text:
cd examples/discontinuous_scaffolds
python run_discontinuous_scaffolds.py

Edit the path and threshold constants at the top of run_discontinuous_scaffolds.py before running; one DiscontinuousScaffoldsPipeline is launched per benchmark input file. The runner launches pipelines disco_p24 through disco_p28.

The runner creates the engine itself over two named backends and hands it to the manager. compute runs every stage: DragonExecutionBackend (from rhapsody.backends) by default; for local testing, swap in the commented-out LocalExecutionBackend(ProcessPoolExecutor(), name="compute"). local is a thread pool for adaptive_decision, which mutates the live pipeline and so cannot run in a process pool:

compute = await DragonExecutionBackend(name="compute")
# compute = await LocalExecutionBackend(ProcessPoolExecutor(), name="compute")
local = await ConcurrentExecutionBackend(
    ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=len(PIPELINE_INDICES)), name="local")

flow = await WorkflowEngine.create(backend=[compute, local])
manager = ImpressManager(flow)

adaptive_task = flow.function_task(backend="local")(adaptive_decision)
# ... PipelineSetup(..., adaptive_fn=adaptive_task) per input file

try:
    await manager.start(pipeline_setups=pipeline_setups)
finally:
    await flow.shutdown()

Child pipelines spawned by adaptive_decision are given the same adaptive_task; passing the bare adaptive_decision raises TypeError.

docs.title: Protein Binding
docs.text:
Location: examples/protein_binding/

An IMPRESS pipeline for iterative computational design of PDZ-domain protein binders against a target peptide. Starting from a set of input PDZ PDB structures, the pipeline runs ProteinMPNN sequence design, Boltz-2 complex structure prediction, and pLDDT/PTM/PAE scoring in a loop. An adaptive decision function compares per-pass scores and spawns child pipelines for proteins whose predicted quality degrades, trying the next-ranked MPNN sequence instead.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input PDB structures are placed in <input_base_path>/prod_in/<name>_in/ (e.g. prod_in/p1_in/), one file per PDZ scaffold. No ligand or .params files are needed — this is protein-peptide, not small-molecule, binder design.

docs.title: Pipeline parameters
docs.text:
ProteinBindingPipeline reads these from its constructor kwargs (i.e. from PipelineSetup.config):

Parameter Default Description base_path os.getcwd() Directory containing scripts/ and mpnn_wrapper.py input_base_path base_path Parent of prod_in/ output_base_path base_path Parent of af_pipeline_outputs_multi/ and the per-pass stats CSVs mpnn_path $MPNN_PATH Path to a ProteinMPNN checkout; raises ValueError if neither the kwarg nor the env var is set peptide_seq "EGYQDYEPEA" Target peptide sequence co-folded with each design max_passes 10 Maximum design/predict iterations per pipeline num_seqs 10 Number of MPNN sequences generated per job seq_rank 0 Index into ranked sequences to fold (0 = best score)

is_child, passes, start_pass, sub_order, iter_seqs, and previous_scores are set by the adaptive function when it spawns a child pipeline; they don't normally need to be supplied.

docs.title: Pipeline Stages
docs.text:
Task Type Script / Tool Resource s1 HPC scripts/s1_mpnn.sh → mpnn_wrapper.py (ProteinMPNN) GPU s2 local Parses MPNN FASTA output, ranks by score, populates iter_seqs CPU s3 local Writes a Boltz input FASTA (designed sequence + target peptide) per structure CPU s4 HPC scripts/s4_boltz.sh (boltz predict, Boltz-2) GPU s4_post_exec local Copies the best-model PDB (renaming Boltz chain IDs pdz/pep → A/B) into best_models/ and mpnn/job_<N>/, and the confidence JSON into best_ptm/ CPU s5 HPC scripts/s5_plddt_extract.sh → plddt_extract_pipeline.py (PyRosetta + BioPandas) CPU
  • s1, s4 and s5 capture their stdio (the framework default). No GPU placement hints are set on the tasks or in the scripts; GPU assignment is left to the execution backend.
  • s1 always designs chain A. On pass 2+ its input is the previous pass's best-model PDB.
  • s3 checks for pre-computed MSAs under ~/boltz/msa_cache/boltz_results_<name>/msa/. If both chain MSAs exist it references them in the FASTA; otherwise it writes empty and Boltz runs in single-sequence mode. This path is hard-coded (protein_binding.py:152) and does not follow delta_env_setup.sh, which writes MSAs to ${WORK_DIR}/boltz/msa_cache; link one to the other until that is fixed (framework backlog F23).
  • s4/s4_post_exec run concurrently across all structures in a pass via asyncio.gather. If every s4_post_exec fails the pass raises RuntimeError rather than scoring empty output.
  • s1, s4, and s5 tolerate spurious backend exceptions: if the task's expected output exists on disk, the error is logged and treated as success.
  • s5 writes avg_plddt, ptm (max iPTM+PTM), and avg_pae (cross-interface predicted aligned error) to a per-pass CSV.

s4_boltz.sh reads these environment variables:

Variable Default Effect BOLTZ_VENV $VIRTUAL_ENV Environment whose bin/ provides the boltz CLI BOLTZ_CACHE_DIR $HOME/.boltz Boltz weights/CCD cache (--cache) BOLTZ_USE_MSA_SERVER unset Set to 1 to add --use_msa_server (off by default)

docs.title: Adaptive Flow
docs.text:
s1 (mpnn) --> s2 (rank seqs) --> s3 (write FASTA) --> s4 (Boltz-2 x N, parallel)
                                                                  |
                                                      s4_post_exec (stage files x N, parallel)
                                                                  |
                                                           s5 (pLDDT extract)
                                                                  |
                                                       adaptive_decision()
                                            +--------------------+--------------------+
                                     score improved                              score degraded
                                  (keep in pipeline)                (spawn child pipeline, seq_rank+1)
                                                                  |
                                                        passes += 1 (up to max_passes)

adaptive_decision() (defined inside impress_protein_bind() in run_protein_binding.py, and declared on the local backend with @flow.function_task(backend="local")) runs after each pass and reads <output_base_path>/af_stats_<name>_pass_<N>.csv:

Pass Condition Action Pass 1 No prior scores Save current scores as baseline; continue Pass 2+ current_score <= previous_score (improved or held) Keep the protein in the current pipeline Pass 2+ current_score > previous_score (degraded) Move the protein to a new child pipeline at seq_rank + 1

When one or more proteins degrade, a child pipeline named <parent>_sub<N> is created: its input directory (prod_in/<parent>_sub<N>_in/) is populated with the degraded proteins' best-model PDBs, and it inherits iter_seqs (skipping s1/s2 on its first pass, since sequences already exist) but uses the next-best MPNN candidate (seq_rank + 1). Children inherit the parent's input_base_path/output_base_path. Nesting is capped at MAX_SUB_PIPELINES = 3. If the parent's tracked protein list is emptied after spawning, it sets kill_parent = True and terminates.

run_protein_binding.py enables ImpressManager telemetry (checkpoint_path="./telemetry/") and emits three custom events from the adaptive function: impress.ProteinScore, impress.ChildPipelineSpawned, and impress.PassSummary. A telemetry summary is printed when the run finishes.

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
<input_base_path>/
  prod_in/<name>_in/                          # input PDB files
<output_base_path>/
  af_pipeline_outputs_multi/<name>/
    mpnn/job_<N>/seqs/                         # MPNN FASTA files for pass N
    mpnn/job_<N>/<protein>.pdb                 # copy of the pass-N best model
    af/fasta/                                  # Boltz input FASTAs (designed + peptide)
    af/prediction/best_models/                 # best-model PDB per structure
    af/prediction/best_ptm/                    # confidence JSON per structure
    af/prediction/dimer_models/<protein>/      # full Boltz outputs
      boltz_results_<protein>/predictions/<protein>/
    af/prediction/logs/
  af_stats_<name>_pass_<N>.csv                 # per-pass scores: ID, avg_plddt, ptm, avg_pae

docs.title: Running It
docs.text:
run_protein_binding.py is configured entirely through environment variables:

Variable Default Description IMPRESS_BACKEND dragon The compute backend: dragon → DragonExecutionBackend; anything else → ConcurrentExecutionBackend(ProcessPoolExecutor()) (both from rhapsody.backends). A second, local thread-pool backend always runs the adaptive callback IMPRESS_N_PIPELINES 16 Number of root pipelines (p1 … pN) IMPRESS_MAX_PASSES 10 max_passes for each pipeline IMPRESS_SCRIPTS_DIR the example directory Passed as base_path IMPRESS_BASE_DIR IMPRESS_SCRIPTS_DIR Passed as input_base_path IMPRESS_OUTPUT_DIR IMPRESS_SCRIPTS_DIR Passed as output_base_path MPNN_PATH — ProteinMPNN checkout (required)

For a local (non-Dragon) run:

cd examples/protein_binding
export MPNN_PATH=/path/to/ProteinMPNN
export IMPRESS_BACKEND=local IMPRESS_N_PIPELINES=2 IMPRESS_MAX_PASSES=2
python run_protein_binding.py

The runner follows the standard IMPRESS pattern: it creates the engine over two named backends, passes the engine to the manager, declares the adaptive callback on the local thread pool, and shuts the engine down itself:

compute = await DragonExecutionBackend(name="compute")
local = await ConcurrentExecutionBackend(
    ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N_PIPELINES), name="local")
flow = await WorkflowEngine.create(backend=[compute, local])
manager = ImpressManager(
    flow,
    telemetry_config={"checkpoint_path": "./telemetry/", "resource_poll_interval": 5.0},
    telemetry_subscribers=[_on_task_event],
)

@flow.function_task(backend="local")
async def adaptive_decision(pipeline): ...

try:
    await manager.start(pipeline_setups=pipeline_setups)
finally:
    await flow.shutdown()

The callback must run on a thread pool, because it mutates the live pipeline object. The decorator rebinds adaptive_decision to the task, so child configs that pass 'adaptive_fn': adaptive_decision carry the task, not the bare function.

docs.title: On NCSA Delta
docs.text:
Two helper scripts target Delta's gpuA40x4 partition:

  • delta_env_setup.sh — run once on a login node (requires WORK_DIR, e.g. /work/nvme/<project>/$USER; options --env-dir, --impress-dir, --python). Creates a Python ≥ 3.11 venv in ${WORK_DIR}/ve/impress with radical-asyncflow, rhapsody-py[dragon,telemetry], IMPRESS (editable), PyTorch, and PyRosetta; builds a separate Boltz conda env in ${WORK_DIR}/ve/boltz; warms the Boltz cache in ${WORK_DIR}/boltz; and pre-computes MSAs into ${WORK_DIR}/boltz/msa_cache for every prod_in/p*_in/*.pdb under $IMPRESS_BASE_DIR (default ${WORK_DIR}/IMPRESS_inputs).
  • delta_gpu_run.sh — the batch job (sbatch delta_gpu_run.sh; create logs/ in the example directory first, since Slurm writes the job logs there; requires WORK_DIR). Sets up Delta's CUDA/MPI/libfabric paths, activates ${IMPRESS_VENV:-${WORK_DIR}/ve/impress}, configures Dragon, exports MPNN_PATH, BOLTZ_VENV, BOLTZ_CACHE_DIR, and the IMPRESS_* path variables (IMPRESS_BASE_DIR=${WORK_DIR}/IMPRESS_inputs, IMPRESS_OUTPUT_DIR=${WORK_DIR}/IMPRESS_outputs), and launches dragon -s run_protein_binding.py (-m for multi-node jobs), or plain python3 when IMPRESS_BACKEND=local.

Note

delta_gpu_run.sh defaults BOLTZ_VENV to ${HOME}/ve/boltz, while delta_env_setup.sh builds the Boltz env in ${WORK_DIR}/ve/boltz. Export BOLTZ_VENV=${WORK_DIR}/ve/boltz before sbatch until the default is aligned (framework backlog F23).

docs.title: Alternate entry point
docs.text: • run_nonadaptive.py — 16 pipelines with no adaptive_fn on DragonExecutionBackend, used as a baseline to measure the benefit of the adaptive strategy. It passes no path config, so it relies on MPNN_PATH and the current working directory.

docs.title: Small Molecule Binding
docs.text:
Location: examples/small_molecule_binding/

An IMPRESS pipeline for iterative computational design of protein binders against a small-molecule ligand. Starting from a ligand-containing target structure, the pipeline runs backbone diffusion, sequence design, energy minimization, structural validation, and fold prediction in a loop, using an ensemble-history-based adaptive router to direct the search toward productive regions of structure-sequence space rather than fixed pass/fail gating alone.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Each pipeline reads its inputs from input_dir when given (absolute, or relative to base_path), else from <base_path>/<pipeline_name>_in/. The runner passes the absolute examples/small_molecule_binding/p{i}_in/, one directory per pipeline.

File Required Description ALR_binder_design.json Yes RFDiffusion3 design config (target structure, hotspot residues, diffusion settings) fixed_residues.txt Yes Space-separated residue indices held fixed during MPNN sequence design <ligand>.params Yes Rosetta ligand parameter file (e.g. ALR.params); filename must match ligand_params <ligand>.smiles Yes (boltz) Ligand SMILES for Boltz-2 co-folding (e.g. ALR.smiles); stem must match ligand_params common_filenames.txt Yes (filter_energy) Accepted filenames for ligand energy filtering input_pdbs/ Optional Target PDB files referenced by the diffusion config

docs.title: Configurable parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description base_path os.getcwd() Root directory for all task subdirectories and inputs input_dir <name>_in Input directory (absolute, or relative to base_path) scripts_path <base_path>/scripts Directory holding the tool wrapper scripts mpnn_dir env MPNN_DIR Path to a LigandMPNN checkout (required; ValueError if unset) foundry_sif_path env FOUNDRY_SIF_PATH Apptainer image containing RFDiffusion3 (required) boltz_cache_path env BOLTZ_CACHE Boltz-2 model cache (required) ligand_params ALR.params Ligand parameter filename (relative to the input directory) mock False Run with lightweight mock tasks — no HPC tools required num_refine_cycles 3 MPNN → PackMin cycles per backbone attempt mpnn_ensemble_size 1 Independent sequence batches generated on cycle 0 diffusion_batch_size 2 Backbone models generated per RFDiffusion3 call rfd3_partial_t 10.0 RFD3 partial-diffusion noise (Å) for guided backbone feedback max_tasks 300 Total ensemble entries before the pipeline stops start_delay 0 Seconds run() waits before its first stage (set by the runner to stagger pipelines sharing a GPU)

These are the class defaults. The runner's PROD config (run_small_molecule_binding.py) overrides several of them and the thresholds below, e.g. diffusion_batch_size=4, num_refine_cycles=2, mpnn_ensemble_size=10, backbone_max_ca_deviation=1.0, fold_min_plddt=75.0.

docs.title: Quality thresholds
docs.text: Parameter Default Metric backbone_max_ca_deviation 2.0 Å Max CA deviation from the diffusion target backbone_min_ss_fraction 0.2 Minimum helix + sheet fraction fastrelax_max_interact 0.0 REU Protein-ligand interaction energy fastrelax_max_total_score 0.0 REU Total Rosetta score fastrelax_max_fa_rep 150.0 REU Steric clash energy interface_min_sc 0.5 Minimum shape complementarity fold_min_plddt 70.0 Minimum mean pLDDT from Boltz-2 fold_min_ligand_iptm None (off) Minimum Boltz-2 protein-ligand interface confidence

docs.title: Pipeline Stages
docs.text:
Task Type Script / Tool Resource rfd3 HPC scripts/rfd3.sh (RFDiffusion3 via Apptainer) GPU analysis_backbone local Reads JSON metrics from the rfd3 output directory CPU mpnn HPC scripts/mpnn.sh → scripts/mpnn_run.py (LigandMPNN) CPU analysis_sequence local Reads .fa headers from MPNN seqs/ output CPU packmin HPC scripts/packmin.sh → scripts/packmin.py (PyRosetta pack + minimize) CPU analysis_packmin local Reads _packmin_score.json CPU fastrelax HPC scripts/fastrelax.sh → scripts/fastrelax.py (Rosetta FastRelax) CPU analysis_fastrelax local Reads the .fasc score file CPU filter_shape HPC scripts/filter_shape.sh → scripts/filter_shape.py (PyRosetta shape complementarity) CPU analysis_interface local Reads shape_complementarity_values.txt CPU boltz HPC scripts/boltz.sh (Boltz-2 protein-ligand co-folding) GPU analysis_fold local Reads Boltz-2 confidence_*.json files CPU

The fold step is still called STEP_AF2 in the state machine; the name predates the switch from ColabFold to Boltz-2.

The pipeline runs as a while self.next_step != STEP_DONE state machine, calling adaptive_decision() after every analysis step:

STEP_RFD3  --> analysis_backbone --> adaptive_decision()
STEP_MPNN  --> refine cycle:
                   for each cycle:
                       mpnn --> analysis_sequence --> adaptive_decision()
                       packmin --> analysis_packmin --> adaptive_decision()
STEP_FASTRELAX --> analysis_fastrelax --> adaptive_decision()
STEP_INTERFACE --> analysis_interface --> adaptive_decision()
STEP_AF2       --> analysis_fold       --> adaptive_decision() --> STEP_RFD3 (loop)

The MPNN + PackMin inner refinement cycle runs num_refine_cycles (default 3) iterations: cycle 0 generates mpnn_ensemble_size independent sequence candidates from the best backbone; later cycles generate one candidate from the current best packed structure. PackMin is skipped on the final cycle.

docs.title: Adaptive Flow
docs.text:
Unlike the other two examples, this pipeline never spawns child pipelines — all adaptivity happens via next_step/state transitions inside a single pipeline instance, and termination is budget-bounded (max_tasks), not convergence-bounded.

Every analysis task appends (type, score, input_path, output_path) to pipeline.state['ensemble']. For a given stage, adaptive_decision() computes:

  • overall_avg — mean score across all prior entries of that type.
  • selective_avg — mean score of prior entries whose structural or sequence similarity to the current result (Kabsch CA-RMSD for structures, per-position identity for sequences) is on the "similar" side of the mean pairwise similarity.

A result is in a productive neighbourhood when selective_avg > overall_avg.

After step Condition Next step backbone Fails hard thresholds STEP_RFD3 — retry backbone No prior data, or selective_avg > overall_avg STEP_MPNN — proceed backbone selective_avg <= overall_avg STEP_RFD3 — unproductive region, retry sequence No prior data, or selective_avg >= overall_avg STEP_MPNN (reset retry count) sequence selective_avg < overall_avg, retries < 3 STEP_RETRY_SEQ — rerun MPNN, same cycle sequence Retries exhausted (>= 3) STEP_RFD3 — abandon this backbone packmin Always STEP_MPNN — continue refinement cycle fastrelax Pass / fail STEP_INTERFACE / STEP_MPNN retry; STEP_RFD3 once retry metrics stop improving, or after 5 attempts interface Pass / fail STEP_AF2 / STEP_MPNN retry; STEP_RFD3 once retry metrics stop improving, or after 5 attempts fold selective_avg > overall_avg STEP_RFD3, with the current fold decoy fed back as rfd3_input_pdb (guided diffusion) fold Otherwise STEP_RFD3, with rfd3_input_pdb cleared (start from scratch)

Fold analysis never sets STEP_DONE — the loop is intentionally open-ended, and the pipeline only terminates when max_tasks ensemble entries have accumulated.

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
<base_path>/                     # the runner's work dir
  <pipeline_name>/
    <N>_rfd3/out/                # backbone diffusion outputs
    <N>_mpnn/out/seqs/           # FASTA files with confidence scores
    <N>_mpnn/out/packed/         # packed PDB structures
    <N>_packmin/out/             # minimized PDB + score JSON
    ...
    <N>_boltz/out/               # Boltz-2 predictions + confidence JSONs

<N> is the pipeline's running task count, so the numbers depend on the route taken, not on the stage.

docs.title: Running It
docs.text:
On NCSA Delta, delta_env_setup.sh builds the environment and sbatch delta_gpu_run.sh launches the runner under Dragon. To run it directly:

cd examples/small_molecule_binding
export MPNN_DIR=... FOUNDRY_SIF_PATH=... BOLTZ_CACHE=...
IMPRESS_BACKEND=local python run_small_molecule_binding.py --n-pipelines 1
Setting Default Description IMPRESS_BACKEND dragon The compute backend: dragon → DragonExecutionBackend; anything else → ConcurrentExecutionBackend(ProcessPoolExecutor()). A second, local thread pool runs the declared adaptive callback --n-pipelines / IMPRESS_N_PIPELINES PROD.n_pipelines (4) Number of pipelines; each needs its own p{i}_in/ --work-dir / IMPRESS_WORK_DIR examples/small_molecule_binding/logs Run directory, passed as base_path MPNN_DIR, FOUNDRY_SIF_PATH, BOLTZ_CACHE — Tool paths (required)

Prefer the command-line flags under Dragon: on a multi-node run, environment variables set by the launcher do not reach the runner. Pipeline thresholds live in the PROD RunConfig at the top of run_small_molecule_binding.py.

An alternate routing mode and a mock entry point are also provided:

  • run_small_molecule_binding.py --nonadaptive (or IMPRESS_NONADAPTIVE=1 sbatch delta_gpu_run.sh) — a fixed routing table (every stage always "passes" and proceeds linearly, with no ensemble comparison or guided backbone feedback), used as a baseline comparison. Everything else (backends, GPU pinning, staggered start, telemetry) is the same as the adaptive run.
  • run_test_small_molecule_binding.py — a mock dry run (mock=True, routing to mock.py's placeholder tasks) that exercises the full state machine and adaptive routing logic with no external HPC tools required; terminates after 100 ensemble entries.

The mock run still constructs the real pipeline class and imports the runner, so set placeholder tool paths and a non-Dragon backend: MPNN_DIR=x FOUNDRY_SIF_PATH=x BOLTZ_CACHE=x IMPRESS_BACKEND=local python run_test_small_molecule_binding.py. It writes p1/ into the current directory, so run it from a scratch copy.

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text:
This page shows you how to set up your environment to use Impress and run asynchronous pipelines with it.

We recommend using a virtual environment to isolate your dependencies.

docs.title: Step 1: Create a Python Environment
docs.text:
Make sure you have Python 3.9 or newer installed. You can check your Python version with:

python3 --version

We recommend creating a virtual environment to keep dependencies clean.

docs.title: Using venv
docs.text:
On Linux/Mac:

python3 -m venv impress-env
source impress-env/bin/activate

On Windows:

python -m venv impress-env
impress-env\Scripts\activate

Your shell prompt should now show (impress-env) indicating the environment is active.

docs.title: Step 2: Install Impress
docs.text:
Clone the repository and install Impress with its required dependencies (including radical-asyncflow>=0.4.0, its workflow engine):

git clone https://github.com/radical-collaboration/IMPRESS.git
cd IMPRESS
pip install .

Use pip install -e . instead if you plan to modify Impress itself.

docs.title: HPC execution backends (optional)
docs.text:
Local runs of your own pipelines only need radical.asyncflow's built-in LocalExecutionBackend. The example runners under examples/ need rhapsody even with IMPRESS_BACKEND=local: their local mode uses its ConcurrentExecutionBackend. HPC backends such as DragonExecutionBackend and RadicalExecutionBackend come from rhapsody, which is not installed automatically. The example workflows under examples/ import it:

pip install "rhapsody-py[dragon,telemetry]"

The protein binding and small molecule binding examples also ship delta_env_setup.sh scripts that build a complete environment (Impress, rhapsody, PyTorch, PyRosetta, Boltz-2, and so on) on NCSA Delta. See Examples.

docs.title: IMPRESS-A (optional)
docs.text:
IMPRESS-A is a second package in this repository, under agent/. The clone above brings it with it, but pip install . does not install it: it is its own distribution (impress_a, Python >= 3.11) with its own dependency set, and it is not on PyPI. It runs on the same middleware as Impress (radical.asyncflow over rhapsody) but does not depend on the impress package.

Install it from agent/:

cd agent
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pip install -e ".[dragon]"   # only where campaigns run on Dragon, e.g. NCSA Delta

agent/scripts/dev_setup.sh does this in a dedicated .venv with the extras its tests need. Check the install with impress-a tools, which lists the registered toolkit.

The two packages are not installed into one merged environment: Impress targets Python >= 3.9 with radical.pilot, IMPRESS-A >= 3.11 with langgraph, rhapsody and biopython.

docs.title: Step 3: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Check that Impress is installed and importable:

python -c "from impress import ImpressManager; print('Impress is installed!')"

You should see:

Impress is installed!

docs.title: Step 4: Run a Sample Pipeline
docs.text: Now you're ready to write and run your own pipelines! Continue with Build A Protein Pipeline for a step-by-step tutorial.

docs.title: Deactivate Environment
docs.text:
When you're done, you can deactivate your virtual environment:

deactivate

Next time you want to work with Impress, just activate the environment again.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Explore the API Reference
  • Read Architecture to understand the core framework
  • Build your own workflows with Build A Protein Pipeline
  • See IMPRESS-A for autonomous campaigns that compose a workflow per cycle

docs.title: Build Asynchronous Protein Pipelines
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you step-by-step through writing and running an asynchronous workflow of multiple protein pipelines using IMPRESS manager.

By the end, you will have a working script that runs N pipelines concurrently, each of which executes 3 tasks asynchronously.

Want to run something first?

The task commands on this page are placeholders for your own tools, so the script below will not execute as written. For a version that runs end to end in a browser tab — real manager, real backend, real adaptive spawning, simulated science — see Run It In Colab.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
We’ll build:

  • A custom pipeline class, ProteinPipeline, which represents one protein analysis pipeline.
  • A script to start all pipelines asynchronously.

You can adapt the number of pipelines (N) and tasks as needed.

docs.title: Step 1: Import the Required Libraries
docs.text:
First, we import the libraries we need:

import asyncio

from impress import PipelineSetup
from impress import ImpressBasePipeline
from impress import ImpressManager

from radical.asyncflow import WorkflowEngine
from rhapsody.backends import RadicalExecutionBackend

We use:

  • asyncio — Python's built-in asynchronous library.
  • WorkflowEngine — the radical.asyncflow engine that submits tasks to an execution backend.
  • RadicalExecutionBackend — an execution backend (from rhapsody) that runs tasks in parallel through RADICAL-Pilot.
  • ImpressBasePipeline — base class for defining a pipeline.
  • ImpressManager — manages and executes multiple pipelines.
  • PipelineSetup — describes one pipeline to submit.

Note

rhapsody is installed separately (pip install rhapsody-py). To try this tutorial without it, use LocalExecutionBackend from radical.asyncflow instead:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from radical.asyncflow import LocalExecutionBackend

async def run_pipelines():
    backend = await LocalExecutionBackend(ThreadPoolExecutor())
    ...

docs.title: Step 2: Define a Custom Pipeline
docs.text:
We now define our custom ProteinPipeline. This simulates a simple workflow operating on dummy protein sequences.

class ProteinPipeline(ImpressBasePipeline):
    def __init__(self, name, flow, **kwargs):
        # Simulated sequence data and scores
        self.iter_seqs = {f"protein_{i}": f"sequence_{i}" for i in range(1, 4)}
        self.current_scores = {f"protein_{i}": i * 10 for i in range(1, 4)}
        self.previous_scores = {f"protein_{i}": i * 10 for i in range(1, 4)}

        super().__init__(name, flow, **kwargs)

Here we:

  • Initialize some dummy sequences and scores.
  • Call the parent constructor to properly set up the pipeline. The constructor calls register_pipeline_tasks(), so any attributes your tasks need should be set before super().__init__().
  • Pass **kwargs through. The manager calls the constructor with the keys of a setup's config dict as keyword arguments, so a pipeline that takes settings declares them as keyword parameters.

docs.title: 2.2 Register Tasks
docs.text:
def register_pipeline_tasks(self):
        @self.auto_register_task()
        async def s1(*args, **kwargs):
            return "python3 run_homology_search.py"

        @self.auto_register_task()
        async def s2(*args, **kwargs):
            return "python3 annotate_domains.py"

        @self.auto_register_task()
        async def s3(*args, **kwargs):
            return "python3 predict_structure.py"

Here we define 3 tasks. Each one is registered on the pipeline by auto_register_task() and becomes callable as self.s1(), self.s2(), self.s3(). A task returns the shell command to execute; the commands above are placeholders for your own tools.

Stdout and stderr are captured to files by default. On rhapsody's backends, await self.s1() therefore returns the path of the stdout file, not the text; register with @self.auto_register_task(capture_stdio=False) to get the text instead. See Architecture.

docs.title: 2.3 Run the Pipeline
docs.text:
async def run(self):  # The tasks will execute sequentially
        s1_res = await self.s1()
        s2_res = await self.s2()
        s3_res = await self.s3()

run() controls the execution order: run s1, then s2, then s3.

register_pipeline_tasks() and run() are the only methods a pipeline must implement. finalize() is optional and is a no-op by default.

Tip

You can change the execution order of your tasks by passing the handle of each task (without await) to the task that depends on it. For example, to make s3 wait for both s1 and s2, which run in parallel:

async def run(self):  # s1/s2 start in parallel; s3 waits for both
    s1_fut = self.s1()
    s2_fut = self.s2()
    s3_res = await self.s3(s1_fut, s2_fut)

docs.title: Step 3: Create and Run Multiple Pipelines
docs.text:
We now create a function that starts N pipelines at once.

async def run_pipelines():
    backend = await RadicalExecutionBackend({'resource': 'local.localhost'})
    flow = await WorkflowEngine.create(backend=backend)
    manager = ImpressManager(flow)

    # start 3 pipelines in parallel and wait for them to finish
    try:
        await manager.start(
            pipeline_setups = [
                PipelineSetup(name='p1', type=ProteinPipeline),
                PipelineSetup(name='p2', type=ProteinPipeline),
                PipelineSetup(name='p3', type=ProteinPipeline)]
        )
    finally:
        await flow.shutdown()

Here:

  • We create an execution backend, build a WorkflowEngine on it, and pass the engine to ImpressManager.
  • We call start() with a list of pipeline setups, each with a unique name (p1, p2, p3) and our ProteinPipeline class. start() returns once every pipeline (and any adaptive work it triggered) has finished.
  • The caller owns the engine: ImpressManager never creates or shuts down the flow, so we shut it down ourselves in a finally block.

You can add more pipelines by adding more entries to the list.

To make a pipeline adaptive, pass adaptive_fn= to PipelineSetup. It must be an engine task declared on a thread-pool backend, e.g. @flow.function_task(backend="local"), not a bare function; see Adaptive Execution and examples/dummy_adaptive.py.

docs.title: Step 4: Run the Script
docs.text:
Finally, add the entry point to run everything with asyncio:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(run_pipelines())

This starts the event loop and runs all the pipelines concurrently.

docs.title: Full Code
docs.text:
Here is the complete script for convenience:

import asyncio

from impress import PipelineSetup
from impress import ImpressBasePipeline
from impress import ImpressManager

from radical.asyncflow import WorkflowEngine
from rhapsody.backends import RadicalExecutionBackend


class ProteinPipeline(ImpressBasePipeline):
    def __init__(self, name, flow, **kwargs):
        self.iter_seqs = {f"protein_{i}": f"sequence_{i}" for i in range(1, 4)}
        self.current_scores = {f"protein_{i}": i * 10 for i in range(1, 4)}
        self.previous_scores = {f"protein_{i}": i * 10 for i in range(1, 4)}

        super().__init__(name, flow, **kwargs)

    def register_pipeline_tasks(self):
        @self.auto_register_task()
        async def s1(*args, **kwargs):
            return "python3 run_homology_search.py"

        @self.auto_register_task()
        async def s2(*args, **kwargs):
            return "python3 annotate_domains.py"

        @self.auto_register_task()
        async def s3(*args, **kwargs):
            return "python3 predict_structure.py"

    async def run(self):
        s1_res = await self.s1()
        s2_res = await self.s2()
        s3_res = await self.s3()

async def run_pipelines():
    backend = await RadicalExecutionBackend({'resource': 'local.localhost'})
    flow = await WorkflowEngine.create(backend=backend)
    manager = ImpressManager(flow)

    try:
        await manager.start(
            pipeline_setups = [
                PipelineSetup(name='p1', type=ProteinPipeline),
                PipelineSetup(name='p2', type=ProteinPipeline),
                PipelineSetup(name='p3', type=ProteinPipeline)]
        )
    finally:
        await flow.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(run_pipelines())

Each pipeline runs its three tasks in order, and all pipelines run concurrently.

docs.title: IMPRESS-A
docs.text:
Autonomous protein design on HPC.

IMPRESS-A conducts scientific exploration of protein design space given a design prompt — "stabilize the given protein" — by repeatedly deciding what experiment to run next, composing a workflow to run it, executing that workflow on HPC, interpreting the result, and updating a population of design candidates.

Run it before you read it

Ten minutes with a mock campaign runs that loop in a browser tab against a laptop surrogate of the small-molecule binding chain — same executor, same gates, same thresholds, no allocation. It walks the four knob arms, then asks you to predict what a campaign will do before you break it.

docs.title: What autonomous means here
docs.text:
Workflow parameters and topology are modified at runtime in response to production data. The agent is not a pipeline with a smart scheduler: it composes a new workflow each cycle from a registry of tools.

That is the distinction from Adaptive Execution, which is IMPRESS's own protocol for a pipeline spawning child pipelines from a decision function you write. There, the shape of the work is fixed and the branching is parameterised. Here, the shape itself is the output of a reasoner, and nothing in the graph is written down ahead of time.

docs.title: One experiment, one variable step
docs.text:
observe ─→ SPECIFY ─→ PLAN ─→ compose ─→ validate ─→ execute ─→ analyze ─→ update ─→ terminate?
          (reasoner halves)   (typed    (5 gates    (one       (QC       (tree,
                               DAG)      + dry-run)  engine)    gates)    Pareto,
                                  │                                       provenance)
                                  └── reject ──→ back to PLAN (bounded retry)

Those steps happen in that order for any one experiment, but the reasoner is not the loop body, so several experiments sit at different steps at once. The executor owns all campaign state and is its only writer.

docs.title: Relationship to IMPRESS
docs.text:
IMPRESS-A is a separate package: impress_a, Python >= 3.11, living in this repository under agent/. It is not on PyPI and is not installed by pip install . at the repository root — see Installation.

It runs on the same middleware as IMPRESS — one radical.asyncflow engine over rhapsody backends, reaching Dragon only through them — but not on the impress package: each Stage is an asyncflow block, and each tool command an engine task placed per backend. One engine per campaign carries named routes — compute for tool commands, local for adapters and QC, and ai when the campaign serves its own reasoner — which is recorded in decision 0015 along with where the control and execution processes divide. The two projects also share science: Small Molecule Binding runs the same rfd3 → LigandMPNN → Rosetta → Boltz chain as a fixed adaptive pipeline, where IMPRESS-A composes it per cycle.

Neither package depends on the other. The two are never installed into one environment as a merged dependency set: IMPRESS targets Python >= 3.9 with radical.pilot, and IMPRESS-A >= 3.11 with langgraph, rhapsody and biopython.

docs.title: This section
docs.text: Architecture The loop, layers, import contract, invariants Resolution How the toolkit, goal, budget and parameters become specified targets and a programmed Stage — step by step, with what refuses each one Observation How a running campaign's state becomes a CampaignObservation, who is shown it, what survives to disk, and how any of it reaches a caller Invocation How a tool spec becomes a command running on a compute node: the adapter, the argv each shipped tool runs, how it is placed, and what is recorded Pluggable Frontends The two frontend axes: which seams are swappable, the protocols they implement, and how to write one Control Models The four reasoners: what each is shown, what it may choose, how its reply is constrained Compute Patterns P1–P8 — normative for every ToolSpec Authoring Tools Writing a tool: the spec, the adapter and its command builder, gates and skill documents Middleware Integration asyncflow / rhapsody seam and its gotchas AuCaM Integration Running as one subordinate workflow under an enclosing campaign manager: the seam, the offer handshake, and the pin The Mock Knob Lab The laptop knob lab and the reasoner axis: what it runs and what its numbers license Known Limitations Known gaps and residual risks, stated plainly Decisions Numbered, immutable architecture decision records Roadmap Standing notes on task-agent training

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text: Stated plainly rather than discovered later.

docs.title: Scientific scope
docs.text:
The loop closes in silico. Nothing in the current toolkit consumes experimental data, so the Pareto front ranks predicted quantities. A campaign's output is a prioritized hypothesis set, not validated designs, and results should be reported that way.

The architecture anticipates this changing: Property carries a source and authority so a measurement supersedes a prediction for the same objective without any change to a campaign specification, and ingest_measurement accepts assay results even after a campaign terminates (decision 0012). What is not built is the other half — nothing selects which designs to send for assay or manages samples.

Some problem classes need a human-supplied hypothesis. Where a design protocol depends on expert mechanistic judgement (catalytic geometry being the clearest case), the agent can vary parameters and run QC around a supplied hypothesis but cannot author it. Autonomy is narrower there, and a campaign should say so.

docs.title: Residual risk in free composition
docs.text:
The validation regime prevents type-incoherent workflows, missing QC gates, frozen-parameter tampering, resource-infeasible and platform-impossible graphs, budget overruns, and every catalogued silent failure. It does not prevent a novel silent failure — one of a kind no ToolSpec anticipated, in a tool combination no human reviewed. Cross-tool consistency and distributional checks are the general defences, and they are statistical, not sound.

The self-promoting interlock buys examination and delay, not soundness: a consistent novel silent failure — one that passes every gate, agrees with a correlated tool, and looks distributionally ordinary on all N runs — will promote. Two consequences: raise the promotion threshold for patterns feeding irreversible or expensive commitments, and weight cross-tool agreement conservatively, since tools sharing training data or architecture may agree because they share a bias.

Since decision 0013, the interlock counts only integrity gates, which ask whether the tool ran and reported real numbers. It ignores acceptance gates, the quality thresholds. That made promotion reachable on a hard target, and it narrowed what trust rests on. For the real toolkits the integrity gates are thin: presence checks, has_secondary_structure, and the Rosetta divergence bounds. There is nothing structural (backlog B1). A tool that emits well-formed, plausibly-scored garbage could already promote; one that emits well-formed, low-scored garbage now can too, as long as it reports its numbers. Acceptance failures still keep such a node off the front.

docs.title: Reproducibility, by layer
docs.text:
Layer Reproducible? Core, composition, validation Bit-exact Model D policies Bit-exact, seeded Tool execution Approximately — pinned versions and checkpoint hashes; GPU non-determinism remains Model A / B policies No — frontier APIs offer no usable seed, and temperature 0 does not guarantee determinism A campaign as a whole Reconstructable, not replayable

An LLM-steered campaign can be audited and reconstructed from provenance; it cannot be re-run to the same answer. Model D exists partly so there is a fully reproducible baseline to compare against.

docs.title: Cost estimates are unmeasured
docs.text:
Validation gate 5 refuses graphs against cost_model figures drawn from literature and documentation, not measurements on the target platforms. Early campaigns should record actual-versus-estimated cost per tool and recalibrate; until then the gate should carry a safety margin rather than be treated as precise.

Two real numbers now exist, and the second one was a latent bug rather than a mis-estimate. rfd3_design cost 0.25 GPU-h against a 0.5 estimate (job 22669509). ligandmpnn_design had walltime_s: 300 - and that same job shows its task spending 276s reaching a ModuleNotFoundError in module-level imports, before allocating a tensor. Roughly 280s of every invocation is import torch paging off a Lustre mount, so the tool could not have finished importing inside its own timeout, and would have failed as timed out after 300s: a message that reads like a hang and blames the tool rather than the budget. Now 1800s, with the measurement recorded in the spec.

The general point is about where these numbers hide rather than about this tool. A walltime_s that is too small does not announce itself as a mis-estimate; it announces itself as a timeout, which is the same shape as a hang. On shared HPC the import cost can dominate a short task entirely, and it is invisible to every local test because no local test pays it. The other four real tools' figures are still literature guesses, and the first thing each one's real run will produce is the true number.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text:
Still the open risk, but now measured. Backtracking works by branching the tree, which avoids needing to cancel in-flight work. The spike has since been done against the installed asyncflow, and the answer is: cancellation exists and is advisory only.

ConcurrentExecutionBackend.cancel_task calls Future.cancel(), which returns False once a callable has started — so queued work is reclaimed and running work is not — and asyncflow's own cancel hook discards that boolean, so a caller never learns which happened. StageExecutor.cancel and the control plane's cancel_run therefore say so in their return value, and a run's terminal state always comes from collecting it, never from the fact that cancel was called.

What this leaves unsolved: reclaiming a GPU from a long-running task that should have been abandoned. That needs cooperative cancellation inside the task agents, or a backend that can kill a process.

Measured again on asyncflow/rhapsody 0.7.0 (2026-11-11). Every tool command is now its own executable task on the engine (exec/launch.py), and asyncflow 0.7.0 sends a cancel to the backend the task was routed to. On the concurrent backend that still does not stop a running command: cancel_task cancels the backend's own coroutine and leaves the child process running (reproduced with a sleep that outlived its cancelled task). That is an upstream gap in rhapsody, not something to work around here.

What holds in place of a cancel is the walltime, but it is enforced by two different mechanisms and the difference matters. On the concurrent backend each command is wrapped in coreutils timeout --kill-after, so it cannot outlive resources.walltime_s by more than the grace period. Under Dragon there is no wrapper - the task itself carries walltime_s + KILL_GRACE_S and Dragon enforces it (exec/launch.py:195, exec/resources.py:139). The wrapper was removed there because it hung a job outright; see the next section. Dragon's own timeout has not yet fired on hardware, so that half is bounded by design and unexercised in practice.

docs.title: A timeout wrapper under Dragon hangs the task it was meant to bound
docs.text:
Job 23814643 submitted two lineages of the smoke, and both stage-1 commands ran to completion on their GPUs - and then nothing finished. The rfd3 processes exited; their timeout parents stayed as [timeout] <defunct>, and the tasks never reached a terminal state until the job was cancelled 22 minutes in.

Coreutils timeout puts itself in a new process group (setpgid) so it can signal its whole child tree. Dragon's local services reaps with os.waitpid(0, WNOHANG) (dragon/localservices/server.py:2604), which collects only children in its own process group. A timeout wrapper therefore becomes a zombie Dragon will never reap, and the task that owns it never completes. The wrapper is applied on the concurrent backend only (exec/launch.py:195), and Dragon is given the bound as the task's own timeout instead. Written up for upstream in the repository at plans/upstream/dragon-unreaped-process-group-leader.md.

The general shape is the one this page keeps repeating: a mechanism that is correct in isolation becomes a hang when it crosses a boundary that owns process lifetime.

docs.title: Not yet implemented
docs.text:
