The MCP control-plane adapter, checkpoint/restart resume (the job ledger now records run state and outcomes, and RunService.reattach reconciles what a previous process left open — but nothing resumes a campaign from it yet), and the P5 network-service governor (caching, per-service concurrency caps, Retry-After backoff).

P6 inlining does not exist, and a P6 declaration is now a load-time error rather than a tool that quietly never runs (tools/spec.py). The composer used to drop P6 tools from every graph with nothing scheduling them in their place, which is the worse of the two failures: a declared stage that vanishes without a word. Inlining is still the intended design; refusal is what holds until it is built.

Engine telemetry is opt-in, per campaign, through CampaignSpec.telemetry_checkpoint_s (0 disables, the default). It needs the [telemetry] extra, and asyncflow's start_telemetry cannot be asked to drain on stop, so a stalled drain is cut short by our own timeout.

A locally hosted reasoner has never run on hardware. CampaignSession.infer and the rhapsody_vllm profile kind are built and tested against a stand-in backend, but the local-dragon profile in models.yaml still names no model, and two questions are open: whether Dragon Inference takes the first num_gpus devices (which StageExecutor.gpu_offset assumes when it keeps tools off them), and whether a model's start-up fits inside backend_startup_timeout_s, which it now shares with the compute backend.

A spec that sets runner: is rejected. It selected between two execution loops; there is one now, and the CLI refuses the key with a pointer rather than ignoring it.

docs.title: The Dragon backend can hang silently during construction
docs.text:
rhapsody's Dragon execution backend builds Batch() (the results DDict, a GPU-affinity worker pool, telemetry) synchronously inside its own constructor, with no await points. A stall there blocks the event loop entirely: not the campaign's own heartbeat, not the process, nothing gets a chance to run until Batch() returns - so a genuinely hung construction is indistinguishable from a process still starting up, right up until whatever wall-clock limit kills the job. This is exactly what happened to job 22318678: the process ran for its full 2-hour SLURM allocation and was killed on the time limit having produced only Dragon's own internal infra-connect log lines - no campaign log, no ledger entry, no heartbeat, nothing else, the entire time.

Bounded now by CampaignSpec.backend_startup_timeout_s (0 = disabled, the default - every existing campaign is unaffected) and backend_startup_heartbeat_s: the backend's synchronous construction runs on a dedicated daemon thread so the calling event loop stays free to heartbeat-log and enforce the timeout, and a stall past the bound raises BackendConstructionTimeout with a clear diagnostic instead of silently consuming the rest of the allocation. Both Delta campaign YAMLs set a 600s bound.

The bound is not purely protective, and getting it wrong costs whole allocations. Only the synchronous construction may be offloaded. A WorkflowEngine captures the running loop in __init__ and puts its run-component dispatch task on it, and a rhapsody backend captures its own loop during async init - so both must be built on the loop that will submit to them. The first version of this bound ran all of make_engine on the daemon thread under asyncio.run(...); that call's exit cancelled run-component and closed the loop, and the caller received an engine that looked healthy and dispatched nothing. Jobs 22328172 and 22328262 - the only two campaigns that had backend_startup_timeout_s > 0 - each logged r0001 submitted and then sat silent for their full walltime. Fixed in exec/backend.py; tests/test_backend_bound.py now runs a real task through a bounded engine, because a dead engine is indistinguishable from a live one until you do.

What this does not solve: why a real construction might stall inside Dragon's own Batch()/Pool() (most likely GPU-affinity worker rendezvous or OFI/libfabric negotiation) is still unknown - see backlog A5.

docs.title: ...and during teardown
docs.text:
The mirror image, and the more expensive one, because by then the campaign has already produced everything it was asked for. Measured on the reference IMPRESS pipeline (job 22491438): flow.shutdown() never returned after all sixteen of its pipelines had finished. The job sat 60 minutes and had to be cancelled by hand - roughly 64 GPU-hours, 37% of its billed total, spent after the science was done. That project's own conclusion was to treat it as reproducible until shown otherwise.

Bounded by CampaignSpec.backend_shutdown_timeout_s (0 disables, as with startup; 300s in both Delta campaigns). On expiry the teardown is abandoned with a warning rather than raised: every result is already durable in provenance and the ledger by that point, so the worst case is leaked backend state in a process that is about to exit - whereas raising would turn a campaign that succeeded into one that reports failure.

Note this is a place where we deliberately diverge from the reference pipeline, which declined the in-code bound and relies on an operator watching the log and issuing scancel. The SLURM wall clock remains our second line of defence, which is part of why scripts/delta_gpu_run.sh asks for 12 hours rather than the partition maximum.

docs.title: ...and when a task's exception cannot be unpickled
docs.text: Dragon hands a worker's exception back by pickling it into a DDict. If it cannot be unpickled, rhapsody's monitor loop logs Critical error in monitor loop and drops every completion in that sweep. No FAILED arrives, and the run sits in flight until the SLURM wall clock kills it (job 22536706, on a LigandMPNN failure). Our own SubprocessError is now pickle-safe. Any other exception with a required-argument __init__ that does not forward those arguments to super() still triggers it, and nothing bounds a single run's wall-clock time. If a campaign log shows that error followed by a heartbeat whose inflight never drops, scancel it. See backlog G6.

docs.title: Dragon removes the root logger's handlers
docs.text:
dragon.native.Pool.__init__ and ProcessGroup.__init__ call setup_BE_logging, which begins with _clear_root_log_handlers() - every handler on the root logger is closed and removed, and handlers are re-added only where DRAGON_LOG_DEVICE_{STDERR,DRAGON_FILE,ACTOR_FILE} asks for them. rhapsody builds Batch() inside the Dragon backend constructor, so on the Delta path this happens during engine bring-up and everything logged afterwards is discarded. This is the second reason jobs 22328172/22328262 produced no diagnostics: even once the hang is fixed, a batch run configured only through logging.basicConfig goes mute the moment the backend comes up.

scripts/delta_run_campaign.py now keeps its handlers (stderr plus a campaign.log transcript in the job working directory) on the impress_a/rhapsody/radical/dragon loggers with propagate = False, out of root's reach, and logs a one-off WARNING naming setup_BE_logging when it notices root has been emptied. Anything that logs to the root logger directly is still lost.

docs.title: Storage was the bottleneck, and it masqueraded as three other bugs
docs.text:
Every path this project reads at runtime used to hang off $SCRATCH, which on Delta resolves under HDD-backed /work/hdd. Measured there: import pyrosetta 471s (a 598 MB rosetta.so, demand-paged), pyrosetta.init 4.5s, get_fa_scorefxn 58.2s - 533.8s before any work, against a packmin budget of 300s. import torch cost ~280s of LigandMPNN's 292.6s.

What makes this worth a section is not the slowness but the disguise. It arrived as a task timeout, which reads as a hung tool; it was about to be "fixed" by raising three walltimes to 1800/3600/1200 with the 533.8s figure written into each spec as justification. Moving $WORK_DIR to /work/nvme (ported from the reference pipeline's PR #67) instead produced, on job 22684607: ligandmpnn_design 292.6s → 18.1s, and packmin - which could not finish importing in 300s - completing in 15.9s, with fastrelax 25.9s and filter_shape 10.2s. The existing walltimes were never wrong. Had the raises shipped, the real cost would have stayed hidden behind timeouts six times larger than necessary.

Two general points. A timeout names a budget, not a cause - which is why run_cmd now preserves whatever a killed process already wrote, and why the Rosetta workers emit phase timings to stderr. And an estimate that feeds a refusal gate is not harmless when it is too high: the cost models were 6-69x over, the gpu side summed past the untrusted-pattern cap, and the budget correction that followed silently truncated boltz_predict - the only producer of two of the campaign's four objectives - off the end of the chain.

docs.title: What has run on real hardware — and what that does and does not establish
docs.text:
Four campaigns have now executed the real six-tool chain on Delta. Job 22692304 ran it end to end (6/6 tasks ok, 2m53s), admitted on the first attempt, every stage passing its gates, terminating with a one-node Pareto front; all four campaign objectives carry real values (total_score -272.0, shape_complementarity 0.591, complex_plddt 0.507, ligand_iptm 0.752), and per-tool cost is measured for all six. Job 22726105 promoted the six-stage pattern after r0002; job 22728140 then ran three consecutive trusted cycles with no demotion. Job 23815248 ran two lineages on the one-engine execution loop: 12/12 tasks ok in 3m45s, lineage 0 pinned to GPU 0 and lineage 1 to GPU 1 by Dragon's placement policy, with GPUs 2 and 3 idle throughout, and a single telemetry block span per Stage carrying every command under it.

They establish that the machinery runs. They do not establish that the science is good, and the sample is still small enough to name exactly:

  • Two lineages, not four. replicas: 2 has executed and the two lineages produced different metrics, so replicas: N really does yield N independent DesignNodes. The declared width of 4 has never completed a campaign, and the budget/signature half of that invariant is untouched.
  • Cycles have run, backtracking has not. Job 22728140 acted on observations across three trusted cycles; backtracking has still never been exercised against real results.
  • Nothing trusted, and for a while nothing could be. The ledger resolved against a relative path inside each job's working directory, so every SLURM job started with an empty one and promotion - three consecutive clean runs in one file - was unreachable on Delta from the first run onward. Fixed; the path is now site-scoped and logged absolutely at campaign start. The trusted code path (no forced dry-run, no 10% cost cap) has now executed and held - three consecutive trusted cycles in job 22728140 - but no real node has reached plain pass: untrusted nodes are always suspect, and all five trusted ones missed an acceptance threshold.
  • No measurement has superseded a prediction. ingest_measurement and the whole predicted-vs-measured calibration story still have no real assay data behind them.
  • Two execution paths are built but unexercised on Dragon. A block cancel reaching a command that is already running, and Dragon's own task timeout firing. Both ran only against the concurrent backend, where the failure modes are different ones.
  • The QC thresholds have one or two observations each. complex_plddt cleared its 0.5 bound by 0.007. filter_shape returned 0.524 against 0.55 on the run before and 0.591 here. Whether these numbers sit in the right place is unknown, and packmin's turned out to be upstream's fastrelax threshold copied onto the wrong stage - it failed +145.3 and +14.8, both healthy.

Cost figures are single samples and should not be tightened. rfd3_design took 145.7s in job 22684607 and 45.0s in 22692304 - same campaign, same allocation shape, same parameters, 3.2x apart. The declared cost_model values deliberately sit 3-5x above measurement because they feed gate 5 and the untrusted-pattern cap, both of which refuse graphs; tuning them to a fast observation is how a campaign starts being rejected for no real reason.

docs.title: Getting here cost four defects, none of which a dry run could have found
docs.text:
The first stage to execute paid for itself immediately. Its real out_dir showed that RFD3DesignAgent's *.cif.gz glob was selecting a diffusion trajectory rather than the design - trajectories carry the same extension and denoised sorts first - so the backbone passed downstream was a multi-frame stack. Discovery now goes through the sidecar *_model_*.json. That turned out to be the expected yield of executing each remaining stage rather than a one-off.

Job 22669509 made the point again and sharpened it. Handed the correct 53 KB backbone, LigandMPNN still failed - in run.py's module-level imports, before parsing an argument: first a missing ml_collections, then np.int, which numpy removed in 1.24. Neither had anything to do with the trajectory bug, which had merely been the plausible-looking explanation for the earlier failure; the two defects were independent. Both are environmental rather than logical - LigandMPNN vendors a copy of openfold written against pre-1.20 numpy, and this venv carries 2.x because Boltz requires it - and the adapter now runs run.py through a shim restoring those aliases, as the reference pipeline always did. The recurring lesson: an adapter checked against a binary's contract is not an adapter that has been run, and what breaks first is usually the environment, not the arguments.

What makes this class expensive is where it was found. A missing module and a removed numpy alias are both knowable on a login node in seconds; both were instead discovered inside a GPU allocation, after a queue wait. impress-a preflight now runs LigandMPNN's real import chain through the same shim the adapter uses - but only for someone who runs it, since no launcher invokes preflight. In the same pass, preflight gained an undetermined state: a probe that times out now reports warn rather than FAIL, because a check that could not be run to a conclusion is not a check that failed, and two meaningless FAILs teach a reader to ignore the column that matters.

A verification pass against the actual installed toolkits on Delta (not just old scripts) found and fixed real contract bugs rather than merely confirming guesses: rfd3_design was invoking rfd3 with flags (--config/--out) that do not exist on the real Hydra-based CLI at all and would have failed immediately - rewritten to the real out_dir=/inputs=/diffusion_batch_size=/ inference_sampler.num_timesteps=/seed= contract. boltz_predict was missing the required --no_kernels flag (a verified CUDA ABI mismatch between the pinned torch and cuequivariance-ops-cu12 versions, not an optional flag). ligandmpnn_design had no way to express a fixed-residue constraint. None of the three Rosetta toolkits (packmin, fastrelax, filter_shape) had a way to pass a ligand .params file, so a real ligand-bearing PDB would likely raise in pose_from_pdb() rather than silently mis-score. All four are now fixed (see each toolkit's SKILL.md); LigandMPNN's own seed/batch flags were checked and confirmed correct as originally written. impress-a preflight still runs cleanly for the ALR benchmark target on a Delta login node. Each of these was a checked contract before it was an executed one, and the executions above are what turned the list from plausible into verified.

Related: the QC gates the real toolkits declare lean almost entirely on metric_in_range against a tool's own self-reported confidence — which is exactly what a confidently-wrong tool passes. Since decision 0013 those are acceptance gates, so trust rests on the integrity gates alone, and there are still no structural ones (is the ligand actually in the output complex, are there chain breaks, does the sequence length match the contig). Known-bad fixtures now exist for every real tool under toolkits/<toolkit>/tools/<id>/tests/, and tests/test_gate_fixtures.py checks each one against the gates it is supposed to fail.

docs.title: Decision Records
docs.text:
Numbered, immutable records of decisions whose rationale should outlive the conversation that produced them.

Named decisions/, not adr/, because radical.adr is a middleware component this project uses and "ADR" would be permanently ambiguous here.

# Decision Phase 0001 IMPRESS is a callable tool, not the control plane 1B 0002 Control model C is control mode 2 1B 0003 Free graph composition, governed by a self-promoting interlock 1B 0004 Population with a Pareto front and backtracking 1B 0005 The active control model is fixed at launch 1B 0006 Task agents are hybrid, declared per tool 1B 0007 One transport-agnostic control plane, with adapters 1B 0008 Polaris/ACCESS primary, Aurora second, Frontier deprioritized 1 0009 Package naming: impress_a 1C 0010 One package, with a CI-enforced import contract 1C 0011 toolkits/ is top-level and declarative 1C 0012 One property, two sources; forward-declare pattern P8 1 0013 Trust counts integrity gates, not acceptance gates (amends 0003) — 0014 An enclosing campaign manager is a caller, not a control model — 0015 One engine, two processes, and where each boundary falls —

docs.title: 0001 — IMPRESS is a callable tool, not the control plane
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1B

docs.title: Context
docs.text: IMPRESS is an async adaptive-pipeline framework already wired to radical.asyncflow.WorkflowEngine and rhapsody.backends.*, with a working per-pipeline adaptive_fn hook and even an LLM-oracle precedent in examples/protein_binding/protein_binding_run.py. It was therefore a plausible candidate to serve as this project's orchestrator.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: IMPRESS is a coarse-grained composite tool (pattern P7). We build our own campaign manager directly on radical.asyncflow. ImpressManager and adaptive_fn are prior art to learn from, not infrastructure to inherit.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The agent owns the WorkflowEngine and the outer loop.
  • IMPRESS pipelines are registered like any other tool; nothing in the registry knows they are special.
  • The Python floor conflict (IMPRESS ≥3.9, foundry ≥3.12) dissolves at the process boundary — see 0010.
  • The oracle precedent informs control model B's requirements rather than supplying its implementation.

docs.title: 0002 — Control model C is control mode 2
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1B

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The specification named two control modes (autonomous, headless) and four control models (A: four-node loop, B: oracle, C: external caller steering, D: explicit policy). Whether these were orthogonal axes was ambiguous.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: They are not orthogonal. Model C is the headless mode. Autonomous mode runs A, B or D; headless mode is C.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Three autonomous policies and one headless mode, rather than eight combinations.
  • Model C's decide blocks on the control plane instead of computing.
  • An external caller is subject to the same validation as any policy — being external confers no privilege.
  • HITL is a special case of C: a caller with a person behind it.

docs.title: 0003 — Free graph composition, governed by a self-promoting interlock
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1B (revised in the Part C decision round)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: "Autonomous" was defined as workflow parameters modified at runtime. Three scopes were considered: parameters only, parameters plus bounded topology, and free graph composition. Free composition offers the most scientific reach and is the hardest to validate — and Part A found that silent failure, not crashing, is the dominant hazard across the entire toolkit.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Free graph composition, with a five-gate validation regime plus dry-run, and a self-promoting interlock as the standing operating posture.

The interlock was chosen over two alternatives. A temporary allowlist switched off once validation proves itself merely postpones the risk. Permanent per-pattern human sign-off eliminates it but caps the agent at reviewed patterns, forfeiting the reason free composition was chosen.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Composition patterns (tool ids plus typed edges, ignoring parameter values) are trusted or provisional.
  • Provisional patterns run under a cost cap, an extended mandatory dry-run, required cross-tool consistency, and are auto-marked suspect regardless of QC outcome.
  • Promotion after N consecutive clean runs; demotion on any failure. Per-pattern, per-site, in provenance.
  • The trust ledger is site-scoped and spans campaigns, since one campaign may not run a pattern three times.
  • Residual risk accepted: a consistent novel silent failure will promote. The interlock buys examination and delay, not soundness.

docs.title: 0004 — Campaign state is a population with a Pareto front and backtracking
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1B

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Alternatives were a single refined lineage (as in the IMPRESS precedent) or a population ranked by a scalarized score.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: A non-destructive tree of design lineages, ranked by a multi-objective Pareto front, with backtracking to any earlier node.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Objectives are declared with directions and hard constraints; constraints prune, directions rank.
  • Cost is a first-class objective, not an afterthought — Part A found a seven-order-of-magnitude spread.
  • QC verdict gates front eligibility: a node failing its gates never ranks, whatever its scores.
  • Append-only storage; backtracking never destroys the abandoned branch.
  • Adopts AgentRosetta's proven pattern; paretoset is a directly adoptable dependency.
  • The front is not monotonic once measurements arrive (see 0012).

docs.title: 0005 — The active control model is fixed at launch
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1B

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Runtime switching between control models would allow escalation (e.g. from an explicit policy to an oracle when the policy stalls).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The control model is named in the campaign specification and cannot change during the campaign.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A campaign has one stated methodology and a result is attributable to it.
  • Two declared-up-front mechanisms exist and are not exceptions: fallback_policy (a model-D policy activated only on oracle or caller unavailability, logged as a state transition) and RequestHuman (suspends the campaign; does not replace the policy).
  • Revisit if campaigns routinely exhaust one policy's usefulness partway through; fallback_policy already proves a controlled transition is implementable.

docs.title: 0006 — Task agents are hybrid, declared per tool
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1B

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Task agents own pre-processing, parameterization, execution and post-processing for a tool. They could be uniformly deterministic, uniformly LLM-driven, or chosen per tool.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Per tool, declared in ToolSpec.agent as deterministic or llm.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Cost and determinism stay predictable: most of the toolkit is deterministic.
  • LLM agents are reserved for tools whose parameterization is itself authorship — RosettaScripts protocol composition, ligand setup, unanticipated failure triage.
  • QC gates are deterministic in both cases. An LLM may author a protocol; it does not judge whether the result passed its clash check.
  • execute() is not overridable by tool adapters — pattern dispatch belongs to the execution layer.

docs.title: 0007 — One transport-agnostic control plane, with adapters
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1B

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Headless mode must serve pipelining-as-a-service, MCP-like exposure, and an in-process HITL agent. Part A surveyed 26 MCP entries and verified 2; every tool running real HPC computation was absent or wrapped only by unaudited third parties.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Define one core CampaignControlPlane protocol; MCP, HTTP+SSE and in-process are thin adapters over it. No adapter may add an operation absent from the core.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• observe() returns the same CampaignObservation a policy's decide receives — informed monitoring means parity of evidence, not a progress bar.
  • MCP exposure is necessarily submit-and-poll, a property of long-running compute rather than of MCP.
  • The project is not hostage to MCP protocol revisions.
  • Measurement ingestion later lands naturally on the same plane (0012).

docs.title: 0008 — Platform priority: Polaris/ACCESS primary, Aurora second, Frontier deprioritized
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1 decision round

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Part A targeted DOE leadership and NSF ACCESS machines, then found the portability picture inverted from expectation. A repo-wide grep of tools/foundry for hip/rocm/amd returned zero hits — no code path, no CI, no documentation — making Frontier a from-source porting spike rather than a rebuild. Aurora, by contrast, has real first-party Intel XPU support in foundry.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Polaris and NSF ACCESS (Delta, Bridges-2, Expanse) are primary. Aurora is second. Frontier is deprioritized and no HIP spike is scheduled.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• frontier stays in the site matrix with gpu.api: hip, so the compose-time portability gate refuses the ML core there rather than failing at runtime — the door stays visible and shut.
  • containers/frontier/ is not created.
  • If revisited: ProteinMPNN first (no cuEquivariance dependency), then RFD3 (cuEquivariance import already wrapped in try/except with a PyTorch fallback), RF3 last (hard CUDA-12 kernel dependency).
  • Part A's risk R1 is accepted and scoped out rather than mitigated.

docs.title: 0009 — Package naming: impress_a
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1C

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The working name impressa sat one character from impress, while impress-a-refcodes/tools/IMPRESS exists in the same workspace.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Role Name Human-facing project name IMPRESS-A Distribution impress-a Import package impress_a Environment variables IMPRESS_A_SHARED, IMPRESS_A_CAMPAIGNS, IMPRESS_A_TOOLKITS

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The underscore supplies the visual break impressa lacked. The hazard applied to human readers and more acutely to LLM agents working in this tree, where the two names are plausible completions of each other.
  • impress_a is the idiomatic Python spelling (PEP 8); uppercase is reserved for prose and env vars.

docs.title: 0010 — One repository, one package, with a CI-enforced import contract
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1C

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Part B's layers have different change rates and audiences. A multi-package workspace would isolate dependencies — but heavy scientific tools are invoked as subprocesses or containers, not imported, so that isolation already exists.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A single package impress_a, with layering enforced by an import-linter rule in CI rather than by directory convention.

Load-bearing rules: policy ↛ tools, policy ↛ exec, compose ↛ exec, core imports nothing internal.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• policy ↛ tools is what keeps control models interchangeable: a reasoner emits abstract intent and cannot reach for a tool adapter.

Amended 2026-11-08 (phase 11). That intent was ExperimentIntent, returned from decide(obs) -> Decision. Both are gone: a reasoner is now a Specifier emitting a SpecRevision and a Planner emitting a Stage of TaskMappings, and the Stage is what "abstract intent" names. The rule is unchanged and the reason is unchanged — a TaskMapping carries a tool id, declared parameters and typed port references, never an adapter, a command line or a resource shape.

ExperimentIntent itself survives, deliberately, as a composer input rather than as anything a reasoner returns. Composer.compose takes a chain and a replica width, which is what two non-policy callers need: impress-a trust --assert computes a pattern signature at a declared width (and the signature includes replica multiplicity, so the width is not optional), and impress-a validate-tasks runs a chain once to prove each Task on real hardware. Neither is a decision about a campaign, so neither needs a Planner — and inventing one for them would mean a validation pass whose result depended on which reasoner validated it. tests/test_layering.py::test_the_decision_union_is_gone_and_nothing_imports_it pins both halves of this: the union is gone, and that one type is not.

  • A new layer, analysis, with one rule of its own: it may not import policy or control. A scorer that could reach a reasoner could score a campaign by asking it, and the whole method of the four-arm comparison is that figures come from the executor's own provenance, the ledgers and the artifacts on disk — never from an arm's bookkeeping.
  • compose ↛ exec is what makes the laptop-runnable mock campaign possible.
  • The only in-process scientific dependencies are the P6 tools (RDKit, Biotite, AtomWorks, US-align, paretoset), which must be co-installable with radical.* on Python ≥3.12.[^0010-floor]

[^0010-floor]: Corrected 2026-11-11. Two things in that sentence are no longer true. The floor is >=3.11, set by radical.asyncflow and rhapsody-py 0.7.0 rather than by the science libraries. And there are no in-process P6 tools: P6 inlining was never built, so a P6 declaration is refused at load (tools/spec.py). The decision itself — one package, one import contract — is unaffected; see decision 0015. - Revisit if policies pull in both LangGraph and Academy, or if a site needs the execution layer without the policy layer. Splitting later is more disruptive than starting split.

docs.title: 0011 — toolkits/ is top-level and declarative
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1C

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Part A produced 52 tool entities. Their specifications are read by four consumers (composer, validator, budget guard, task agent) and edited mainly by scientists.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Tool specifications live in a top-level toolkits/ directory, discovered from a configurable path, as declarative spec.yaml plus behavioural agent.py per tool. Skill documents live in their toolkit directory beside the tools they describe.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Specs are reviewable in a pull request by someone who does not read Python, and diffable when a parameter range changes.
  • A site or third party can add a toolkit without forking the package.
  • Registration never requires editing the composer, validator or manager — the test of correct factoring.
  • Skill-doc drift becomes a CI failure: required sections are checked, and tools and docs must reference each other.
  • Cost: a non-trivial packaging story for non-package data.

docs.title: 0012 — One property, two sources; forward-declare pattern P8
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-21 · Status: accepted · Phase: 1 decision round

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Developability surrogates (solubility, expression, aggregation) were added to close a Part A coverage gap, with the requirement that they be designed so they can later be replaced or supplemented by tools querying experimental results from a robotic lab.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A predicted value and a measured value for the same quantity are the same Property type with different source, authority and confidence — not two unrelated quantities. Objectives are declared against the property name, never its source.

Pattern P8 (external experiment) is added to the taxonomy as a forward declaration: latency of days to weeks, out-of-band completion, routinely outliving the campaign. Nothing in the current roster is P8.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A campaign objective is satisfiable by a surrogate today and an assay tomorrow with no spec change.
  • Measurements supersede predictions for ranking; the prediction is retained, because a systematic surrogate-versus-assay gap is itself the calibration signal.
  • The Pareto front is not monotonic — a node promoted on an optimistic prediction can be demoted by its own assay.
  • ingest_measurement is added to the control plane; measurements are accepted even after campaign termination, which is why campaign storage is append-only on a shared filesystem.
  • Not a closed design–build–test–learn loop: nothing here selects designs for assay or manages samples.

docs.title: 0013 — Trust counts integrity, not acceptance
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-07 · Status: accepted · Amends: 0003's "clean run"

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
0003 promotes a composition pattern after N consecutive clean runs, and until now a clean run meant every QC gate passed. On Delta that made promotion unreachable for reasons unrelated to the pattern. Job 22702568 ran the six-stage chain five times, and all 30 tasks succeeded. The ledger nevertheless recorded failure, clean, failure, failure, clean, so nothing was promoted. Every one of those failures was a design-quality threshold: - Boltz pLDDT 0.486 and 0.426 against 0.5; - ipTM 0.327 against 0.4; - LigandMPNN confidence 0.355 against 0.4; - shape complementarity 0.519 against 0.55.

None was a tool breaking. Promotion had become a function of how hard the target is. At the observed ~43% all-gates rate, a 6-cycle campaign had a ~17% chance of ever admitting a trusted graph.

The interlock asks whether a novel composition behaves: whether its tools ran, produced output and reported numbers that mean what they say. Whether the resulting design is good is a separate question, answered by the QC verdict and the Pareto front.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Each QC gate declares a role in its tool spec: - integrity (the default): a FAIL means the tool or the pipeline broke. Examples are output_present, has_secondary_structure, metrics_reported, and the Rosetta divergence bounds. - acceptance: a FAIL means the tool worked and the design fell short. These are the quality thresholds on self-reported confidence and on shape complementarity.

Only integrity failures are evidence against a pattern. A run is clean when no task failed and no integrity gate failed (runtime/executor._record_evidence). Acceptance gates still FAIL the node, and a FAIL node is still never eligible for the front; that invariant is untouched.

Classifying the gates surfaced a hazard. Two known-bad fixtures were caught only by thresholds that would have become acceptance gates, and both recorded a run breaking, not a weak design: - Boltz run with no ligand chain, where the adapter fell back to iptm and then to 0.0; - an unparsed LigandMPNN header, where the adapter reported 0.0/0.0.

In both cases the adapter fabricated a number for a value it never read. So: - adapters omit a value they cannot read, and never report 0.0 in its place; - a new integrity gate, metrics_reported, fails when a named metric is absent or non-finite; - ToolSpec validation refuses an acceptance metric_in_range whose metric no integrity metrics_reported gate names, so the presence check cannot be forgotten; - every .bad.json fixture must fail an integrity gate unless it declares acceptance_only: true.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Promotion is reachable on hard targets. Replaying 22702568's recorded per-task metrics through the new rule promotes at its third run (tests/test_validation.py).
  • Trust now rests on the integrity gates, and they are thin (backlog B1: no structural gates). A tool emitting well-formed, confidently-scored garbage could already promote under 0003. Now one emitting well-formed, low-scored garbage can too, as long as it reports its numbers.
  • The policies' own notion of a good run (ExecutionResults.all_gates_passed, used by policy/explicit.py and policy/agentic.py) still counts every gate. Search quality and pattern trust are different questions, and each uses its own answer.
  • Provenance records each node's failed_gates, with their roles, and each admission's scrutiny. A run that resets trust now says why.

docs.title: 0014 — An enclosing campaign manager is a caller, not a control model
docs.text: Date: 2026-11-10 · Status: accepted · Relates to: 0001, 0002, 0007

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
IMPRESS-A is meant to be invoked by an agentic caller, and an important class of caller is orchestrating many heterogeneous workflows toward a higher campaign goal with IMPRESS-A as one constituent among them. The canonical such superstrate is AuCaM (radical-project/campaign_manager), which launches a workflow as an async def taking a reporter, sizes it from a declared cost, and reads its progress back through reporter.emit().

The tempting reading is that this is control model C — we already have a headless mode, an external half and a control plane, so an outer manager would be one more external caller. That reading is wrong, and the distinction is worth a record because every design that follows from it differs. Model C is a reasoner over CampaignSession: it publishes Specs, submits Stages, answers a rejection through replan, and is refused by the same six gates as any policy. An enclosing campaign manager does none of those things. It launches, bounds a budget, allots resources, pauses, cancels, and reads reports. It has opinions about whether this campaign deserves to be running, and none about which tool runs next.

Two facts fix the shape of the integration. The caller has no preflight protocol: AuCaM's declared_spending, spending_limit and resources are static dicts fixed when the caller builds its own spec, so nothing can be negotiated at launch. And the observation already crosses a process boundary (control/http.py:200), so being told does not need a new operation — see observation.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
An enclosing campaign manager owns one whole IMPRESS-A campaign as a single subordinate workflow — launching it, bounding its budget and resources, pausing and cancelling it, and reading one projected observation per absorbed cycle — and is therefore not control model C: it steers no Spec and plans no Stage, CampaignControlPlane gains no operation, and the preflight handshake is a caller-side function call made before the caller's own spec exists.

Concretely:

  • One invocation is one whole campaign. Its own cycle loop, its own termination. 0001 is untouched: the agent still owns the WorkflowEngine and the outer loop, and the executor still decides when the campaign has ended, because budget, stagnation and repeated failure are facts about state only it holds.
  • The handshake is impress-a offer, a synchronous function of a toolkit and a campaign spec with no campaign to address. It is not a plane operation, and 0007 is not in play. It reports a cost model and the goal vocabulary the toolkit can address, and it reports its basis: declared figures sit multiples above measurement on purpose, because they feed gates that refuse graphs, so an offer states what it is and never passes for a prediction.
  • Being told is a projection, not an operation. A caller receives a digest of the CampaignObservation that observe() already returns, taken by a pump that reads the executor's await-free snapshot API and awaits its sink outside the executor. No await enters a mutating block, and 0007 stays out of play for the same reason adding a field to the observation does (core/decision.py:127-131).
  • An enclosing owner gets no privilege over campaign state, which is 0002's rule extended rather than bent. A caller's spending limit arrives as a budget: it narrows CampaignSpec.budget, and is then enforced by reserve and gate 5 against the same estimate as any policy's. The campaign refuses its own unaffordable graph before a task runs, rather than being cancelled from outside after one has.
  • Pause gates admission only. In-flight runs are allowed to finish, because cancellation is advisory and a reclaimed GPU is not something this system can promise. A paused campaign therefore keeps spending for up to one cycle, and the offer declares that.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An outer manager is told measured cost, not declared. BudgetLedger.spent holds the declared figure (runtime/executor.py:1127), which is inflated deliberately, so reporting it upward would misinform the caller by the full headroom and leave its own learned-cost estimate permanently wrong. ExecutionResults.cost_measured is already summed per run and folded into no ledger; this decision makes aggregating it part of the integration.
  • Our tasks are invisible to the caller's per-task telemetry. We build our own engine through the only sanctioned constructor, and the loop that owns an engine must be the loop that uses it — two allocations were lost to learning that (jobs 22328172, 22328262). So spending must travel in our own reports. Sharing an engine with an enclosing manager is a separate question and is not answered here.
  • Liveness runs outward, not inward. control_liveness_timeout_s cannot protect a campaign under an enclosing manager, because observe() refreshes the clock it reads (runtime/executor.py:489) and a pump that polls observe() holds it open forever. The adapter therefore does not register a control plane — which is also what would arm the bound — and relies on the caller's own stale timeout. Recorded as finding 7 of observation.md.
  • A second superstrate costs an adapter, not a redesign. The pump reports to a sink protocol that names no AuCaM vocabulary, so an off-process variant — a campaign inside its own sbatch, reporting over Redis or Dragon — is another adapter over the same seam.
  • The MCP adapter 0007 anticipated is still unbuilt, and this decision does not change what it would be: submit-and-poll over the same core operations.

docs.title: 0015 — One engine, two processes, and where each boundary falls
docs.text: Date: 2026-11-11 · Status: accepted · Amends: nothing; records what 0010 and 0014 assumed but never stated

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
IMPRESS-A was conceived as three loops — a Spec Loop, a Planning Loop and an execution loop — and the reason given for separating them was that spec resolution, planning and task computation must be mutually non-blocking. That requirement is older than any of the code: the phase-1 architecture record asks for "async, non-blocking submission — the outer loop must observe and remain steerable while work runs", and for a long time nothing implemented it. The reasoner was the loop body of a serial cycle, and three awaits on one coroutine serialised it.

"Mutually non-blocking" bundles three different hazards, and they do not have the same remedy:

Hazard Does a process boundary fix it? What fixed it here A synchronous call on a shared event loop Yes Async structure: AsyncOpenAI for live reasoners, asyncio.to_thread for the blocking backend construction and the ledger's flock Serialisation by awaits — one coroutine doing everything in order No. Two processes with the same await chain are equally serial Structure, in one process: manager.run races executor.pump() against the reasoner's conduct() as two tasks CPU contention between roles Yes Never an observed problem; the roles do almost no CPU work

The only measured precedent for the first row is job 22534628, where a synchronous decision body took 67% of wall clock (p99 56 s) — and that is the sibling example's synchronous client, replaced by an async one before IMPRESS-A ever ran a live reasoner. It argues for async structure. It does not, by itself, argue for a process boundary.

Two mechanical facts constrain any answer. A WorkflowEngine captures the loop it is built on and schedules its dispatch there, so an engine built elsewhere looks healthy and dispatches nothing — jobs 22328172 and 22328262 each wrote r0001 submitted and then burned a full allocation in silence. And admission is synchronous because the dry-run instantiates task agents, so it has to run where the toolkit is installed.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Two processes, not three, and CampaignSession is the split. The Spec Loop and the Planning Loop are co-resident in a control process, because they are independent of execution but not of each other: a plan consumes the revision respecification just made, and in the shipped driver they are sequential awaits inside one conduct (runtime/roles.py). The Reviewer and Deployer are execution-side, because admission needs the toolkit. A third process for the Planner is therefore out of scope by construction rather than deferred. What separates the processes is the session boundary — a second WorkflowEngine or a second event loop is not, and must never become the mechanism.

One engine per campaign, on the execution process's loop, carrying named routes. compute is Dragon on an allocation and rhapsody's concurrent backend off one; local is a thread pool for adapters and QC; ai is added when the campaign serves its own reasoner. A decorator names its route, and an unknown name fails at decoration.

A Stage is one @flow.block. The block's future is the graph's result, its members inherit its uid as workflow_id, and cancelling it cascades to every unfinished member with each cancel sent to the backend that member was routed to (radical.asyncflow 0.7.0).

Each tool command is an executable task placed per backend. exec/launch.Launcher submits it, exec/resources.Placement says where it runs — a Dragon Policy(gpu_affinity=[g]), or a child environment carrying CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES on the concurrent backend — and thread caps travel with it rather than with the process.

What this replaced. The previous engine had a single backend and ran each graph node as one opaque function_task carrying adapter, subprocess, post-process and QC together, with no task_description at all: exec/resources.to_backend_description had no caller, no Policy was ever built, and on Delta every GPU tool saw every GPU. Thread caps were written into the campaign process's environment at start-up. A cancel cancelled a side-channel future, so a run was reaped FAILED and its budget released while its tasks kept running. A second, opt-in execution loop ran on the root project's ImpressManager with a 0.5 s poll and a single-slot child mailbox, and never ran on hardware. exec/dispatch.Dispatcher, runtime/runner.py, runtime/pipelines.py and CampaignSpec.runner are deleted; a spec that sets runner: is refused with a pointer here.

The root impress package is no longer a dependency. tests/test_layering.py::test_nothing_imports_impress and tests/test_toolchain.py::test_impress_is_not_a_dependency keep it that way; the second because impress is on no index, so declaring it again would be a dependency-confusion exposure.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Non-blocking is delivered by async structure first, and by route separation inside the execution process second. The process boundary adds one guarantee on top: tolerance of a reasoner that blocks synchronously. That guarantee is not covered by the test tier — the planned test used a synchronous stall, and what shipped (tests/test_split_process.py) stalls with await asyncio.sleep, which one process already survives.
  • Whether the boundary costs or buys anything is measurable and unmeasured. Arms B and C share a client and a profile and differ only in topology, so a B-vs-C gap is plane latency and round trips, never decision quality. Arm C has never run on Delta.
  • Co-residency has a measured cost, and it is not blocking. control_liveness_timeout_s reads a clock that an in-process campaign's own role driver refreshes, and that driver is silent exactly when it is busy awaiting the tasks it asked for: job 23671367 lost arms A, B and D after one cycle each. The bound now arms only once a plane has registered and is suspended while work is in flight. Job 23675997 showed the mirror image, running two reasoners against one executor.
  • A locally hosted reasoner puts the model execution-side. CampaignSession.infer is a prompt_task on the ai route: the decision stays in the control process, the weights sit beside the tools, sharing that process's GPUs (StageExecutor.gpu_offset keeps tools off them) and its backend_startup_timeout_s. A stalled vLLM bring-up would stall the loop Dragon's Batch() stalled. This path has not run on hardware.
  • The local route brought its own coupling. asyncflow's LocalExecutionBackend.shutdown joins its pool synchronously on the engine loop, so an adapter thread still waiting on a command deadlocks teardown; exec/stage._settle and Launcher.idle drain first. Filed upstream.
  • An enclosing campaign manager gets two surfaces, not one. AuCaM builds a single-backend engine and asyncflow fixes backends at creation, so an in-process AuCaM run cannot share its engine and IMPRESS-A's tasks stay invisible to AuCaM's per-task telemetry.
  • Cancellation stays advisory for running work on the concurrent backend, where rhapsody's cancel_task leaves the child process alive. A run's terminal state always comes from collecting it.
  • cost_measured changed meaning. It now excludes the time a command spent queued, recorded separately as usage.phases["queued"], so figures recorded before this change are not comparable with figures recorded after it.
  • The Python floor moved to 3.11 and both middleware pins to 0.7.0, with Dragon as the [dragon] extra so CI and the laptop tier need none of it.

Evidence. Job 23815248 ran the two-lineage Delta smoke on this loop: 12/12 tasks ok in 3m45s, lineage 0 on GPU 0 and lineage 1 on GPU 1 under Dragon's placement policy with GPUs 2–3 idle, one telemetry block span per Stage with every command under it, Dragon up in 4.5 s and torn down in 2 s. Job 23814643 is the failure that preceded it: a coreutils timeout wrapper, correct on the concurrent backend, became an unreaped process-group leader under Dragon and hung stage 1. Commits e69e982, 8d22cf8, 0e3d945, d9420bc, ed0fde2.

docs.title: The outer loop
docs.text:
One experiment, driven by impress_a.runtime.executor.CampaignExecutor. The steps below happen in this order for any one experiment — but the reasoner is no longer the loop body, so several experiments can be at different steps at once:

observe ─→ SPECIFY ─→ PLAN ─→ compose ─→ review ─→ execute ─→ analyze ─→ update ─→ terminate?
           (Spec      (Stage   (typed     (coverage, (asyncflow) (QC       (tree,
            revision)  of       DAG)       5 gates,              gates)    Pareto,
                       Tasks)              budget,                         provenance)
                          │                dry-run)
                          └── reject ──→ back to PLAN (bounded retry, with the gate and reason)

How the campaign's inputs become that Spec and that Stage — the toolkit, the goal, the budget and the parameters, step by step with the refusal guarding each — is resolution.md.

Only the reasoner differs between control models. Everything below the policy layer is shared, which is what makes frontends pluggable rather than parallel implementations.

There are two ways to be a reasoner:

  • a Specifier and a Planner - two halves, with separate contracts. The Specifier turns the caller's Goal into a mutable Spec of atomic objectives and revises it as data arrives; the Planner maps the objectives that are ready onto Tasks and emits a candidate Stage. runtime.roles.RolesDriver runs both as the Listener, Specifier, Planner and Deployer over one CampaignSession. This replaced decide(obs) -> Decision, which answered "what should the campaign be trying to achieve" and "which tool should run next" in a single call - so no transcript could say which half of a control model earned its cost, which is exactly what the four-arm comparison needs to say. What each shipped model does with the two contracts, and what it is shown when it does, is control-models.md.
  • conduct(session) - drive yourself. The reasoner runs as its own coroutine and reaches the executor through core.session.CampaignSession: submit as many experiments as it wants, then collect them with as_completed in the order they finish. This is what makes a federation of task agents generating an ensemble in parallel expressible at all.

The executor owns all campaign state and is its only writer; it also decides termination, because budget, stagnation and repeated failure are facts about state a reasoner cannot see. A reasoner may request a stop.

Step Owner Notes observe manager Builds a CampaignObservation — front, population stats, budget, failures, and the ToolkitView a reasoner chooses from specify policy Specifier.revise returns a SpecRevision — objectives to add, delete or re-status. The executor applies it and is the only writer plan policy Planner.plan returns a candidate Stage of TaskMappings, or None. replan answers a rejection; RequestHuman and a stop request remain available through the session compose manager A Stage (or abstract intent) → concrete typed DAG. P6 inlining is designed but not built, so a P6 declaration is refused at load review manager Coverage against the applied Spec, six gates, budget, then dry-run; rejection returns the gate and reason to the Planner execute exec layer The Stage runs as one asyncflow block on the campaign's single engine; each node's adapter is a task on the local route and each tool command an executable task on compute, placed per backend analyze task agents Typed metrics extracted; QC gates enforced update manager Nodes appended, front recomputed, provenance written, budget charged

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
control/    CampaignControlPlane + transport adapters
policy/     the decision frontend: specifiers/ + planners/ (one module per control
            model), the reasoning seam, and the role wrappers
manager.py  the outer loop
core/       tree · pareto · budget · qc · decision · provenance · artifacts
compose/    TaskGraph · composer · five gates · self-promoting interlock
tools/      ToolSpec · registry · gate library · task agents
exec/       engine + named backend routes · Stage-as-block · command launcher ·
            placement · job ledger
analysis/   per-Task validation and the four-arm scoring harness. May not import
            `policy` or `control`: a scorer that could reach a reasoner could score a
            campaign by asking it

docs.title: Import contract
docs.text:
Asserted by tests/test_layering.py, which walks the source with ast and checks every internal import against this table. ast.walk is used deliberately: the real adapters defer their science imports into run() bodies, and a deferred from ..exec import ... inside compose would be exactly as fatal as one at the top of the file.

cli          → control, manager, runtime, policy, compose, tools, core, analysis
control      → manager, runtime, core
policy       → core                           (NOT tools, NOT exec, NOT runtime)
manager      → runtime, policy, tools, core   (a facade; the executor owns the work)
runtime      → policy, compose, exec, tools, core
compose      → tools, core                    (NOT exec)
tools        → exec, core
exec         → compose, tools, core
analysis     → runtime, exec, compose, tools, core   (NOT policy, NOT control)
integrations → cli, manager, runtime, tools, core    (NOT exec)
core         → (nothing internal)

__main__ imports cli and nothing else. integrations is a second composition root, like cli: nothing else in the package imports it, so an adapter may name another project's types without any layer of IMPRESS-A knowing that project exists. exec is absent from its row on purpose — an integration drives the executor, it does not dispatch.

Three notes on accuracy. exec → compose, tools has been true since the first prototype (exec/stage.py imports TaskGraph, exec/dispatch.py imports TaskAgent); this line records what the code does rather than what an earlier version of this document claimed. And policy → core is what forced core/session.py and core/results.py to exist: a reasoner may hold a RunOutcome, so RunOutcome cannot live in exec/ beside the ExecutionResults it projects from. And manager → tools is real — manager.py imports Registry — and was missing from this table until the layering test was written; cli and __main__ appeared in no row at all. Both are recorded above rather than quietly tolerated, because a contract with undocumented edges is not a contract.

Two rules carry real weight:

  • policy ↛ tools, policy ↛ exec. Policies emit abstract ExperimentIntent; turning intent into a concrete DAG is the composer's job. If a policy can reach a tool adapter, the seam rots and control models stop being interchangeable.
  • compose ↛ exec. Composition and validation must be testable with no backend at all — that is what makes the whole laptop test tier possible.

docs.title: One engine, and two boundaries
docs.text:
All task work in a campaign is deployed by one long-lived radical.asyncflow WorkflowEngine, which reaches Dragon only through rhapsody. It carries named routes: compute (Dragon on an allocation, rhapsody's concurrent backend off one), local (a thread pool for adapters and QC), and ai when the campaign declares a locally hosted reasoner. A Stage is one @flow.block, so the block's future is the graph's result and cancelling it cascades to every unfinished member on the backend that member was routed to.

The other boundary is between processes. impress-a run keeps the reasoner and the executor in one process as two asyncio tasks — the executor's pump raced against the reasoner's conduct — and impress-a serve + impress-a control splits them, with CampaignSession as the seam. What does not split is the engine: it belongs to the loop it was built on, and a second engine or a second event loop is not how the processes are separated. The Reviewer and Deployer stay execution-side because the dry-run instantiates task agents and must run where the toolkit is installed.

Both boundaries, what each one buys, and what it does not, are recorded in decision 0015.

docs.title: Composition and validation
docs.text:
The agent composes arbitrary typed DAGs at runtime. Six gates run before anything executes, then a dry-run in which every task agent parameterizes without executing — which proves parameter values are legal and nothing about the command that will run (invocation.md, step 3):

Gate Rejects 1 type An edge whose producer output type does not unify with the consumer input type 2 structure Cycles, empty graphs, a tool composed without its QC gates 3 parameter Out-of-range values, unknown parameters, any frozen_parameters 4 resource P6 scheduled (unreachable now that a P6 declaration fails at load, and kept as a backstop), resource shapes exceeding the site, unproven GPU portability, disallowed external submission 5 budget An estimate exceeding remaining budget in any dimension 6 tool delivery Mock tools in a campaign that declares tool_delivery: real, and the reverse

Rejection is cheap and informative: the policy receives a structured ValidationFailure through on_rejected and gets another attempt within the same cycle, bounded by max_attempts.

docs.title: The self-promoting interlock
docs.text:
Novel composition patterns are never blocked and never trusted on sight. A pattern is the graph's shape — tool ids plus typed edges, parameter values excluded, so tuning a parameter does not reset accumulated trust.

Trusted Provisional Cost ceiling Normal budget rules Capped fraction of remaining budget Dry-run Standard Mandatory Result marking Normal QC verdict Auto-marked suspect regardless of outcome

Promotion is mechanical — N consecutive clean runs, where clean means no task failed and no integrity gate failed. Demotion is symmetric and immediate on any integrity failure. Acceptance gates (quality thresholds) still fail the node and keep it off the front, but say nothing about whether the pattern is sound, so they do not touch trust (decision 0013). The trust ledger is site-scoped and spans campaigns, because one campaign may not run a pattern N times.

docs.title: Campaign state
docs.text:
An append-only tree of design lineages ranked by a multi-objective Pareto front, with non-destructive backtracking.

  • Constraints prune, directions rank. Cost is a first-class objective, not an afterthought.
  • A node whose QC verdict is FAIL is never eligible for the front, whatever its scores. This is the single most important coupling in the system: these tools fail silently, so a successful exit code is never sufficient evidence.
  • replicas: N means N independent lineages, one design node each.
  • A measurement supersedes but never deletes a prediction (decision 0012), so the front is not monotonic once assays arrive — a node promoted on an optimistic prediction can be demoted by its own measurement.

docs.title: Task agents
docs.text:
Per tool, four phases: pre-process → parameterize → run → post-process, driven by TaskAgent.__call__. An adapter overrides run() only; the inherited parameterize and post_process are what make parameter checks and QC gates impossible to skip. ToolSpec.agent declares whether the agent is deterministic code or LLM-driven, and nothing reads it yet: every shipped adapter is deterministic code.

Inside run() the adapter builds its tool's command in one pure function and hands it to run_cmd, which submits it to the engine as a placed task — an adapter that started a process any other way would run it on the campaign host, unplaced and unrecorded. The whole path from a spec to a running command, with each shipped tool's command written out, is invocation.md.

QC gates are deterministic in both cases. An LLM may author a protocol; it does not judge whether the result passed its clash check.

docs.title: AuCaM Integration
docs.text:
How IMPRESS-A offers itself to an enclosing campaign manager as one subordinate workflow, and what that relationship is not.

AuCaM (radical-project/campaign_manager) is the canonical superstrate: it orchestrates many heterogeneous workflows toward a higher goal, launches each as an async def taking a reporter, sizes it from a declared cost, bounds its spending, may pause or cancel it, and reads its progress back through reporter.emit(). One IMPRESS-A campaign is one such workflow.

docs.title: The seam
docs.text:
AuCaM  ── launches the block ──►   impress_a_<spec>(reporter, context)
     │       declared_spending            │
     │       spending_limit ──────────────┤  narrows CampaignSpec.budget
     │       resources ───────────────────┤  fits concurrency
     │                                    │
     │  ◄── reporter.emit(score, ─────────┤  one CampaignDigest per absorbed cycle
     │       metrics, iteration)          │
     └──── PAUSE / RESUME ───────────────►┘  gates admission only
                                          │
                                   the campaign keeps its own engine,
                                   its own cycle loop, and the decision to stop

Two modules, and the split is deliberate:

Module Role integrations/reporting.py Transport-neutral. The CycleSink protocol, JsonlSink, the Bridge pump and run_with_sink. Names no superstrate's vocabulary — an in-process block function, an HTTP poller and a subprocess reporting over Redis are three sinks, not three payloads integrations/aucam.py The adapter. The only module in the package that imports AuCaM, which tests/test_layering.py asserts, so the dependency stays optional and one file wide

The pump never touches the executor. It reads observe(), which is synchronous and await-free by invariant, and awaits the sink outside it, so no await enters a mutating block and the one-writer property is untouched.

The trigger is observe().seq, the absorption watermark, not cycle. cycle is incremented in _dispatch, so it counts submissions, and a report fired there would carry no results. seq advances once per lineage absorbed, which is exactly when there is something new to say. The report_interval_s is therefore a floor and not the only trigger: a cycle of the real chain runs minutes of tasks with nothing absorbed, and a caller's staleness bound has to stay satisfiable while that happens.

run_with_sink sends one report before the campaign starts, so a caller has a liveness anchor before there is any work to describe, and one after it ends — and the last one must be the real one, because the stores a caller reads these through keep only the last value per workflow.

Whatever the sink, the digests are also kept on disk: JsonlSink writes one JSON line each under the campaign root at reports/<sink>.jsonl, deliberately not under provenance/, where the executor is the only writer — a report is a record of what somebody else was told, not a campaign record. So a campaign can be asked afterwards what it reported, and when.

What integrations/aucam.py exposes:

Function What it is for workflow_config(spec_path, …) An AuCaM WorkflowConfig for one whole campaign, built from the same impress-a offer a caller could read for itself make_impress_worker(spec_path, …) The block function AuCaM launches. Builds the campaign inside the coroutine launch_bounds(offer) {dimension: (floor, ceiling)} for the caller's own LaunchRequest.bounds reward_fn(result) A WorkflowResult as a reward in [0, 1], for BanditSchedulingPolicy(reward_fn=…) report_once(manager, reporter) One digest on demand, for a campaign somebody else is driving

launch_bounds is separate from workflow_config because bounds is a LaunchRequest field and not a WorkflowConfig one: the controller attaches it per launch, and SchedulingPolicy.size() then picks a point inside it using learned costs this side never sees.

reward_fn exists because AuCaM's default bandit reward is 1.0 if returncode == 0 else 0.0 — throughput — and no shipped AuCaM policy can rank a dict. A cancelled or failed campaign scores 0 whatever it had found, because the bandit is choosing whether to launch this arm again and a run that could not finish is not evidence that it would.

docs.title: A caller, not a control model
docs.text:
The tempting reading is that an outer manager is control model C: there is already a headless mode, an external half and a control plane. That reading is wrong, and decision 0014 is the record of why — every design that follows from it differs.

Model C An enclosing campaign manager What it is a reasoner over CampaignSession the owner of the process What it does publishes Specs, submits Stages, answers a rejection through replan launches, bounds a budget, allots resources, pauses, cancels, reads reports What it is refused by the same six gates as any policy nothing: it proposes no graph Its opinion which tool runs next whether this campaign deserves to be running

So CampaignControlPlane gains no operation, and the adapter registers no control plane at all. See Control Models for what model C actually is, and Pluggable Frontends for where each kind of caller plugs in.

Three consequences of that ruling are visible in the adapter and worth knowing before you read it:

A spending limit arrives as a budget, not as a kill switch. _narrow_budget applies min(current, limit) to CampaignSpec.budget — the adapter's load-bearing line. A limit enforced from outside can only cancel a campaign after it has overspent; the same number as a budget is refused from the inside by reserve and gate 5 before a task runs, and the campaign stops itself with a reason naming the dimension instead of being killed with work in flight.

The caller is told measured cost, not declared. BudgetLedger.spent holds the declared figure, which is inflated on purpose because it feeds gates that refuse graphs. Reporting it upward would misinform the caller by the full headroom and leave its learned-cost estimate permanently wrong, so the digest carries cost_measured under cpu_hours/gpu_hours — the keys AuCaM's own _spent_so_far reads.

Pause gates admission only. In-flight runs are allowed to finish, because cancellation is advisory and a reclaimed GPU is not something this system can promise. A paused campaign therefore keeps spending for up to one cycle, and the offer declares that.

docs.title: Sizing an invocation
docs.text:
impress-a offer campaigns/<spec>.yaml           # what one invocation would cost, and which
                                                # goals the toolkit could address
impress-a offer campaigns/<spec>.yaml --json    # the form a caller reads to size its own spec
impress-a offer campaigns/<spec>.yaml --validation validate_tasks.json

The handshake is a caller-side function call made before the caller's own spec exists, not a plane operation — AuCaM's declared_spending, spending_limit and resources are static dicts fixed when the caller builds its spec, so there is nothing to negotiate at launch.

A different question from preflight: that asks whether this machine can run the binaries, this asks what a caller is buying.

--validation is the only route by which a measured figure enters an offer. Everything else is declared, and the payload says so. Declared cost models sit multiples above measurement on purpose, because they feed gates that refuse graphs — so an offer states its basis and never passes for a prediction. workflow_config logs the offer's warnings rather than discarding them, so a caller that never read the offer still hears that the estimate is parameter-blind.

The offer also declares report_interval_s, so a caller's staleness bound can be a multiple of it. workflow_config sets stale_timeout_s to 4× that interval rather than AuCaM's stated 3× minimum, because 3× is the floor the contract names rather than a margin, and a child of this process can spend minutes in import pyrosetta alone off slow storage.

docs.title: Installing it
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[aucam]"
python -c "import src.aucam, impress_a.integrations.aucam"    # the check CI runs

Both scripts/dev_setup.sh and CI install this extra, so a skipped tests/test_aucam.py is a real failure rather than an absent optional — see the first gotcha below.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
The import name is src.aucam, not aucam. The distribution is named aucam, but upstream's [tool.setuptools.packages.find] declares include = ["src*"], so the importable package is the generic name src — which setuptools itself warns about at install time. This repository has src/ at its root and agent/src/ under it, neither a package, so a same-named namespace portion sits ahead of AuCaM's on the path whenever the working directory is either one. It resolves because a regular package beats a namespace portion. _aucam() tries src.aucam, then aucam in case upstream ever renames, and otherwise raises an error naming the resolved src.__path__ — because when this breaks, the message must say so rather than blame the adapter.

A skip is not a pass. tests/test_aucam.py opens with pytest.importorskip("src.aucam"), so without the extra the whole file exits 0 and the suite looks green. CI therefore installs the extra and runs the import check above as its own step, which fails loudly instead.

The pin is a fact about a moment, not a version. The extra pins a 40-character commit, and tests/test_toolchain.py::test_the_aucam_extra_pins_a_commit_not_a_branch holds it that way — a branch pin reinstalls something different next week and moves this tier under us. What that test cannot express is which ref the commit came from:

Ref Relationship to the pin aucam-v2 the pinned commit is this branch's tip devel (upstream default) a different, older commit — the pin is ahead of it main / master, newest tag v0.2.1 the pre-v2 line

So the adapter is written against an in-progress branch that upstream has not merged or tagged, and three things follow. aucam-v2 will advance, so the pin needs deliberate bumping and the adapter may need to move with it. There is no tag to pin instead, because the v2 work is untagged. And if that branch is rebased, force-pushed or deleted once it lands, a pinned SHA can stop being fetchable and pip install -e ".[aucam]" fails — a red CI run whose cause is in another repository. aucam is not on PyPI, which is why the extra is a git requirement at all.

The adapter does not take AuCaM's engine. AuCaM passes its shared WorkflowEngine to a block that asks for one; this block does not declare flow. WorkflowEngine.__init__ captures the loop it is built on, and the executor builds its own through the only sanctioned constructor, exec.backend.make_engine_bounded, which also bounds Dragon's synchronous startup. There is no "use this engine instead" seam, and inventing one is how two allocations were spent on an engine that dispatched nothing. The cost of not taking it is that our tasks are invisible to AuCaM's per-task telemetry, so its task-level charging never applies — which is why spending travels in our own reports.

Liveness runs outward. control_liveness_timeout_s cannot protect a campaign under an enclosing manager: the pump calls observe(), and observe() calls touch(), which refreshes the very clock that bound reads. A campaign with a pump attached therefore cannot detect a lost caller by silence, and liveness has to come from the enclosing manager's own staleness bound. Recorded as finding 7 of Observation.

wall_hours is declared but never offered as a limit. It is an input to AuCaM's proration, not a dimension it bills, and offering it as a limit would cancel a campaign for taking the time it said it would take. It is reported in declared_spending, at the offer's ceiling, because too small a figure makes AuCaM's proration exceed 100% and cancel a campaign that is behaving normally.

docs.title: What is not built
docs.text:
The off-process path. Everything above runs the campaign in the caller's process, as a block function. A campaign inside its own sbatch, reporting to an AuCaM running elsewhere, is the variant that is not built: CycleSink is already the seam for it — it names no superstrate — and the implementation would be a reporter over a Redis or Dragon DataBackend reachable from the compute node. The backlog holds it open deliberately, as worth doing only after the in-process path has run once on real hardware.

That is also the honest status of this page: the adapter is exercised on every push, by a real AuCaM campaign driving a real IMPRESS-A one, but on CI runners rather than in an allocation.

docs.title: What the tests prove
docs.text:
tests/test_aucam.py drives a real campaign through a real AuCaM WorkflowReporter — no fake reporter and no stub config, because a test written against a double would not have caught the thing that actually bit, the src.aucam import name. Eight tests:

  • a WorkflowConfig the real AuCaM accepts
  • a campaign runs as one AuCaM workflow and reports through its reporter
  • the score is a float a bandit can rank
  • the metrics carry measured spending under the keys AuCaM charges against
  • the caller's spending limit becomes the campaign's own budget
  • a PAUSE from AuCaM is translated into the bridge's own vocabulary
  • the bounds a caller attaches are not on the WorkflowConfig
  • an AuCaM campaign launches a whole IMPRESS campaign and charges what it reported

tests/test_toolchain.py adds the two packaging guards: that the extra pins a commit rather than a branch, and that src.aucam resolves to the installed AuCaM rather than to a directory in this repository.

docs.title: What a tool is, to the system
docs.text:
A tool is three things, read by three different readers:

part where read by says the spec toolkits/<tk>/tools/<id>/spec.yaml the planner, the composer, the gates what the tool accepts and produces: typed ports, parameters and their bounds, metrics, QC gates, cost the adapter the TaskAgent subclass entry: names the engine, once per task how to stage inputs, run the tool and read its output back the command builder one pure function in the adapter's module a person, and a test the exact argv the tool runs

The division matters because a spec does not say what gets executed — it has no command, executable or environment field. A reasoner chooses a tool and its parameter values from the spec alone and never sees a command line. The adapter turns those values into a command, and the engine places that command on a compute node. So the adapter is the only place where "which command does this system run" can be answered, and the rules below exist to make that answer short enough to read.

invocation.md walks the whole path — spec, request, parameters, argv, placed process, recorded command — with the shipped tools' commands written out. Read it once before writing an adapter; this page is the how-to that follows from it.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Tools are declarative data plus a behaviour class. A toolkit is a directory:

toolkits/<toolkit>/
├── SKILL.md                     # agent-facing guidance for the whole toolkit
└── tools/<tool_id>/
    ├── spec.yaml                # the ToolSpec  (data)
    └── tests/                   # fixtures, including known-BAD outputs

The behaviour class lives wherever entry: points. In practice every shipped tool points into the package (src/impress_a/tools/<toolkit>_agents.py) rather than co-locating an agent.py here, because several tools in a toolkit share helpers and a subprocess worker.

Toolkits are discovered from, in precedence order: an explicit path, $IMPRESS_A_TOOLKITS, installed impress_a.toolkits entry points, then the bundled toolkits/ directory. A site or third party can add a toolkit without forking the package.

docs.title: Adding a tool
docs.text:
1. Run the real tool by hand first, and keep the command that worked. Every flag in an adapter should be one somebody has executed: RFD3 was once invoked with --config/--out, flags its CLI does not have, on the strength of its documentation.
  2. Write spec.yaml (below). Declare a parameter only if step 3 will pass it to the tool.
  3. Write the command builder: a module-level function taking the resolved params and the paths it needs, returning the argv, with no I/O in it.
  4. Write the TaskAgent subclass around it — override run() only — and set entry: to its dotted path.
  5. Add known-bad and known-good fixtures under tests/ (see QC gates).
  6. Mention the tool in the toolkit's SKILL.md.
  7. Pin the command: add the tool to _build in tests/test_real_toolkits.py, which gives it the golden-argv test and the declared-parameters test.
  8. Teach impress-a preflight about any environment variable or executable it needs, then run impress-a validate-tasks on hardware. Admission cannot tell you the binary is missing (invocation.md, finding 1).

If you find yourself editing the composer, validator or manager to add a tool, the layering is wrong.

docs.title: spec.yaml
docs.text:
id: example_fold
toolkit: prediction
version: "0.1"
pattern: P1                                  # see reference/compute-patterns.md
entry: mypkg.agents.FoldAgent
resources: {gpus: 1, cores: 4, walltime_s: 60}
gpu_portability: {cuda: proven, hip: unproven, sycl_xpu: unproven}
inputs:
  sequences: {type: ProteinSequence}
outputs:
  complex: {type: Complex}
parameters:
  recycles: {type: int, default: 3, min: 1, max: 12, trades: "accuracy vs wall-clock"}
frozen_parameters:
