  checkpoint: "Mixing checkpoints within a campaign makes designs non-comparable."
qc_gates:
  - {id: output_present, params: {key: result}}
  - {id: has_secondary_structure, params: {min_ss_fraction: 0.25}}
cost_model: {unit: invocation, cost: {gpu_hours: 0.03}}

docs.title: What a parameter is for
docs.text:
A parameters entry is a promise in two directions. To a planner it is a knob: the trades sentence is how a planner decides whether it may move it (quality and diversity, yes; breadth and identity, no — resolution.md step 6), and the bounds are how far. To the adapter it is a key that will arrive in params, already validated. A parameter that reaches no command breaks the first promise silently — a planner can tune it forever with no effect — so the test suite refuses one unless it is exempted by name with a reason.

Give a parameter a null default only when "unset" is a real state, as with seed. It is then absent from params unless something set it, so read it with params.get(...).

Inputs that identify the campaign's target — a ligand SMILES, an input-spec path, a params file — are ordinary parameters with an empty-string default. The campaign's params: block supplies them, so a reasoner never has to know a tool's parameter names to run a campaign correctly.

docs.title: frozen_parameters matters as much as parameters
docs.text: Settings an agent must never touch — a scorefunction's reference weights, a checkpoint identity, a retry backoff floor. Freezing them declaratively means the composer cannot propose them and gate 3 rejects any graph that tries. Each entry carries its reason, which is surfaced in the rejection.

docs.title: Loading is validating
docs.text: A malformed spec, a default outside its own declared range, an unknown QC gate id, a P1 tool declaring no GPU, or a SKILL.md missing a required section is a load-time error. A toolkit that fails anywhere registers nothing — never a partial set.

docs.title: QC gates
docs.text:
Gates are shared by id from impress_a.tools.gates, not reimplemented per tool, so there are not fifty subtly different versions of the same check:

from impress_a.tools import gates
from impress_a.core.qc import GateOutcome, GateResult

@gates.gate("my_check")
def _my_check(out: dict, params: dict) -> GateResult:
    v = (out.get("metrics") or {}).get("thing")
    ok = v is not None and v >= params.get("min", 0)
    return GateResult(gate="my_check",
                      outcome=GateOutcome.PASS if ok else GateOutcome.FAIL,
                      observed=v, threshold=params.get("min"))

Gates are mandatory for non-P6 tools — gate 2 refuses a tool composed without them. They are the boundary at which a tool's output enters campaign state, and the only defence against silent failure.

Each gate has a role — integrity (the default) or acceptance:

qc_gates:
  - {id: output_present, params: {key: result}}
  - {id: metrics_reported, params: {metrics: [complex_plddt]}}                 # integrity
  - {id: metric_in_range, role: acceptance, params: {metric: complex_plddt, min: 0.5}}

An integrity failure means the tool or pipeline broke, and it demotes the composition pattern. An acceptance failure means the tool worked and the design is not good enough: the node still FAILs, and is never rankable, but the trust ledger ignores it (decision 0013). Use acceptance only for a quality threshold; anything that detects a malfunction stays integrity. Load-time validation enforces one rule here: every acceptance metric_in_range must have its metric named in an integrity metrics_reported gate. That rule exists because a value the adapter never read must be an integrity failure, never a low score. Adapters therefore omit a metric they could not read rather than reporting 0.0.

Write gates against the failure you have actually seen. A gate that has never seen the output it was written to catch is an assertion, not a test — so every non-mock tool carries known-bad fixtures under tests/, and tests/test_gate_fixtures.py fails if a new one does not. A .bad.json must fail at least one integrity gate; one that records a genuinely weak design, caught only by acceptance, says so with "acceptance_only": true.

toolkits/<tk>/tools/<id>/tests/
├── <name>.bad.json     # a raw run() payload this tool's OWN gates must FAIL
├── <name>.good.json    # a raw run() payload they must PASS
└── raw/                # tool-native artifacts (a real FASTA, a real out_dir listing);
                        # never collected as fixtures

The filename suffix is authoritative, never a field inside the file: a typo'd "expect": "pass" would be silently wrong, a wrong suffix cannot be. Each file has three keys:

{
  "why": "the failure this records, and where it was observed",
  "failing_gates": ["output_present", "metric_in_range[ligand_iptm]"],
  "output": {"result": null, "count": 0, "outputs": {}, "metrics": {}}
}

output is verbatim what the agent's run() returns, and outputs is always {} — these fixtures cover the QC contract; the artifact contract is _as_artifacts, covered in test_real_toolkits.py. failing_gates is an exact set of rendered GateResult.gate labels, so metric_in_range entries take the metric_in_range[<name>] form. A fixture cannot claim to demonstrate one gate while tripping another.

toolkits/mock/tools/mock_noodle/tests/ is the worked example, and the one fixture pinned directly to the code that produces it.

docs.title: Task agents
docs.text:
class FoldAgent(TaskAgent):
    async def pre_process(self, req): ...        # stage inputs, check preconditions
    def parameterize(self, req): ...             # usually inherited: defaults + range + frozen checks
    async def run(self, req, params): ...        # the only required override
    async def post_process(self, req, raw): ...  # usually inherited: metric extraction + gate execution

The driver is TaskAgent.__call__, which runs the four phases in order and times each. Override run() and nothing else: no shipped adapter overrides another phase, and the inherited parameterize and post_process are what make parameter checks and QC gates impossible to skip. run() returns a plain dict with outputs, metrics, and whatever keys the gates inspect.

docs.title: The shape of an adapter
docs.text:
def fold_command(params, *, input_fasta, out_dir, weights) -> list[str]:
    """THE command `example_fold` runs. Pure: every path is an argument.

    `fold` comes from PATH and `weights` from $FOLD_WEIGHTS; neither is in the spec.
    """
    cmd = ["fold", "predict", str(input_fasta), "--out", str(out_dir),
           "--weights", str(weights), "--recycles", str(params["recycles"])]
    if params.get("seed") is not None:
        cmd += ["--seed", str(params["seed"])]
    return cmd


class FoldAgent(TaskAgent):
    async def run(self, req, params):
        weights = os.environ.get("FOLD_WEIGHTS")
        if not weights:                                   # 1. fail loudly, before any work
            raise RuntimeError("FOLD_WEIGHTS is not set - see scripts/delta_env_setup.sh")
        sequences = input_path(req, "sequences")          # 2. inputs, by declared port
        work = workdir_for(req, "fold")                   #    and a directory of its own
        cmd = fold_command(params, input_fasta=sequences, out_dir=work, weights=weights)
        await run_cmd(cmd, env=child_env(req),            # 3. the engine runs it, placed
                      timeout_s=float(self.spec.resources.walltime_s))
        return {"result": "complex",                      # 4. read the output back
                "outputs": {"complex": work / "model_0.pdb"},
                "metrics": _read_confidence(work)}

docs.title: The adapter's contract
docs.text:
Each rule is here because breaking it failed quietly at least once.

rule why Every command goes through run_cmd. Never subprocess, never os.system run_cmd submits the command to the engine, which places it on the node's GPU with its thread share and records its argv. A command started any other way runs on the campaign host, unplaced and unrecorded, and nothing says so Build the argv in one pure function It is the only place a reader can learn what the tool runs, and the only form a test can pin without the binary Every declared parameter reaches the command — a flag, a config-file key or a positional argument Otherwise it is a knob connected to nothing Pass timeout_s=spec.resources.walltime_s The walltime bounds a command only because the adapter passes it. A call without it is unbounded Never pin a GPU or cap threads yourself Placement is the engine's, and differs by backend: an environment variable under the concurrent backend, a Policy under Dragon. An adapter that set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES under Dragon would name a device it was never given Pass env=child_env(req), or a filtered copy of os.environ if the child must not see yours The environment given to a child replaces its own, so pass a whole one. child_env carries no pinning; the engine adds that Write under workdir_for(req, prefix), and pass absolute paths tempfile.mkdtemp() is local to one node and unreachable from wherever the next task runs. Most commands run with no cwd, so a relative path resolves against the campaign's directory, not the tool's Read inputs with input_path(req, port) It resolves by your own declared input port — the wiring the composer computed and gate 1 type-checked. Scanning the upstream payloads mis-wires a node with two typed inputs Check environment variables first, and raise A missing variable should name itself, not surface as a tool's own confusing failure Keep heavy imports inside run() The module is imported at registry load and in the dry run, on a login node, where import pyrosetta costs minutes or does not exist Omit a metric you could not read — never report 0.0 A fabricated zero turns "the tool broke" into "the design is weak" If the tool produces N candidates, select one and say how many Report ensemble_size; breadth across designs comes from replicas, never from a tool's internal N

docs.title: Outputs are typed handles, not strings
docs.text:
Return a pathlib.Path for anything written to disk, and a plain value for anything small enough to carry inline. post_process turns both into ArtifactRefs, taking the type from the spec's declared output port — so a handle can never disagree with the contract the composer type-checked the graph against, and an adapter never has to repeat itself.

return {"result": "backbone",                       # what `output_present` looks for
        "outputs": {"backbone": work / "design.pdb"},   # a Path: a file
        "metrics": {"ss_fraction": 0.62}}

Returning a Path is how an adapter declares a file; returning str(path) makes it an inline value instead. Files get their size and a content digest recorded, which is what lets a reasoner in another process tell whether the bytes behind a path are still the ones the campaign reasoned about.

An output your spec does not declare is a load-bearing error, not something to drop quietly: nothing downstream could consume it and the composer never type-checked it, so post_process raises rather than let a spec bug surface later as a missing input.

To consume an upstream artifact, _subprocess.input_path(req, port) returns the thing to open, resolved by your own declared input port — the wiring the composer computed and gate 1 type-checked. It replaces a helper that scanned the dependency payloads for a matching output name, which is right only while a node has exactly one upstream: with two typed inputs it returned whichever dependency came first, and that type-checks at composition and mis-wires at runtime.

docs.title: Checking what your tool ran
docs.text: After a run, provenance/tasks.jsonl has one row per task, and its commands field lists each command as the backend was handed it — your builder's argv, with a timeout prefix where the engine added one, the GPU it was placed on and its exit code. work/<prefix>_<node>/ holds what you staged and what the tool wrote. Compare the first against your builder and the second against what run() returned; a tool that exits 0 having written nothing is the failure these files are for.

docs.title: Skill documents
docs.text:
SKILL.md is agent-facing guidance, not an API reference — the spec is the reference. Required sections: Purpose (and when not to use the toolkit), Canonical sequences, Cost posture, Pitfalls.

Every tool in the toolkit must be mentioned, and every tool mentioned must exist; the registry checks both. Co-location is what keeps docs and specs in step: one pull request touches both.

docs.title: Compute Patterns
docs.text: Normative. Every ToolSpec declares one. Validation keys off it today — whether QC gates are mandatory, whether a P6 tool was scheduled, whether external submission is allowed. Dispatch does not: every node takes the one path described in invocation.md, whatever its pattern (that page's finding 6).

docs.title: Why patterns rather than categories
docs.text: A tool's compute pattern is not what it computes — it is what kind of scheduling commitment a call to it represents. Two tools share a pattern if and only if the execution layer must treat them the same way. An autonomous agent cannot reason about "run AlphaFold" as an undifferentiated action; it has to know whether the call consumes a GPU it already holds, blocks for hours, can fail because a remote host is down, or can be retried for free.

docs.title: The patterns
docs.text: ID Pattern Scheduling implication Examples P1 GPU-node-local, in-job Placed on a GPU the agent already holds, one device per lineage; contends with other P1 work Diffusion generators, inverse folding, structure prediction P2 CPU-parallel fan-out, in-job Scales by replica count; the natural knob for adaptive batch sizing Physics ensembles, structural search, per-design scoring P3 MPI multi-node, in-job Needs a reserved rank topology; not resizable mid-run Molecular dynamics, MPI-parallel design protocols P4 External HPC job Async submit/poll; outlives the agent; needs a durable ledger entry Long production runs, work needing a different queue P5 Network service over HTTPS No local resource cost; fails by latency, quota, outage, schema drift Structure/sequence databases, MSA services, a hosted LLM oracle P6 In-process library call Must never be scheduled — overhead would exceed the work Cheminformatics, structure parsing, metric computation P7 Composite pipeline Parameterize and launch; internal stages are not individually steered A whole externally-defined multi-stage pipeline P8 External experiment Latency of days to weeks; completes out-of-band, often after the campaign ends Wet-lab or robotic-lab assay

docs.title: The three that change how code is written
docs.text:
P4 is not P1–P3 with a longer timeout. P1–P3 run inside the allocation the agent already holds. P4 leaves it, so the work can outlive the agent process. That demands a durable job ledger (exec/ledger.py) and introduces queue wait as a cost term unrelated to the science.

P6 is an instruction to inline — and inlining is not built. A tool that takes 30 ms does real damage if treated as a task: the orchestration layer pays scheduling, serialization and filesystem cost orders of magnitude greater than the work. The composer was supposed to inline P6 tools, and never did: it dropped them from every graph instead, with nothing running them in their place, so a declared stage vanished without a word. A P6 declaration is therefore a load-time error now (tools/spec.py), and a whole toolkit that declares one registers nothing. Gate 4 still rejects a scheduled P6 node, as a backstop against a composer bug. The pattern stays in the taxonomy because the intent is unchanged; what a reader must not assume is that declaring P6 gets a tool run.

P8 is forward-declared. No tool in the current registry is P8. It exists so the data model, the storage layout and the control plane are shaped correctly now, when that is nearly free, rather than retrofitted later. A measurement arrives out-of-band as an update to an existing design node, not as a task result — see decision 0012.

docs.title: Orthogonal attributes
docs.text:
Pattern alone is insufficient. ToolSpec also declares:

Attribute Why it matters gpu_portability (cuda / hip / sycl_xpu) Checked at compose time against the site's gpu_api. A tool with no proven path on the running platform is refused before it consumes anything resources Become a per-command Placement (exec/resources.py): the GPU, the thread share and the environment one command runs with. Backends do not share a resource vocabulary, so the translation is per backend — a Dragon Policy, or a child environment on the concurrent backend cost_model Feeds the budget gate and the cost objective qc_gates Mandatory for every tool that can be registered; gate 2 refuses a tool composed without them

A campaign that serves its own reasoner reserves the first devices for the model, and StageExecutor.gpu_offset shifts every tool's placement past them — so a tool never lands on the GPU the model is holding. That reasoner is not P5: it runs inside the allocation on the engine's ai route, with none of P5's latency, quota or outage failure modes and all of P1's contention.

docs.title: Classification rules
docs.text:
1. Classify by dominant cost, not capability. A tool that can use a GPU but is normally run on CPU is P2.
  2. A secondary pattern is allowed for genuinely dual-mode tools — record as P2 (primary) / P4 (when the ensemble exceeds remaining walltime). Never more than two.
  3. Wrappers inherit what they wrap. A Python API over an MPI binary is P3.
  4. Egress-dependent tools are P5 even with a local fallback. Record the fallback under failure modes.

docs.title: Control models: what each reasoner is shown, and what it may choose
docs.text:
The four reasoners, as they run today. resolution.md is the pipeline all of them drive — caller inputs to specified targets to a programmed Stage; this page covers the four places a model's choice enters it, what the model is shown when it does, and how its answer is constrained before the engine acts on it.

Anything true of every campaign is in resolution.md and is not repeated here.

docs.title: The letters
docs.text:
Every reasoner is a Specifier half and a Planner half (policy/registry.py:385, build_roles). decide(obs) -> Decision was deleted in phase 11 and nothing else is a reasoner; manager._reasoner raises TypeError on anything that is neither a pair nor a conduct implementation.

letter Specifier half Planner half calls/cycle status A four-node loop hypothesize (call) → analyze select_tasks (call) → parameterize 2 partial B oracle one SPEC_SCHEMA call per signal one STAGE_SCHEMA call per planning round 2 partial C external a {"role": "specifier"} inbox a {"role": "planner"} inbox 0 — a caller is the model implemented D explicit Goal → Spec, deterministically Tasks by output type 0 implemented null an empty Spec never asked 0 implemented replay re-authors a recorded specs.jsonl re-authors a recorded stages.jsonl 0 partial

A letter is a decision frontend, not a deployment topology. Any of them runs either in one process (impress-a run) or split across impress-a serve + impress-a control; the one exception is C, which run refuses because it means an external caller steers and run attaches no plane. Where the model is hosted is a third, separate axis: a --model-profile names a hosted endpoint (kind: openai_compat) or a model served inside the allocation on the campaign's own engine (kind: rhapsody_vllm, e.g. the local-dragon profile), and the latter is reached through session.infer rather than over the network.

null and replay are shipped deciders outside the four-model taxonomy, which is why "exactly one of four" and --model's choices do not agree. replay reads the two executor-written records rather than anything a reasoner kept, so the record exists for every model whether or not it takes notes and a reasoner cannot write itself a flattering one; it needs --replay-from, and it diverges loudly rather than improvising — a recorded Stage refused where the original was admitted means the campaign differs from the one recorded.

Model A makes two calls per cycle, not four. Its four nodes are two per half, and analyze and parameterize are deterministic: they act on the strategy the node before them chose. Measured on Beam, that is the same per-cycle call count as B.

impress-a models prints this table from policy/registry.MODELS, which is the mechanism that keeps the status column honest — a claim nobody can see goes stale quietly, and docs/ once described four working control models while two had no LLM behind them.

ReasonerModel.llm_calls is the count with no --model-profile attached, which is why every row in the registry reads 0. Nothing in this repository constructs a live client unless a profile names one; A then runs its rule cascades and B runs RehearsalOracle, and both report zero calls. tests/test_reasoner_registry.py holds the field at 0 for exactly that reason, so it cannot rise by accident.

docs.title: What A, B and C share with D
docs.text:
Chain resolution, typed port wiring and replan come from ThresholdPlanner, held by each as self._mechanics and used by composition rather than reimplemented. Those are correctness — which tool produces the artifact another consumes, and which port it arrives on — and two implementations would be two things to keep in step. A four-arm comparison's one-variable claim is about decisions, not about whether a graph is wired correctly; an arm that wired it differently would be a different engine, not a different reasoner.

What is genuinely each model's own: breadth, the parameter vector, and — for B alone — which subset of the declared chain to run.

And none of them decides when the campaign is done. No shipped half overrides BaseSpecifier.satisfied, so satisfaction is computed from the data registry (resolution.md step 8). The protocol permits an override, and says such a Specifier owes an explanation in provenance; nothing takes it.

docs.title: What reaches a half
docs.text:
policy may import core only (ADR 0010), so CampaignSpec — which lives in runtime/ — can never reach a reasoner. Two plain-data objects cross the boundary, by two different routes.

impress-a run      CampaignSpec ─┬→ _options_for()   → ReasonerOptions → build_roles()
                                 └→ goal_from_spec() → Goal → initial_spec()
impress-a control  CampaignObservation → _role_pair() + a Goal rebuilt from the observation

ReasonerOptions (policy/registry.py:53, filled by cli._options_for:243) is the construction-time half. Every field is optional because most models use two or three:

option from read by stages stages: all four planners. Without it every model falls back to its built-in default, which is the mock chain — so a campaign naming real toolkits would load them, validate them, and then execute mocks replicas replicas: all four planners, as base_replicas oracle and reasoner --model-profile B's single-call seam and A's per-node seam. One client fills both, because OpenAICompatOracle implements reasoning.NodeReasoner; a letter picks one shape or the other, so a second client would only be a second connection to the same endpoint. A rhapsody_vllm profile fills them with SessionOracle instead, which calls session.infer rather than an endpoint timeout_s, on_timeout control_liveness_timeout_s: C only records, spec_records, stage_records --replay-from replay only fallback built by the caller B and C sink always whichever halves record their own reasoning max_cycles, target_front max_cycles:, target_front: nothing in policy/ reads either — see resolution.md, finding 4. target_front reaches a Specifier through the Goal

impress-a control takes the second route (cli/__init__.py:601): it passes only stages, the client, replicas and a sink, because a remote driver has no CampaignSpec — the campaign's bounds arrive as obs.max_cycles, obs.target_front and obs.replicas from the observation instead, and a Goal is rebuilt from it. Dropping any of those made a remotely driven arm run to a different bound from the in-process arms it was being compared with.

The campaign's params: reaches no reasoner at all — the executor merges it as defaults under the policy's choices (resolution.md step 6). A reasoner never has to learn a tool's parameter names.

docs.title: What each model is shown
docs.text:
This is where A and B actually differ, and it is a bigger difference than their judgement.

A — hypothesize / select_tasks B — SPEC_SCHEMA / STAGE_SCHEMA Specifier side goal, cycle, open objectives, count satisfied, the front with its metric values, population stats, and toolkit.ids only the same, plus the declared objectives as data and two machine-readable lines (FRONT_IDS, METRICS), plus budget remaining Planner side goal, cycle, ready objectives, what is being refined, the chain as bare ids, in-flight count, budget remaining, max lineages the chain plus each enabled tool's full card: outputs, metrics, and every tunable parameter with type, default, min, max, trades and kind chooses a strategy word, and a lineage count the chain subset, the width, and every parameter value

Model A's Specifier is shown tool ids and no cards on purpose: that node chooses a strategy, and tool detail belongs to the half that chooses tasks. Its Planner is shown no cards either, because its parameter vector is computed by the deterministic parameterize node from the strategy word — explore sets quality knobs to 83% of each declared range and diversity to 35%, exploit 39% and 5%, which are FourNodePolicy's own shipped numbers re-expressed as fractions so they mean the same thing on a chain nobody wrote them for.

B's prompt filters by tunable(), which does not look at kind. So B is shown the breadth parameters that _knobs forbids A and D to touch, labelled kind: breadth, and it raises them — num_designs to 2, 3, 4 and 8 on the mock lab's live arms. rfd3_design's own spec records that num_designs stays at 1 because its adapter keeps index 0, and cost_model is per invocation, so nothing prices the extra draws either. A-vs-B is therefore partly a filtered knob set against an unfiltered one, not only one model's judgement against another's. Backlog H10, with three ways to close it: filter the prompt by kind, mark the real breadth parameters operator_only, or make the cost models scale.

What no model is shown, on any path: a parameter marked operator_only. tools/view.card_for puts it in TaskCard.frozen with its reason, so tunable skips it, B's prompt omits it, and B's schema check refuses a reply naming it (resolution.md step 3).

docs.title: How a reply is constrained
docs.text:
A reasoner never constructs a Stage. It returns a JSON object, and _to_stage (policy/planners/oracle.py:156) passes three of its fields — stages, replicas, params — as arguments to ThresholdPlanner.plan. Task ids, lineage indices, typed port inputs, objective attribution, deferrals, cancels and parent_node are all engine-authored and unreachable from a reply. Most of the format cannot be violated because the model was never given the pen.

What it can get wrong is caught in six layers. All of model A's calls use the same machinery with a two-field schema.

layer where what it does, and the defect it exists for the schema, stated twice policy/llm.py:198, _render:224 prose in the request and response_format: json_object. An endpoint rejecting the parameter with 400 is retried once without it rather than failing the decision — "OpenAI-compatible" is not a uniform surface parsed, never brace-sliced :303 json.loads, absorbing only a `` fence. The predecessor tooktext[find("{"):rfind("}")+1]`, which accepts a prose answer containing two braces and builds a decision from whatever was between them bounded corrective retry policy/reasoning.ask:75 isinstance dict → required keys non-empty → the node's own validate, all inside the loop, with the rejection appended to the prompt. Two attempts; a third has nothing new to add while costing a round trip. Every attempt is recorded, rejected ones with ok: false the state-bound validator planners/oracle.py:109 built per call against this cycle's enabled chain and view: a tool outside the chain (the error names the chain), replicas out of bounds (names the bound), params naming a tool not in the stage, then frozen → unknown → range, in that order, and parent_node refused outright as the Specifier's decision the typed model core/spec.py:325 Stage is pydantic: wrong types raise at construction, omitted optional fields take defaults guard, then Reviewer policy/wrappers.StageGuard:65, runtime/reviewer.py forbid_tools, which refuses rather than edits; then coverage against the applied Spec, gates 1–6, budget and the dry-run (resolution.md step 7)

Two details worth keeping. The frozen-before-unknown ordering was a real fix: card_for leaves a frozen parameter out of parameters and reports it under frozen, so the "declares no parameter" branch fired first and a model naming difficulty was told the tool has no such parameter — which is false, and a corrective retry cannot act on a correction that is a lie. And one exchange is scoped to one decision (ask calls the client's reset): the live client carries earlier turns because a reasoning model may require its own reasoning content back on a follow-up, and nothing was ending the exchange, so by cycle fifty the prompt carried fifty decisions with both halves' exchanges interleaved inside one client.

A model-supplied chain is intersected, never substituted. ThresholdPlanner.plan computes enabled = [t for t in declared if t in view and t in self.stages], and self.stages stays the campaign's chain. The oracle and external planners used to assign self._mechanics.stages = reply before delegating, so one reply naming a subset narrowed the campaign for every later cycle — including the cycles planned by the fallback, which is that object — and a degrade afterwards could not restore it, because nothing held the original. A tool the campaign never enabled cannot enter by this route whatever a reply says.

The corrective-retry path has never fired against a live endpoint. Across 140 live calls (Beam-501B-A23B, 2026-11-10) there were zero retries and zero degraded turns, so layers 3 and 4 are proven by tests and by the offline rehearsal, not by a model getting it wrong in production.

docs.title: Degraded mode is declared, never improvised
docs.text:
Models A, B and C each depend on something outside the job, and each has a defined answer when it does not arrive.

  • A — a node that exhausts its attempts raises NodeRefused, falls back to that node's own rule cascade, and records a reasoner_degraded transition. The campaign continues.
  • B — either half falls back to a model-D half, sets degraded = True, and records the same event. A declared fallback is mandatory for a real run: an API outage must degrade explicitly, never stall a multi-GPU allocation.
  • C — on_timeout defaults to stop, and ExternalPlanner refuses on_timeout="fallback" with no fallback declared. fallback is what makes "a model-C arm that silently became a model-D arm" possible, and such an arm is byte-for-byte a D campaign and invisible in the result. impress-a run --model C is refused outright rather than timing out (backlog C6).

reasoning.degraded writes one event name for every model, so a single query over transitions finds every degraded decision in a campaign whatever made it. That is what makes the pre-registration's "a degraded arm is void" rule enforceable at all — before the sink was subscribed, no campaign on any machine recorded a prompt, a reply, a model id, an attempt count or a timing, and the rule could not fire on a laptop or on Delta.

Check degraded_events before reading any live arm's yield. A non-zero count means what the arm produced is not that model's result.

docs.title: Writing another one
docs.text:
Two protocols and a registry row. frontends.md has the procedure and a worked example, including why a new Planner should compose ThresholdPlanner rather than reimplement chain resolution.

What belongs here rather than there is the constraint that shapes such a half: a reasoner reads only ReasonerOptions, never a CampaignSpec — see "What reaches a half" above — so a builder that needs a campaign field wants another option, not an import.

docs.title: Pluggable Frontends
docs.text:
IMPRESS-A has two independent frontend axes. Both plug into the same engine; neither requires changes below the layer it occupies. The substrate beneath them is not a third axis — nothing above it chooses it — but it is selected by name rather than hard-coded; see the end of this page.

        ┌──── INTERFACE FRONTEND ─────┐        who talks to the campaign
        │  in-process · HTTP+SSE · MCP │
        └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                       │  CampaignControlPlane (one protocol)
        ┌──────────────┴───────────────┐
        │     DECISION FRONTEND        │        who decides what runs next
        │   A · B · C · D · your own   │
        └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                       │  Specifier + Planner (two protocols)
        ════════════════════════════════        everything below is shared
          manager · compose · validate
          tools · exec · rhapsody backends

docs.title: 1. The decision frontend — control models
docs.text:
Exactly one is active per campaign, fixed at launch (decision 0005): a campaign has one stated methodology and its results are attributable to it.

Four ship — A, B, C and D — plus null and replay outside the taxonomy. Three run autonomously; model C is the headless mode (decision 0002), not an extra option bolted onto the side. Model D is the one that is reproducible end to end, which is what makes it the baseline the other three justify their cost against.

The roster itself is not duplicated here. It lives in policy/registry.MODELS, which impress-a models prints and tests/test_reasoner_registry.py checks — a table in prose is a claim nobody runs, and this page once described as "implemented" something nobody could run (backlog C5). For each model's halves, call count and status, run impress-a models or see control-models.md, which also covers what each model is shown, what it may choose, how its reply is constrained, and which campaign fields reach a half. For the pipeline all of them drive — caller inputs to specified targets to a programmed Stage — see resolution.md.

docs.title: Two contracts, and why not one
docs.text:
class Specifier(Protocol):
    name: str
    async def initial_spec(self, goal: Goal) -> Spec: ...
    async def revise(self, spec: Spec, ev: SpecEvidence) -> SpecRevision: ...
    async def satisfied(self, spec: Spec, ev: SpecEvidence) -> list[str]: ...

class Planner(Protocol):
    name: str
    async def plan(self, spec: Spec, ctx: PlanningContext) -> Stage | None: ...
    async def replan(self, stage, rejection, spec, ctx) -> Stage | None: ...

There was one contract, decide(obs) -> Decision, and it was deleted in phase 11. It answered "what should the campaign be trying to achieve" and "which tool should run next" in a single call, so nothing in a transcript could say which half of a control model earned its cost — and that is precisely what a four-arm comparison of control models has to be able to say.

A reasoner still emits abstract intent, never a concrete DAG: a Stage of TaskMappings, which the composer turns into a typed graph. That is what keeps a reasoner out of tool-invocation details and genuinely swappable, and tests/test_layering.py asserts the import contract that enforces it — policy may import core and nothing else.

replan is the counterpart of the old mandatory on_rejected: validation can refuse a composed graph, and every Planner needs a defined answer to "your proposed experiment is illegal, too expensive, or type-incoherent". Returning None — "I have no better Stage" — is a valid answer and ends the campaign with the gate that refused it named.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text:
Implement the two protocols — or subclass BaseSpecifier/BasePlanner, whose defaults are a fixed Spec and a planner that gives up loudly — then add a row to policy/registry.MODELS with both builders. Nothing else changes.

from impress_a.core.goal import Goal
from impress_a.core.spec import Spec, Stage
from impress_a.policy import registry as reasoners     # policy/__init__ re-exports nothing
from impress_a.policy.planner import BasePlanner, PlanningContext
from impress_a.policy.planners import ThresholdPlanner
from impress_a.policy.specifier import BaseSpecifier, SpecEvidence


class MySpecifier(BaseSpecifier):
    name = "mine-spec"

    async def initial_spec(self, goal: Goal) -> Spec:
        ...                      # Goal -> Spec; see policy/specifiers/explicit.py
    # `revise` defaults to "nothing has changed my mind", which is the common case, and
    # `satisfied` to the rule-driven answer off the data registry. Overriding the second
    # means arguing a campaign's stop condition rather than computing it.


class MyPlanner(BasePlanner):
    name = "mine-plan"

    def __init__(self, stages: list[str] | None = None, base_replicas: int = 0) -> None:
        # Type-driven chain resolution and typed port wiring are correctness, not
        # strategy: compose them rather than reimplementing them, as models A, B and C do.
        self._mechanics = ThresholdPlanner(
            stages=stages, **({"base_replicas": base_replicas} if base_replicas else {}))

    async def plan(self, spec: Spec, ctx: PlanningContext) -> Stage | None:
        return await self._mechanics.plan(spec, ctx, lineages=2)


reasoners.MODELS["mine"] = reasoners.ReasonerModel(
    letter="mine", name="my control model", mode="autonomous",
    llm_calls=0, llm_shape="none", status="implemented",
    specifier=lambda o: MySpecifier(),
    planner=lambda o: MyPlanner(stages=o.stages, base_replicas=o.replicas),
    note="what is true of this model that a reader would otherwise have to discover")

ReasonerOptions (o above) is the only configuration a builder sees, and cli.POLICIES is derived from MODELS, so the letter becomes a valid --model with no second list to update. A builder that needs something only CampaignSpec has wants another ReasonerOptions field, not an import — policy may import core only.

docs.title: Composable wrappers
docs.text:
A half is decorated rather than subclassed. impress_a.policy.wrappers provides:

  • StageGuard — an unconditional external guard on a Planner half, attached by the CLI unless --no-guard is passed. It carries forbid_tools and refuses rather than edits: dropping a forbidden tool would leave a hole where a producer was, and a Stage is wired by port, so removing a task leaves its consumers pointing at nothing. Two of its predecessor's three corrections moved somewhere they cannot be bypassed — the replica cap is applied by the executor against the campaign's own replicas, and a task serving no objective is refused by the Reviewer's coverage gate — because --no-guard could switch both off and should never have been able to. forbid_tools itself is a stopgap for phase 10's gate 6, which refuses a mock-toolkit node under tool_delivery: real and cannot be disabled at all.
  • LoggingSpecifier / LoggingPlanner — provenance decorators, recording that a half authored a revision or a Stage. Not redundant with the executor's own records, which say what it applied: the four-arm comparison reads the second to tell a model that proposed nothing from one whose proposals were refused.
  • NullSpecifier / NullPlanner — the no-op baseline. An empty Spec makes complete() true, so the campaign ends through the designed path rather than a Stop the driver must recognise.
pair.planner = StageGuard(pair.planner, forbid_tools=("mock_noodle",))

docs.title: Degraded mode is declared, not improvised
docs.text:
Every model that depends on something outside the job has a defined answer when it does not arrive, and the transition is an explicit logged state change — never a silent no-op that leaves an allocation idling while the campaign quietly stops adapting. reasoning.degraded writes one event name whatever degraded, so one query over transitions finds them all.

Which models, and what each one does, is in control-models.md. Read it there rather than here: this section used to say "Models B and C" and omit model A's rule cascade, and to describe a fallback as what a caller timeout activates when on_timeout in fact defaults to stop and ExternalPlanner refuses fallback unless one is declared (policy/planners/external.py:56).

docs.title: 2. The interface frontend — control-plane adapters
docs.text:
One transport-agnostic protocol; adapters translate transport only (decision 0007). No adapter may add an operation absent from the core, or the semantics fork between consumers.

Operation Purpose submit / pause / resume / stop Lifecycle observe Returns the same CampaignObservation an in-process half is given events Append-only stream with a resumable cursor steer Inject a directive — this is model C's planning call, routed to a half by its role key artifacts / provenance Retrieve results and the audit trail ingest_measurement Out-of-band P8 arrival; accepted even after termination infer One prompt to the campaign's locally hosted reasoner, answered as text

infer is in the core protocol, and therefore in every adapter, for the reason decision 0007 gives: an operation that only one transport carries forks the semantics. It also makes a split that is easy to miss — the model runs on the execution side, as a prompt_task on the engine's ai route, sharing that process's GPUs; only the prompt and the answer cross the socket. A reasoner in the control process therefore decides where the campaign goes while its weights sit beside the tools. A campaign that declares no local model refuses the call rather than falling back to a hosted one.

The observe symmetry is the point: an external caller, an LLM oracle and a user-written half all consume the identical observation and answer in the identical vocabulary — a SpecRevision from the Specifier side, a candidate Stage from the Planner side. "Informed monitoring" means parity of evidence, not a progress bar.

Adapter Status Fits in-process implemented HITL agents co-located in the job; tests; the reference implementation HTTP + SSE implemented (control/http.py) A reasoner outside the allocation; pipelining-as-a-service MCP not yet built An external agent driving a campaign, submit-and-poll

The HTTP adapter is exercised end to end by tests/test_http_adapter.py on loopback, deliberately: a transport nothing runs looks finished while rotting. It is built on asyncio.start_server rather than a web framework, speaks JSON plus one SSE stream, and is not public-facing — no auth, no TLS, bind it to localhost or a private interface.

Run operations are part of the core protocol, not something a transport adds: submit_run, list_runs, run_result, cancel_run. Admission is synchronous — 202 with a run id, or 409 with the ValidationFailure that refused it — because a rejection severed from the request that caused it leaves nothing to bound retries against.

docs.title: Steering carries no privilege
docs.text: A caller's directive is composed, type-checked, gated and budget-checked exactly as any Planner's Stage is — including the Reviewer's coverage check against the applied Spec. A rejection comes back to the caller through replan with the gate and the reason, for another turn. A caller may add and delete objectives but may not declare one satisfied: satisfaction is computed, not asserted (see resolution.md step 8).

docs.title: The substrate beneath the two axes
docs.text: Backends are selected by name from site configuration and resolved through rhapsody.backends.get_backend(), so no backend class is named outside exec/backend.py: concurrent for laptop and mock, dragon / radical / dask on HPC. That name selects the campaign's compute route; the same engine also carries local for adapters and QC, and ai when a local reasoner is declared.

docs.title: Running the two processes
docs.text:
The interface frontend described above is reachable from a shell as of phase 7 of plans/control-plane-refactor.md. Until then it was reachable only from tests/, and this document described it as implemented anyway (backlog C5).

impress-a serve campaigns/<spec>.yaml            # execution: executor, Reviewer, Deployer,
                                                 # stage executor, the one asyncflow engine.
                                                 # No reasoner.
# it prints: campaign <id> serving on http://127.0.0.1:<port>
impress-a control --connect <url> --campaign <id> --model D

What the split is and is not for. It is tempting to read it as the thing that keeps reasoning from blocking execution. That independence is already there in one process: impress-a run races the executor's pump against the reasoner's conduct as two asyncio tasks, and the shipped test for this seam (tests/test_split_process.py) exercises the same property either way — "in one process that independence is a property of the loop; across a socket it is a property of the process boundary." What the boundary adds is tolerance of a reasoner that blocks synchronously, and honesty for model C, where an external caller really is a separate program. Note also what does not move: the Spec Loop and the Planning Loop are co-resident because a plan consumes the revision just made, and the Reviewer and Deployer stay execution-side because the dry-run instantiates task agents and needs the toolkit. See decision 0015.

Four more things worth knowing before using it.

Loopback is the security boundary. The plane has no auth and no TLS, so both ends belong on the same compute node; --host exists for a deliberate choice rather than a casual one (backlog C7).

The execution side keeps the engine, and only the engine's loop matters. WorkflowEngine.__init__ captures the loop it is built on, and an engine built elsewhere dispatches nothing while looking healthy - two allocations were lost to that. The control process has its own loop and never touches an engine, which is why it is free to have one.

A lost control process drains and stops. control_liveness_timeout_s on the campaign spec bounds the silence; on expiry the executor stops admitting, lets in-flight work finish and be absorbed, and stops with a reason naming the loss. Draining rather than aborting is deliberate: cancellation is advisory, so that work will finish whether or not anyone collects it.

The bound arms only once a plane has registered, and is suspended while work is in flight. Both conditions were learned the expensive way: in a single-process campaign the "caller" is the role driver in the same process, silent exactly when it is busy awaiting the tasks it just asked for, and job 23671367 lost three arms after one cycle each to a 120 s bound against ~180 s of normal task time.

impress-a run --model C is refused, because run attaches no plane and model C means an external caller steers. It used to time out every five seconds and run its fallback, reporting a model-D campaign as model C (backlog C6).

docs.title: Invocation: from a tool spec to a running command
docs.text:
resolution.md ends with an admitted graph, and observation.md begins when a run is absorbed. This page is the part between: how one node of that graph — a tool id and a parameter dict — becomes a command line running on a compute node, and what is written down about it.

Every step says what it takes, who owns it, what it produces and what refuses it, in the order a task executes them. If this page and the code disagree, the code is right and this page is a bug.

Two things to read it for. Knowing what the system actually executes, from the source rather than from a finished run's logs — step 4 is the answer, one table per tool, each anchored to the single function that builds that tool's command. And adding or changing a tool safely, for which authoring-tools.md is the how-to and this page is the reason behind each rule in it.

The one fact to carry through the rest: a spec declares what a tool accepts; it does not declare what the tool runs. There is no command template in spec.yaml. The executable, the flag names, the config-file schema and the environment contract live in Python, in the adapter entry: points at — and in exactly one function of it.

toolkits/<tk>/tools/<id>/spec.yaml ──→ ToolSpec                              step 0
ToolSpec.entry ──importlib──→ a TaskAgent subclass (the adapter)             step 1
TaskGraph node ──node_task──→ TaskRequest + Placement    (a `local` thread)  step 2
TaskRequest.params ──parameterize──→ resolved params      (= the dry run)    step 3
resolved params ──<tool>_command()──→ argv                 (pure, in Python) step 4
argv ──run_cmd → Launcher──→ an executable task on `compute`, placed         step 5
files in work/<tool>_<node>/ ──post_process──→ ArtifactRefs, metrics, QC     step 6
Launcher.records ──→ provenance/tasks.jsonl `commands`                       step 7

Anchors are relative to agent/src/impress_a/.

docs.title: Step 0 — what a spec says about invocation, and what it does not
docs.text:
In: toolkits/<toolkit>/tools/<id>/spec.yaml. Owner: tools/spec.ToolSpec:109. Out: the typed contract every later step reads.

declared what it does for invocation entry: (:131) the dotted path of the adapter class — step 1 parameters, frozen_parameters the only keys a node may set, with their bounds — step 3 inputs / outputs ports which upstream file the adapter opens, and the type its results are filed under — steps 4 and 6 resources gpus decides whether the command is pinned to a device; walltime_s becomes its timeout — step 5 qc_gates, metrics what the adapter's return value is held to — step 6

Not declared, anywhere in a spec: the executable, its flags, its environment variables, its container image, its working directory. ToolSpec has no field for any of them. So a spec can be valid, load cleanly and be planned against while naming a parameter no command ever receives — finding 2 — and nothing at load time can compare a spec with the CLI it fronts.

docs.title: Step 1 — entry: becomes a class
docs.text:
In: a tool id. Owner: tools/registry.Registry.agent_for:90. Out: a TaskAgent subclass.

mod, _, cls = spec.entry.rpartition(".")
return getattr(importlib.import_module(mod), cls)

An ordinary import, so the adapter has to be importable from the campaign's environment: toolkit directories are not put on sys.path. Every shipped tool points into the package (impress_a.tools.<toolkit>_agents). A spec with no entry: gets EchoTaskAgent (tools/agent.py:266), which runs nothing.

Adapters keep heavy imports (PyRosetta, gemmi, Biopython) inside run(), never at module scope. This import happens at load, on a login node, and in the dry run; a module-level import pyrosetta would cost minutes there and fail where PyRosetta is not installed.

docs.title: Step 2 — a graph node becomes a request, and a placement
docs.text:
In: an admitted TaskGraph. Owner: runtime/executor._dispatch:1036 → exec/stage.StageExecutor.submit:119 → exec/dispatch.node_task:144. Out: one TaskRequest (tools/agent.py:28) and one Placement (exec/resources.py:86) per node.

node_task is the single factory for every node of every graph — there is no per-tool and no per-pattern dispatch (finding 6). For each node it builds:

field of TaskRequest from tool, params the node, i.e. the planner's TaskMapping with the campaign's params: merged under it (resolution.md step 6) node_id <run_label>:<task id> — also the name of the task's work directory seed the lineage's seed, from the composer inputs, input_ports the composer's typed wiring: this tool's own input port → the upstream payload, and which of its output ports was meant seed_inputs artifacts from outside the graph: the parent design a refinement starts from gpu_index informational only; the placement is what pins

The Placement is decided here, once per node: the lineage's GPU (round-robin over site.gpus_per_node, and only if the tool declares gpus > 0), a host, and the thread share.

A node is two kinds of engine work, and this is the step that splits them. The adapter runs as a function task on the engine's local route (exec/dispatch.py:222) — a thread in the campaign process. Each command it starts is a separate task on the compute route (step 5). So nothing about the adapter is pickled, and the backend schedules binaries rather than an opaque Python callable.

docs.title: Step 3 — parameters are resolved, and that is all admission proved
docs.text:
In: TaskRequest.params. Owner: tools/agent.TaskAgent.parameterize:151, inherited by every adapter. Out: the params dict run() receives.

  1. Start from the spec's defaults — only those that are not null. A parameter whose default is null (seed, everywhere) is simply absent, which is why adapters read it with params.get("seed").
  2. For each key the node set: refuse it if it is in frozen_parameters, refuse it if the spec does not declare it, refuse it if ParameterSpec.validate_value (tools/spec.py:57) rejects its type, choice or range. Otherwise it overrides the default.
  3. If the request carries a seed, the spec declares seed, and the node did not set one: seed = req.seed % 2**31.

Each refusal is a ValueError naming the tool and the key. These are the same rules gate 3 applied at admission; this is the second, authoritative application, in the process that is about to act on them.

The dry-run gate is this step and nothing after it. compose/validate.Validator.dry_run:186 calls agent.dry_run (tools/agent.py:260) — pre_process then parameterize — on a TaskRequest holding only the tool and its params: no inputs, no work directory, no seed. An admitted graph has therefore been shown to have legal parameter values. Whether the binary exists, the environment variable is set, or the flag is one the real CLI has, admission never asked (finding 1). impress-a preflight and impress-a validate-tasks ask it, outside the loop.

docs.title: Step 4 — the adapter builds the command
docs.text:
In: resolved params and the request. Owner: each adapter's run(), which is the only method an adapter overrides — and inside it, one pure function per tool that returns the argv. Out: a list[str].

run() does four things in order: check the environment and fail loudly if a variable is unset; stage files into the task's work directory (workdir_for, step 6) and find its inputs (input_path(req, port)); call its command builder; hand the result to run_cmd. The builder takes params and paths as arguments, reads no environment and touches no disk, so the command below can be read — and is tested — without a binary, a GPU or an allocation.

Where the executable comes from is never the spec and never sites/*.yaml:

tool executable supplied by rfd3_design apptainer exec … <image> rfd3 design apptainer on PATH; image from $FOUNDRY_SIF_PATH ligandmpnn_design <python> mpnn_run.py <checkout> sys.executable; checkout from $MPNN_DIR boltz_predict boltz predict boltz on PATH (the campaign's venv); weights from $BOLTZ_CACHE packmin, fastrelax, filter_shape <python> worker.py sys.executable; PyRosetta is an import inside the worker

scripts/delta_env_setup.sh is what sets those variables on Delta.

docs.title: rfd3_design — tools/rfd3_agents.rfd3_command:198
docs.text:
apptainer exec --nv --bind <tree>:<tree> … $FOUNDRY_SIF_PATH \
  rfd3 design out_dir=<work> inputs=<work>/<staged spec>.json skip_existing=False \
  dump_trajectories=False prevalidate_inputs=True \
  diffusion_batch_size=<num_designs> inference_sampler.num_timesteps=<diffusion_steps> \
  [seed=<seed>]
parameter becomes input_spec_path inputs= — not the file itself but a copy staged into the work directory with its relative paths made absolute (_inputs_with_absolute_paths:143) num_designs diffusion_batch_size= diffusion_steps inference_sampler.num_timesteps= seed seed=, when set

rfd3 design takes Hydra overrides, not --flags. Binds are $WORK_DIR, the input spec's directory and the work directory, de-duplicated (_binds:172). Environment: the campaign's, minus PYTHONPATH / PYTHONUSERBASE / PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE, plus PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1 (_container_env:28), so the container imports its own Python stack. No cwd.

docs.title: ligandmpnn_design — tools/ligandmpnn_agents.ligandmpnn_command:133
docs.text:
<sys.executable> <work>/mpnn_run.py $MPNN_DIR --model_type ligand_mpnn \
  --checkpoint_ligand_mpnn $MPNN_DIR/model_params/ligandmpnn_v_32_010_25.pt \
  --checkpoint_path_sc     $MPNN_DIR/model_params/ligandmpnn_sc_v_32_002_16.pt \
  --pdb_path <upstream backbone> --out_folder <work> \
  --temperature <temperature> --batch_size <batch_size> --number_of_batches <number_of_batches> \
  [--seed <seed>] \
  [--pack_side_chains 1 --pack_with_ligand_context 1 --number_of_packs_per_design 1] \
  [--fixed_residues <fixed_residues>]
parameter becomes temperature, batch_size, number_of_batches the flags of the same name pack_side_chains when true, the three packing flags, each fixed at 1 fixed_residues --fixed_residues, when non-empty seed --seed, when set num_seqs nothing — declared, validated, never passed (finding 2)

mpnn_run.py is MPNN_SHIM (:69), written into the work directory at run time: it patches the numpy aliases LigandMPNN's vendored openfold still uses and then runs $MPNN_DIR/run.py. --pdb_path is the artifact wired to this tool's backbone port. Runs with cwd=$MPNN_DIR and the campaign's whole environment.

docs.title: boltz_predict — tools/boltz_agents.boltz_command:112, boltz_input:93
docs.text:
boltz predict <work>/boltz_input.yaml --out_dir <work>/out --cache $BOLTZ_CACHE \
  --devices 1 --accelerator gpu --diffusion_samples <diffusion_samples> \
  --output_format pdb --no_kernels [--seed <seed>] [--use_msa_server]

Two parameters reach the tool through a config file rather than a flag:

parameter becomes diffusion_samples --diffusion_samples seed --seed, when set use_msa_server --use_msa_server, and msa: auto (else empty) in boltz_input.yaml ligand_smiles a ligand: {id: [B], smiles: …} entry in boltz_input.yaml, when non-empty

The protein sequence in that file is extracted from the artifact on the structure port. A flock on the cache is held across the first run, because Boltz extracts its component dictionary inside boltz predict. No cwd; the campaign's whole environment.

docs.title: packmin, fastrelax, filter_shape — tools/rosetta_agents.worker_command:278
docs.text:
<sys.executable> <work>/worker.py <positional args…> <work>/result.json

PyRosetta is a Python API, not a binary, so each tool writes a worker script (_PACKMIN_WORKER :20, _FASTRELAX_WORKER :72, _FILTER_SHAPE_WORKER :171) into its work directory and runs it in a fresh interpreter. Its arguments are positional:

tool builder arguments, in order packmin packmin_args:331 structure, out pdb, cycles, seed|none, ligand_params_path|none fastrelax fastrelax_args:337 structure, out pdb, relax_cycles, nstruct, seed|none, ligand_params_path|none filter_shape filter_shape_args:343 structure, ligand_params_path|none

The flags Rosetta itself sees are assembled inside the worker and passed to pyrosetta.init: -mute all, plus -run:constant_seed -run:jran <seed> when a seed was given, plus -extra_res_fa <ligand_params_path> -ignore_unrecognized_res -ignore_zero_occupancy when a ligand params file was. No cwd, and no env (finding 5).

docs.title: Mocks stop here
docs.text:
The mock adapters (tools/mock_agents.py, tools/mock_smb_agents.py) override run() and return seeded draws. They never call run_cmd, so steps 5 and 7 do not happen for them: no executable task is submitted and their commands list is empty.

What refuses a change here: tests/test_real_toolkits.py pins each builder's argv at its spec defaults, and test_every_declared_parameter_reaches_its_command compares each spec's parameters against the keys its builder reads. A parameter that is declared and unread must be added to that test's exemption table with a reason.

docs.title: Step 5 — the command becomes an engine task
docs.text:
In: run_cmd(argv, cwd=, env=, timeout_s=). Owner: tools/_subprocess.run_cmd:48 → exec/launch.Launcher.run:123 → _submit_and_wait:194. Out: (stdout, stderr), or a SubprocessError carrying the command line, the exit code and both streams.

run_cmd does not start a process. Inside a node it finds that node's Launcher in the LAUNCHER context variable (tools/_subprocess.py:30, set at exec/dispatch.py:198) and hands the command over; the Launcher submits it to the engine as an executable_task on the compute route. A context variable rather than an argument, so that no adapter can forget to pass it — one that shelled out with subprocess directly would run its binary on the campaign host, unplaced, and nothing would say so.

What is added to the adapter's argv on the way, by backend (exec/resources.Placement.describe:116):

concurrent backend Dragon walltime argv is prefixed timeout --kill-after=10 <walltime_s> the task's own timeout, walltime_s + 10; never the wrapper GPU CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<index> in the environment Policy(gpu_affinity=[index]); the variable is not set threads OMP_/MKL_/OPENBLAS_/NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS, OMP_WAIT_POLICY=PASSIVE the same environment the adapter's env, or os.environ, replaced whole only what differs from the campaign's, merged into the node's concurrency bounded by workers (exec/stage.command_slots:44) the backend's own

The walltime only reaches a command because each adapter passes timeout_s=spec.resources.walltime_s; a run_cmd call without it is unbounded. Why the wrapper is refused under Dragon, and what a cancel does and does not kill, are in middleware-integration.md and limitations.md and are not repeated here.

Outside a node — impress-a preflight, the gate fixtures, a direct test — no Launcher is set and run_cmd runs the child itself with asyncio.create_subprocess_exec.

docs.title: Step 6 — files come back as typed results
docs.text:
In: whatever the command wrote, and run()'s return dict. Owner: tools/_subprocess.workdir_for:159, then tools/agent.TaskAgent.post_process:203. Out: a TaskResult.

Every real adapter writes under workdir_for(req, prefix):

<campaign process CWD>/work/<prefix>_<run_label>_<task id>/

created on demand and never cleaned — it holds the campaign's results. The root is the process CWD because TaskRequest.workdir is never set (finding 4); on Delta the launcher has already changed into a per-job directory on shared storage.

The adapter reads its tool's native output there (a sidecar JSON, FASTA headers, a confidence file, the worker's result.json) and returns {"outputs": …, "metrics": …} plus whatever keys its gates inspect. post_process then, without the adapter's help:

  • turns each output into an ArtifactRef whose type is the spec's declared output port (_as_artifacts:175); a Path is hashed as a file, anything else is an inline value, and an output name the spec does not declare raises;
  • runs the spec's QC gates over the return value;
  • records the declared cost beside the measured one.

An adapter omits a metric it could not read; the metrics_reported gate is what turns the omission into an integrity failure rather than a low score.

docs.title: Step 7 — what is written down
docs.text:
In: the Launcher's records and the TaskResult. Owner: runtime/executor._log_task_telemetry:1319. Out: one row per task in provenance/tasks.jsonl.

question where it is answered which parameters did the planner choose? provenance/stages.jsonl, mappings what command ran? provenance/tasks.jsonl, commands where and for how long? the same row: host, pid, cuda_visible_devices, wall_s, phases what did it write? work/<prefix>_<node>/, and the node's ArtifactRefs in results.jsonl

commands has one entry per run_cmd call, in order, as the backend was handed it:

{"argv": ["timeout", "--kill-after=10", "900", "apptainer", "exec", "--nv", "…"],
 "cwd": null, "backend": "concurrent", "host": null, "gpu_index": 0,
 "placement_env": {"OMP_NUM_THREADS": "4", "…": "…", "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES": "0"},
 "timeout_s": 900.0, "exit_code": 0, "queued_s": 0.01, "ran_s": 44.9}

argv is the realized form of what step 4's builder returned — the timeout wrapper is there when one was added — so the page above can be checked against a run instead of trusted. The environment recorded is only what the placement added: adapters pass their child a copy of os.environ, and provenance is not the place for whatever that holds.

docs.title: What invocation does not enforce
docs.text:
Seven places where the implementation does not do what a reader of the design would reasonably assume. Each is verified against the source at the anchor given. Read this section before changing any step above.

# the reasonable assumption what the code does anchor item 1 An admitted graph is one whose commands can run Admission's dry run calls parameterize on a request with no inputs, no work directory and no seed. It proves parameter values are legal and nothing about the binary, the environment variable, the container image or whether a flag exists. Four defects reached hardware through this gap; preflight and validate-tasks exist because of it, and run outside the loop compose/validate.py:186-195, tools/agent.py:260 J1 2 A parameter a spec declares changes what the tool does Nothing connects a spec's parameters to its adapter. ligandmpnn_design.num_seqs is validated, shown to a planner, written to stages provenance, and passed to no command. A test now refuses a new one; this one is exempted by name tools/ligandmpnn_agents.py:133, tests/test_real_toolkits.py (_NOT_IN_THE_COMMAND) J2 3 Asking a tool for N candidates yields N to choose from rfd3_design passes num_designs as the diffusion batch size and converts cif_models[0] only: N are paid for and one is kept. LigandMPNN and Boltz do select. The spec says so, and the planner may not move it (resolution.md step 6) tools/rfd3_agents.py:198, toolkits/rfd3/tools/rfd3_design/spec.yaml — 4 Where a tool writes is the campaign's decision StageExecutor is built without workdir, so TaskRequest.workdir is always None and every task writes under the process CWD. Correct only because the launcher scripts cd first; nothing in the package enforces it runtime/executor.py:1459, tools/_subprocess.py:159 J4 5 Every tool's child sees the same environment contract The three Rosetta tools pass no env to run_cmd; the others pass child_env(req). Equivalent today on both backends, by the fallback in Placement.describe rather than by intent tools/rosetta_agents.py:290, exec/resources.py:116 J5 6 A tool's compute pattern selects how it is dispatched exec/ never reads ToolSpec.pattern. Every node takes the one path in step 2. Pattern is read by gates 2 and 4 only — whether QC gates are mandatory, whether P6 was scheduled, whether external submission is allowed exec/dispatch.py:144, compose/validate.py:94,121,125 J6 7 Every command a campaign ran is on the record A task whose adapter raises records its error string — which contains the failing command line — and no commands list; a command run outside the engine records nothing; and the base environment is never recorded, by decision exec/dispatch.py:213, exec/launch.py:121 J7

Two properties that are by design and are listed so they are not mistaken for the above. The executable's location is an environment contract rather than a spec field or a sites/*.yaml entry, because the right value is machine-specific and a spec is shared across machines; the cost is that only impress-a preflight checks it (backlog J3). And filter_shape returns its input structure as its output: it is a filter, so the artifact it passes downstream is the one it was given, with the same content hash.

docs.title: Seeing it on disk
docs.text:
impress-a mock-lab --only arms --stage sweep writes one campaign per arm in about half a minute with no allocation, and shows steps 2, 3, 6 and 7 — with commands: [], because mocks run none. Steps 4 and 5 need a tool that shells out: tests/test_placement.py runs real commands through a real engine on a laptop, and a Delta run shows the science tools.

step where it landed 2 provenance/graphs.jsonl — the admitted graph, each node with its tool; provenance/tasks.jsonl — each task's lineage and seed 3 provenance/stages.jsonl, mappings — the parameter vector before defaults are filled in; a refusal carries its gate 4, 5 provenance/tasks.jsonl, commands[].argv — the builder's argv, plus the timeout wrapper where one was added 5 the same entry's backend, gpu_index, placement_env, queued_s, ran_s, exit_code; telemetry/, when on, has a span per command named <node>.<program> 6 work/<prefix>_<node>/ — the staged inputs (boltz_input.yaml, mpnn_run.py, worker.py) and the tool's own outputs 7 provenance/tasks.jsonl — one row per task

A step whose output cannot be pointed at in one of those files is a step this page has described wrongly.

docs.title: Middleware Integration
docs.text: How IMPRESS-A sits on radical.asyncflow and rhapsody, and the behaviours that are easy to get wrong.

docs.title: The seam
docs.text:
campaign manager  ── validated DAG ──►  radical.asyncflow.WorkflowEngine
        ▲                                   │      │        │
        │                             compute    local      ai
        │                          (Dragon or   (thread   (rhapsody
        │                           Concurrent)  pool)     vLLM)
        └──── typed results, QC ───────┴────────┴─────────┘

One engine per campaign, carrying named routes. exec/backend.make_engine builds compute first, so it is the default; local is asyncflow's own LocalExecutionBackend over a thread pool, for work that must not be pickled and must not sit on the engine's loop; ai is added only when the campaign declares a locally hosted reasoner. A decorator names its route (backend="compute"), and an unknown name fails at decoration rather than at submission.

The agent owns the WorkflowEngine directly, and keeps several graphs in flight on it at once. StageExecutor.submit (exec/stage.py) runs a graph as one asyncflow block and returns the block's future without awaiting it; collect waits for one. Inside a node, the adapter runs on the engine's local route and each tool command is an executable task on compute, placed per backend (exec/launch.py, exec/resources.py). Backends are constructed by exec/backend.py and named only in site configuration.

Two things make concurrent graphs safe on one engine, both verified against 0.7.0. Task names come from fn.__name__ and collide across graphs, but they are only labels: components are keyed by a unique uid and dependencies resolve by future identity, never by name. And workflow_id= tags every task of a run, which is what keeps a log readable when two identical chains are running — though asyncflow exposes no way to look tasks up by that tag, so the run table stays the index.

docs.title: Runtime-composed DAGs
docs.text:
A graph described as data is dispatched with one generic factory — no code generation:

async def _run(*deps):
    ...
_run.__name__ = node_id            # asyncflow reads the task name from __name__
task = flow.function_task(_run)
futures[tid] = task(*[futures[d] for d in deps])   # unawaited futures express edges

Two idioms, both needed and not interchangeable:

Idiom Expresses passing unawaited futures as call arguments edges in the DAG asyncio.gather awaiting independent work (replica fan-out)

docs.title: A node is two kinds of engine work
docs.text:
The factory above builds only half of a node. The adapter — pre-process, parameterize, post-process and the deterministic QC gates — is a function_task on local, a thread in the campaign process under its own asyncio.run. Every command that adapter starts through tools/_subprocess.run_cmd is a separate executable_task on compute, submitted by exec/launch.Launcher and found through a LAUNCHER contextvar rather than passed down every call site.

That split is what puts a binary where the placement says and keeps the adapter's Python off both the engine's loop and the backend's pickle boundary. An adapter that shelled out any other way would run its binary on the campaign host, unplaced and uncounted.

A whole Stage is one @flow.block (exec/stage.StageExecutor): the block's future is the graph's result, its members inherit its uid as workflow_id, and cancelling it cascades to every unfinished member with each cancel sent to the backend that member was routed to (0.7.0, asyncflow #118).

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Rhapsody backends are awaitable and must be awaited. __await__ triggers _async_init(), which registers the backend's task states with StateMapper. Constructing one synchronously appears to succeed and then fails later with an unrelated-looking error:

backend = await ConcurrentExecutionBackend(ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4))  # correct
backend = ConcurrentExecutionBackend(ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4))
# ... later: ValueError: Backend 'concurrentexecutionbackend' not registered. Available backends: []

Real backends live in rhapsody, not asyncflow. asyncflow exports only NoopExecutionBackend and LocalExecutionBackend. ConcurrentExecutionBackend, DragonExecutionBackend, RadicalExecutionBackend and DaskExecutionBackend come from rhapsody.backends, and are resolved by name through rhapsody.backends.get_backend() so that site configuration, not source code, selects them.

Task decorators accept no name= kwarg. flow.function_task(name=...) raises TypeError. Setting __name__ before decorating is what allows a single generic factory to serve every node.

Resource shapes are not portable. RADICAL takes {"ranks", "gpus_per_rank"}; Dragon takes process_template / process_templates. There is no shared vocabulary, so exec/resources.py owns the translation from ToolSpec.resources. Treat site-level resource defaults as required, not convenience.

What a node needs is decided once, at submission (Placement), and rendered per command (Placement.describe), because a tool's commands differ in environment and working directory but share their GPU and their thread share. Two asymmetries are easy to get backwards:

  • Who sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. Under Dragon, nothing here does: the placement carries Policy(host_name=…, gpu_affinity=[g]) and Dragon sets the variable itself. Setting it in the template's env does not work — local services merges the template env and applies the policy layout afterwards, and a policy with no gpu_affinity resolves to every GPU on the node. On the concurrent backend the env is the only pinning mechanism, so there it carries the variable.
  • How much of the environment travels. The concurrent backend replaces a child's environment, so it is given the whole thing. Dragon merges a template's env into the target node's own, so it is given only what differs from ours — sending the head node's entire environment would overwrite the remote node's.

Thread caps (thread_caps, thread_share) are part of a placement and therefore per command. They used to be written into the campaign process's own environment at start-up and inherited by every child, which meant one campaign's caps leaked into its siblings under an enclosing manager.

asyncflow provides no retry primitive and no durable job state. Engine state is in-process and cleared at shutdown. Retry policy and the external-job ledger (exec/ledger.py) are ours.

Dragon backend construction is fully synchronous and can block the event loop indefinitely. DragonExecutionBackend.__init__ builds Dragon's own Batch() (results DDict, GPU-affinity worker pool, telemetry) with no await points - a stall there blocks the calling thread's event loop entirely, so nothing else on that loop (a heartbeat task, an asyncio.wait_for deadline) gets a chance to run until Batch() returns. Measured, not theoretical: job 22318678 ran its full 2-hour SLURM allocation this way, producing only Dragon's own internal infra-connect log lines the whole time - the campaign's own heartbeat never fired once. exec/backend.make_engine_bounded works around this by running the construction on a dedicated OS thread, so a timeout and heartbeat on the calling loop stay effective regardless of what the backend's own constructor does.

The engine and a backend's async init belong to the loop they are built on. WorkflowEngine captures self.loop = get_event_loop_or_raise(...) in __init__ and _start_async_components schedules its run-component dispatch task on exactly that loop; a rhapsody backend likewise captures its own loop for cross-thread result delivery. So an engine built on a different loop from the one that will submit to it is already dead when you get it - and it does not look dead: construction returns normally, flow.function_task decorates normally, and the first task future simply never completes. This is how the bound above went wrong: make_engine_bounded originally ran all of make_engine on the daemon thread under asyncio.run(...), whose exit cancelled run-component and closed the loop. Jobs 22328172 and 22328262 both wrote r0001 submitted to the ledger and then burned their walltime in silence. Only the synchronous _construct_backend_sync() may be offloaded; await backend and WorkflowEngine.create() run on the caller's loop. tests/test_backend_bound.py guards this the only way it can be guarded - by putting a real task through the engine.

flow, be = await make_engine_bounded("dragon", cfg, 600, 60)
assert flow.loop is asyncio.get_running_loop()   # false => every submit hangs forever

A coreutils timeout wrapper must not be used under Dragon. timeout leads its own process group; Dragon's local services reaps only its own, so a wrapped command exits, its wrapper becomes [timeout] <defunct>, and the task never reaches a terminal state. Job 23814643 hung at stage 1 exactly this way. The wrapper is applied on the concurrent backend only; Dragon is handed walltime_s + KILL_GRACE_S as the task's own timeout and enforces it itself (exec/launch.py, exec/resources.py).

Telemetry starts and stops with the engine, and its stop does not drain. flow.start_telemetry takes a checkpoint path; the executor points it at <campaign root>/telemetry/ when telemetry_checkpoint_s > 0. stop() does not forward rhapsody's drain_on_stop, so a stalled drain can only be cut short by a timeout of ours, and stopping telemetry from a task other than the one that started it makes OpenTelemetry log Failed to detach context. Counts read off a checkpoint can double-count across flushes — read a span's shape, not its totals.

LocalExecutionBackend.shutdown joins its pool synchronously on the engine loop. If an adapter thread on the local route is still waiting on a command, teardown deadlocks: the command's completion needs the loop that is blocked in the join. exec/stage._settle and Launcher.idle wait for in-flight commands before shutdown for that reason.

Version drift is real. Check the installed version before trusting any API note here; this integration was first written against radical.asyncflow 0.5.1 and rhapsody-py 0.5.0.
