Verified on 0.7.0 / 0.7.0 (2026-11-11, Python 3.12.12, both installed editable from sibling checkouts): the whole local tier is green, including the loop-ownership guard in tests/test_backend_bound.py that puts real work through a bounded engine, and job 23815248 ran the stack on Delta with dragonhpc 0.15.0. agent/pyproject.toml floors both at >=0.7.0, because the execution loop relies on 0.7.0 specifically: a cancel reaches the backend a task was routed to, a block cancel cascades to its members, future.uid exists at call time, and every task event names its real backend.

Session directories. asyncflow writes an asyncflow.session.* directory into work_dir on every engine run, and work_dir defaults to the CWD. exec/backend.make_engine and make_engine_bounded both take a work_dir and pass it to WorkflowEngine.create; the executor passes the campaign root, so the session dir sits beside that campaign's provenance. Construct an engine without one and it lands in whatever directory you ran from.

docs.title: Python floor
docs.text:
Python ≥3.11, unconditionally: radical.asyncflow and rhapsody-py 0.7.0 both require it, so the floor no longer depends on whether Dragon is in use. Dragon itself is the [dragon] extra (rhapsody-py[dragon]), which keeps CI, the laptop tier and the knob-lab notebook runnable with no Dragon installed. Heavy scientific tools run in containers or as subprocesses and do not constrain the agent environment.

The root impress package is a separate matter: it is >=3.9 with radical.pilot, and this project does not depend on it. That is the dependency firewall, not a conflict.

docs.title: The mock knob lab
docs.text:
A measuring harness, not a result. It runs the laptop surrogate of the small-molecule binding chain across a grid of knob settings, flattens what the executor wrote into four CSVs, and draws six figures from them. The whole thing finishes in about half a minute on a laptop and needs no allocation.

Read campaigns/README.md first for what the surrogate campaign is and what each knob does. This page is about the harness around it: what it runs, what it measures, and which of its numbers mean anything.

To drive it rather than read about it, Ten minutes with a mock campaign runs the four arms in Colab and walks the two traps below — the G14 stop-reason gap and the decision-0013 trust split — as a predict-then-run exercise.

docs.title: What a figure from here is allowed to claim
docs.text:
Every metric the six surrogates report is a seeded random draw (toolkits/mock/SKILL.md). A response surface drawn here is a statement about the surrogate's own arithmetic. It is not evidence about any molecule, and the disclaimer is printed on every figure from analysis/mock_lab.DISCLAIMER rather than typed into a caption a reader could drop when they paste the PNG into a slide.

What is measured honestly is the campaign's behaviour — how many cycles it took, which gate refused what, whether the Pareto front filled, how long the control plane spent deciding — because that is the same executor, the same composer, the same five gates and the same interlock the Delta arms run. A behaviour observed here is the behaviour the real campaign would show; a number observed here is not a measurement.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
impress-a mock-lab                                   # sweep, collect, figures
impress-a mock-lab --only arms --stage sweep         # the four arms, nothing else
impress-a mock-lab --stage figures                   # redraw from the tables already there
impress-a mock-lab --repeats 6 --jobs 8              # a tighter band, same wall clock

Figures need the optional extra: pip install -e ".[figures]". The sweep and collect stages do not — they write CSVs with the standard library, so a machine with no plotting stack can still produce the tables.

Output lands in campaigns/_runs/_analysis by default, which is gitignored:

manifest.json          every cell, its knob setting, its exit code, its run directory
specs/<cell>.yaml      the campaign that cell actually ran
runs/<cell>/           that campaign's own run root - provenance, ledger, trust
logs/<cell>.log        its stdout and stderr tail
tables/*.csv           lineages, tasks, cycles, campaigns, phases
figures/*.png          the six figures

docs.title: The two kinds of cell
docs.text:
Four arms, which are the settings the ten-minute activity walks through and the four hues in analysis/plot_style.py. Each is one reproducible campaign a person can re-run by hand and get back.

They are named for what the campaign DOES, not for what the surrogate reports. Every mock metric is a seeded random draw, so a name like "low-plddt" would be naming noise, while "aborted after three all-failed runs" is a control-plane outcome that reproduces. The tier each arm takes in the palette follows the same rule and is assigned once, in analysis/plot_style.py, never per figure.

Arm Setting What the campaign does baseline shipped defaults clears every bar; the Spec is satisfied; the front fills rescued difficulty: 0.55, plus diffusion_steps: 200, packmin.cycles: 5, diffusion_samples: 25 the same difficulty, bought back by three knobs hard difficulty: 0.55 acceptance shortfall; the front stays empty; trust untouched hopeless difficulty: 0.85 integrity failure; CampaignAborted after three all-failed runs

Two things the table cannot say. hard and rescued are a matched pair at identical difficulty, differing only in the three knobs raised to buy it back — which is what separates "can knobs recover this campaign?" from "is this campaign hard?". Under a one-dial sweep those two questions are the same column, which is why the pair exists as arms rather than as sweep points.

One caveat on rescued, measured from its own stages.jsonl rather than assumed: two of its three knobs only hold for cycle 1. Exploring emits no parameters, so the arm's values stand; from cycle 2 the planner escalates diffusion_steps and packmin.cycles from the tool spec's defaults (50 and 1) and the policy wins the merge, so they become 88 and 2 — below what the arm declared. diffusion_samples survives at 25 because it is a breadth knob no planner may touch. The campaign is real and the measured behaviour is real; what the label overstates is how much of it is held across cycles. Backlog G17, which is where the fix is being argued.

And hard versus hopeless is the acceptance/integrity line, not a matter of degree. Between roughly 0.5 and 0.75 the dial only misses the 0.5 acceptance threshold: the node FAILs and the pattern's trust is untouched. Above about 0.75 it drives ss_fraction under the 0.3 has_secondary_structure floor, which is an integrity failure — the node FAILs and the pattern is demoted (decision 0013). Reaching for the dial to "make the campaign fail" without noticing which kind of failure you bought is the mistake the mock toolkit exists to make visible.

Sweep cells, one campaign per knob value per repeat, each repeat under a different seed salt. These carry the ensembles: 8 lineages a cell times 3 repeats is 24 independent draws per point at the default settings.

Two deliberate differences from the shipped campaign, applied to every cell equally:

  • replicas: 4 (arms) or 8 (sweeps), because one lineage per cycle is not a distribution. This changes the pattern signature, so every cell runs untrusted under the interlock's 10% cost cap — the same interlock for all of them.
  • A sweep cell runs exactly one cycle. ThresholdSpecifier.revise adds a refinement objective as soon as the front is non-empty, so a multi-cycle cell mixes the knob's response with the planner's escalation away from it, and a sweep that cannot separate those is not a response surface.

docs.title: Isolation, and why it is not tidiness
docs.text:
Each cell runs as a subprocess of impress-a run with its own IMPRESS_A_RUN_ROOT, IMPRESS_A_TRUST_DIR and IMPRESS_A_SEED_SALT.

The trust directory is the one that bites. The trust ledger is cross-run state: a cell that promoted a pattern changes the interlock every later cell runs under, so a shared ledger makes the sweep a function of its own iteration order rather than of the knob. The salt is what makes --repeat draw different lineages instead of the same ones again (backlog G7).

The four arms always run one at a time, whatever --jobs says, because every wall-clock figure comes from them. Run eight-wide, one arm's first cycle came back at 0.10s against 1.10s for the other three — scheduling noise presented as a property of the knob setting. Sweep cells are read only for the metrics their tools drew, which CPU contention cannot change, so they run in parallel.

docs.title: The reasoner axis
docs.text:
The six surrogates mock the tools. --reasoners mocks nothing: it varies the control model above them, so the four knob arms run under each named reasoner and the lab measures the half the four-model taxonomy is actually about.

impress-a mock-lab --reasoners D --reasoners null                    # offline, free
impress-a mock-lab --reasoners D --reasoners B --model-profile beam  # live
letter what drives the campaign needs a profile repeated D ThresholdSpecifier + ThresholdPlanner; rules end to end no no null an empty Spec, so the campaign stops at cycle 0 no no A the four-node graph; two nodes call the model (hypothesize, select_tasks) yes --reasoner-repeats, default 3 B two schemas, one call each (SPEC_SCHEMA, STAGE_SCHEMA) yes --reasoner-repeats

C is absent: it needs impress-a serve plus an impress-a control sidecar waiting on the 0600 control_plane.url, which is two processes per cell, and its caller-side reasoner records have nowhere to land (backlog H8).

Sweeps stay on D whatever the axis says. They measure the surrogate's own response surface, which no reasoner changes, so running them under four models buys four readings of one piece of arithmetic.

docs.title: Three rules the live path enforces
docs.text:
A live model with no profile is refused, not quietly run. --model A without one runs its rule cascades and --model B runs RehearsalOracle. Both report zero LLM calls — which is exactly what a degraded live arm reports. A figure labelled "model B" drawn from the rehearsal is the pre-registration's §8 void outcome manufactured on purpose, so the lab exits 2 and names the models it refused, before spending anything.

One probe call before any live cell. cli._client_for opens no socket, so without this the first failure lands inside a campaign cycle, where reasoning.ask retries twice, writes reasoner_degraded and runs model D's cascade — and the campaign exits 0. Every live cell would do the same and the lab would draw a full set of figures for a model that never answered. One round trip up front is the difference between "the endpoint is down" and twenty-four quietly degraded arms.

A cap on what it may spend. --max-llm-calls (default 400), counted from what each cell actually recorded rather than estimated — a corrective retry is a second call and a degraded node is two calls that bought nothing. A cell the cap stopped is named in the manifest and carries a skipped reason, because one silently missing from a figure reads as a model that had nothing to show.

docs.title: What the lab reads about a reasoner
docs.text:
Nothing recorded a control model's behaviour until 890829d: ReasonerOptions.sink had writers throughout policy/ and no subscriber, so a campaign left no prompt, no reply, no model id, no timing and no degraded event. Two of the collected tables exist because of that fix.

  • decisions.csv — one row per LLM call: node, attempt, whether it was accepted, the model_id that answered, elapsed_s, and prompt/completion tokens as deltas. The prompt and reply bodies stay in decisions.jsonl; a CSV is for counting.
  • params.csv — the parameter vector each Planner chose, from stages.jsonl's mappings. source separates campaign from reasoner, because mappings holds the effective vector and _apply_campaign_defaults merges the campaign's params: into it before composition. Without the split every model would read as having set every knob.
  • campaigns.csv gains llm_calls, llm_retries, llm_s, llm_share, token totals, s_per_llm_call, degraded_events, and model_id — read from the records rather than from the flag the lab passed, so a cell that asked for beam and was answered by something else shows it.

Check degraded_events before reading any live arm's yield. A non-zero count means the arm fell back to model D's cascade, and what it produced is not that model's result. That is the pre-registration's void rule, enforceable for the first time now that anything writes these events.

docs.title: What the live runs found
docs.text:
Beam-501B-A23B via profile beam, 2026-11-10: model B alone (20 calls), then D + A + B at one repeat (31), then three repeats of every live cell (89 calls, 28 cells), which is the run the figures are drawn from. Zero retries and zero degraded turns in all three, and no allocation.

model D model A (live) model B (live) seconds per decision 0.33 9.23 19.36 seconds per call — 2.8 7.2 completion tokens per call — 386 1110 share of campaign wall clock at the endpoint — 84–99% 93–99% cycles run 2–4 1–1 1–6 knobs it moved 3, all quality 4, all quality 9, mostly breadth front on hard, over 3 repeats 0 of 12 3–4 of 4 0 of 16 predicted GPU-h per campaign 1.4–2.0 0.68, flat 0.68–4.1

A live model is not a function, and three repeats is the smallest number that shows it. Model B ran the rescued arm as one cycle with an empty front twice and as six cycles with four designs on the front once — same arm, same salt, same endpoint. Model A was identical in all three. Any single-repeat figure here would have been a draw reported as a property; the repeats are what let f7 and f11 draw a range instead of a bar.

A and B differ in what they are shown, not only in what they choose. Model A's parameter vector comes from parameterize, a deterministic node the model steers only by naming a strategy, and _knobs.tunable keeps breadth parameters away from it. Model B is handed the whole task card and picks for itself. So A raising four quality dials and B raising num_designs is a comparison of a filtered knob set against an unfiltered one.

Two things worth carrying off the laptop. The endpoint is the campaign on this tier: the six tools return in milliseconds and 94–99% of each live cell's wall clock was one model thinking. And model B raises breadth parameters that models A and D are forbidden to touch — num_designs to 2, 3, 4 and 8 — because OraclePlanner._prompt filters what it shows by tunable, which does not look at kind. rfd3_design's own spec records that num_designs stays at 1 because its adapter keeps index 0, and its cost_model is per invocation, so nothing prices the extra draws either. Backlog H10.

And a live Specifier can skip the abort rule. On hopeless — difficulty 0.85, the arm whose backbone breaks — model A stopped at cycle 1 on "every spec objective satisfied" with all four lineages failing the ss_fraction integrity gate and an empty front, where the deterministic control ran on and aborted on three consecutive all-failed runs. Its Specifier emitted no refinement objective, so nothing was left unsatisfied and a third cycle never came. The quality dials it had raised made the numbers good on a structure difficulty 0.85 had already destroyed — which is visible in f10, where that arm clears every band but ss_fraction.

Over three repeats it is A 3 of 3 and B 1 of 3, so it is not a model-A property: it is what any live Specifier does when it declines to add a refinement objective, and B does that one time in three. Backlog H11 — G14's mechanism with a safety consequence rather than a reporting one.

docs.title: difficulty is operator_only
docs.text:
OraclePlanner shows a live model every tunable parameter with its range and its trades sentence, and _apply_campaign_defaults states that a policy wins on any key it set. The dial reads "how hard this campaign is", 0.0 to 1.0. A model asked to satisfy the objectives turns it down, the hard arm quietly becomes the easy one, and nothing says so.

So it is marked operator_only in mock_rfd3_design/spec.yaml: the campaign may declare it, a reasoner may not propose it. Enforced in one seam, tools/view.card_for, which reports it under TaskCard.frozen and leaves it out of TaskCard.parameters — _knobs.tunable skips it, B's prompt omits it, and B's schema check refuses a reply naming it with the reason the spec gave. Gate 3 reads ToolSpec.frozen_parameters, which stays empty, so the campaign path is untouched and no seeded draw moves.

Checked rather than assumed: campaigns.csv carries difficulty_proposed, which is empty unless a reasoner's value reached a deployed stage or a rejection named the dial as frozen, and f9-knobs-moved.png asserts that it appears for nobody.

docs.title: The tables
docs.text:
File One row per Carries lineages.csv DesignNode the whole chain's metrics merged, the QC verdict, and the failed gates split into failed_integrity / failed_acceptance tasks.csv task its stage_index in the chain, verdict, gates, timing, both sides of its cost, and every metric it reported prefixed m_ cycles.csv composed graph signature, whether it was trusted, the interlock's scrutiny, the estimate, and the gate that refused it if one did campaigns.csv cell stop reason, whether it aborted, cycles, front size, verdict counts, wall clock, busy time, overhead, decisions and tasks per second phases.csv cycle where that cycle's wall clock went, segment by segment

Two things in there are easy to get subtly wrong, so they are done once and tested:

  • Busy time is a union of intervals, not a sum of durations. workers: 4 overlaps tasks, so a sum double-counts; and wall - sum can go negative and then reads as negative overhead. The union is correct at any concurrency.
  • A metric a tool did not report is None, never 0.0. A tool omits a metric it could not read (the metrics_reported invariant), and fabricating a zero turns "the tool broke" into "the design is weak".

docs.title: The figures
docs.text: File Shows f1-metric-ensembles.png each campaign objective against difficulty, mean ± 2σ population spread, with its acceptance bar and the arms marked f2-knob-response.png complex_plddt against the four knobs that have a real counterpart, on one shared y-axis so the spans are comparable f3-stage-funnel.png per-stage pass rate per arm, and the failures split into acceptance shortfalls and integrity failures f4-decision-rate.png elapsed seconds against decision index — slope is seconds per decision — and decisions/s against tasks/s f5-control-time.png where a cycle's wall clock goes, cycle 0 against every cycle after it f6-stop-vs-front.png what each arm's campaign said against what it actually had on the front f7-reasoner-yield.png front size per arm per control model — does a reasoner rescue a campaign the rules cannot? f8-decision-cost.png what one decision costs in seconds and in tokens, by who made it f9-knobs-moved.png which knobs each model moved, and how far up their declared ranges f10-protein-metrics.png every metric a live arm is tiered on, per arm per model, against tiers' own T2/T3 bands f11-predicted-cost.png what the same decisions would have cost on hardware, at the real specs' rates

docs.title: f10 and f11: the comparison as a live campaign will make it
docs.text:
analysis/compare_arms.py scores a Delta arm on two axes, and these two draw the same axes on the surrogate — with the two places the surrogate cannot follow stated rather than papered over.

f10, the protein axis. The seven metrics tiers.T2_THRESHOLDS and T3_THRESHOLDS test, read at import rather than retyped, one panel each, a mark per arm per model and the band shaded on the side that clears. What it does not draw is a tier count: the live headline is distinct_t2/distinct_t3, which is tiers after clustering at 90 % sequence identity and 2.5 Å Cα RMSD, and the surrogate emits neither a sequence nor a structure. A count here would be an upper bound wearing a measured number's name. The yield comparison stays in f7, where the denominator is the Pareto front and nothing is implied about distinctness.

f11, the cost axis. compare_arms charges an arm AllocNodes × gpus_per_node × Elapsed_h from sacct. There is no allocation here, and the laptop's clock is not a stand-in — 82–99 % of it is one model thinking, which inverts completely on hardware. What does transfer is the decision: which tools ran and how many times. Charged at the real toolkit's declared rates (rfd3 0.1 GPU-h, ligandmpnn 0.02, boltz 0.05, fastrelax 0.25 CPU-h), that is the same arithmetic gate 5 and the untrusted-pattern cap do before admitting a graph. Every number on it is labelled predicted. The mock specs' own cost models are deliberately uniform at 0.002 and carry no information, so they are not used.

It also shows H10 without having to argue it: models A and B cost the same predicted GPU-hours in every arm, because the estimate is per invocation and B's num_designs: 4 does not enter it.

f3, f4 and f5 are drawn for one control model. They pool by arm, and an arm stops being one campaign once the reasoner axis exists: averaging D's 0.14s decision with B's 20.5s one under the arm's hue measures the endpoint, not the knob. When a lab has more than one model these three keep the deterministic control — D, or the first model on the axis if D is not on it — and say so in the caption. A single-model lab is unaffected, caption included.

The control model does not get a hue. The four validated colours are spent on the four knob arms and colour follows the entity, so in f7–f9 a model takes the fill channel — hatch and face alpha inside the arm's own colour (plot_style.MODEL_FILLS). It survives every CVD simulation by construction, reads in greyscale, and the arm identity a reader learned in f1–f6 carries straight across.

Colour follows analysis/plot_style.py and means the same thing in all nine: blue is the best-performing configuration, magenta is the run that did not complete, and a sweep line is drawn in the neutral grey because a sweep is a measure rather than one of the compared entities. Bands are ± 2σ population spread over lineages, never a standard error — at 24 lineages the two differ by about five times, and a band read as a confidence interval makes adjacent knob settings look separated when they are not.

docs.title: Three things the lab found
docs.text:
Worth knowing before you read its output, because two of them are defects in the system it measures rather than in the surrogate.

  1. hard stops on "every spec objective satisfied" with an empty Pareto front. Not a bug in the lab. DataRegistry.ingest records a task's metrics whatever the QC verdict and SatisfactionRule counts those readings, while core/pareto correctly refuses a FAIL node a place on the front. f6-stop-vs-front.png exists to make that gap unmissable. Backlog G14.
  2. An aborted campaign's provenance says reason: completed. hopeless raises CampaignAborted and the only durable trace of why is the process's stderr, so collect derives aborted from the exit code instead. Backlog G15.
  3. About one first cycle in eight stalls for an extra ~1.0s inside asyncflow's run-component loop, which waits on its component-change event with a 1.0s timeout. Irrelevant on hardware, 90% of the first cycle here, and the reason every wall-clock caption says so. Backlog G16.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text: Add a knob to SWEEPS in analysis/mock_lab.py — the tool, the parameter and the values — and it sweeps. Add an arm to ARMS and it must also get a hue in plot_style.RUN_STYLES; style_for raises on an unknown arm rather than inventing one, because a silent fifth hue would break the colour identity every figure in a report depends on. A fifth categorical colour has to be re-validated first — see the campaign-plot-style skill's references/palette.md.

docs.title: Observation: what a caller is told, and when
docs.text:
resolution.md runs one direction — toolkit, goal, budget and parameters become specified targets and a programmed Stage. This page runs the other: how the state of a running campaign becomes a CampaignObservation, who is shown it, what of it survives to disk, and by what mechanism any of it reaches a caller outside this process.

Every step says what it takes, who owns it, what it produces and what refuses it, in the order a cycle executes them. Anything true of how a decision is made from an observation is in control-models.md and is not repeated here. If this page and the code disagree, the code is right and this page is a bug.

Two things to read it for. Wiring IMPRESS-A beneath an enclosing campaign manager, which needs to know the cadence, the shape and the cost of being told — see decision 0014. And changing any of this safely, for which the thing to preserve is named in each step: the observation is assembled inside a window where the executor is not mutating anything, and almost every rule below exists to keep that window shut.

   absorb a run ────────────────────────────────────────────────  step 1
        │  await-free: tree, ledger, provenance, _absorbed
        ▼
   observe()  ──→  CampaignObservation  ─────────────────────────  step 2
        │             (built fresh, never stored)
        ├──→  the reasoner's two halves, in-process  ────────────  step 3
        ├──→  prov_sink  ──→  the plane's event list  ───────────  steps 4, 5
        └──→  GET /observe?since=  ──→  another process  ────────  step 6
                  │
   provenance/*.jsonl, jobs/*.jsonl  ─────────────────────────────  step 7
                  │
   what a caller must do today  ──────────────────────────────────  step 8
        │
   Bridge ──→ CampaignDigest ──→ a sink, per absorbed cycle  ─────  step 9

docs.title: Step 1 — a run is absorbed, and the window is shut
docs.text:
What ran between admission and this step — each task's command, and where it is recorded — is invocation.md.

In: ExecutionResults from the backend. Owner: runtime/executor._absorb:578. Out: DesignNodes on the tree, one results provenance record each, and one id appended to _absorbed per lineage (:601).

The executor is the only writer of campaign state, and every mutating block is free of await. Its own module docstring (runtime/executor.py:1-16) states the rule and the reason: "adding an await inside observe or _absorb would reintroduce torn reads, and they are nearly impossible to diagnose from provenance afterwards." That property is a discipline, not something the language enforces, and it is the single constraint that shapes everything below — an observation cannot be pushed anywhere from inside the code that produces the state it describes. A sink that must be awaited cannot be called here.

_absorbed (:318) is an append-only list of node ids in absorption order, and _cursor (:319) is how far the last consumer read. Those two integers are the whole of the campaign's notion of "what is new", and step 2 is where they are read.

docs.title: Step 2 — observe() assembles the snapshot
docs.text:
In: the executor's own state, plus an optional since watermark. Owner: runtime/executor.observe:540. Out: a CampaignObservation (core/decision.py:75).

Synchronous, read-only, and the only place in the package that constructs one. It computes the Pareto front over live nodes, builds PopulationStats (core/decision.py:66) inline, and reads recent out of _absorbed[cursor:] (:549) with seq = len(_absorbed) (:550).

since is the one subtle parameter. Omitted, it reports from _cursor — what the last consumer saw. Given, it reports from that watermark instead, without moving the cursor, so an observer can read the same evidence a policy is about to read without disturbing it. The docstring calls this parity of evidence, and ADR 0007 makes it binding rather than incidental.

Two declared fields are never populated by this method: failures (core/decision.py:87) and PopulationStats.diversity (:71). And one thing a reader would expect is absent — the parameter values a planner chose. Those reach stages provenance under mappings (runtime/executor.py:1005, written at :1019) and nowhere else, so an observation says what a campaign found and not what it tried.

docs.title: Step 3 — the two halves are shown it, whole
docs.text:
In: the observation. Owner: runtime/roles.py:86 (obs = await session.observe(), once at the top of every turn). Out: SpecEvidence (policy/specifier.py:36) and PlanningContext (policy/planner.py:37).

Both wrappers hold the observation rather than summarising it — SpecEvidence's own docstring says observation is the object observe() returned, not a digest of it. So there is exactly one description of campaign state in the system, and a reasoner, an external caller and a test all read the same fields. That is what makes the control models comparable: a difference in their behaviour is a difference in judgement, not in what they were told.

What refuses a second shape here: nothing mechanical. The discipline is the import contract — policy may import core and nothing else (tests/test_layering.py), so a half cannot reach the executor to ask a narrower question.

docs.title: Step 4 — provenance is mirrored to every listener
docs.text:
In: every provenance record. Owner: runtime/executor._log:356. Out: a write to provenance/<kind>.jsonl, then a guarded call to each registered listener.

def _log(self, kind: str, record: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    self.prov.append(kind, record)
    for sink in list(self._prov_listeners):
        try:
            sink(self.spec.campaign_id, kind, dict(record))
        except Exception as broken:
            self.prov_dropped += 1
            log.warning(...)

This is the only synchronous hook out of a running campaign, which is why a sink that must be awaited cannot be one — that is step 9's job. It was a single slot until recently, and two call sites assigned it without checking for each other: control/plane.py:104 for the event stream and cli/__init__.py:890 for the log heartbeat. Last writer won, in silence, so serving a campaign over HTTP turned off its own progress log. Both now call add_prov_listener, prov_sink remains as a property over the first listener so no caller had to move, and each call is guarded and its failures counted — _log runs on every settlement and every absorption, so a listener that raised was aborting a campaign from inside the record of work already done (finding 3).

docs.title: Step 5 — the event stream is that mirror, kept in memory
docs.text:
In: prov_sink calls. Owner: control/plane.InProcessControlPlane.emit:112, into self._events (:94). Out: events() (:143), by cursor page or as a tail.

_events is a dict[str, list[Event]] in the serving process. It is unbounded, never persisted and lost when the process exits. events(stream=True) polls its own list every 50 ms, and the SSE layer polls that at 100 ms (control/http.py:151). The method's own docstring is honest about it: it polls "because provenance is appended to rather than published. A push-based source would replace the body of this loop and nothing else."

What refuses an addition here: ADR 0007 — no adapter may add an operation absent from the core protocol. A new way to be told would be a change to CampaignControlPlane, not an adapter's business.

docs.title: Step 6 — the observation crosses a process boundary intact
docs.text:
In: GET /campaigns/<cid>/observe?since=. Owner: control/http.py:200 server side, ControlPlaneClient.observe:304 client side. Out: the same CampaignObservation, rebuilt from model_dump(mode="json").

This already works and is exercised end to end. It is the only machine-readable, serialisable description of campaign state the system has, and anything that wants to tell a caller something should start from it rather than invent a second vocabulary.

Its cost is the other half of the fact. The payload embeds the whole ToolkitView — every TaskCard, and each toolkit's full SKILL.md text (tools/view.view_of:67) — plus the applied Spec and every DesignNode on the front, rebuilt on every call, with no projection and no field selector. ToolkitView.skills is read by no prompt and no consumer (resolution.md finding 6), so the largest part of what crosses the wire is read by nothing at either end.

docs.title: Step 7 — what is actually durable
docs.text:
In: records from _log and the two ledgers. Owner: core/provenance.append:24, exec/ledger.py, exec/task_ledger.py. Out: append-only JSONL under the campaign root.

file holds provenance/campaign.jsonl the spec, goal, objectives and budget, once at start provenance/specs.jsonl each Spec generation and its rationale provenance/graphs.jsonl each composed graph, its signature, trust and estimate provenance/stages.jsonl the deployed Stage — the only record of chosen parameters provenance/executions.jsonl settlement and run-finished events provenance/results.jsonl one row per absorbed node: QC verdict, failed gates, metrics provenance/tasks.jsonl per task, including cost_estimated and cost_measured provenance/decisions.jsonl the reasoner's transcript provenance/transitions.jsonl promotions, demotions, stops, losses jobs/ledger.jsonl, jobs/tasks.jsonl run and task state, folded on read

append opens, writes and closes per record, so a record is durable when the call returns. The log is truth; checkpoints are an index.

There is no observations.jsonl. An observation is computed on demand and discarded, so cycle N's view of the campaign cannot be read back — it has to be re-derived from graphs, results, executions and specs. Nothing today needs to replay one, which is why this is recorded as a property rather than fixed.

docs.title: Step 8 — so what must a caller do today
docs.text:
In: a wish to be told. Out: one of three unsatisfying options.

option how what it costs Assign prov_sink mgr.prov_sink = fn, as cli/__init__.py:890 does for the log heartbeat one slot, synchronous, unguarded; the caller must reconstruct cycles from provenance records Run impress-a serve and poll serve_campaign:459, then GET /observe a second process and a socket, and the whole ToolkitView on every poll Hold the manager and schedule a task mgr.observe() through the _DELEGATED allowlist (manager.py:46) the caller must write the pump, and nothing tells it when something landed

The third is the one that works, and the precedent for it is already in the tree. cli._heartbeat:758 does exactly this for logging, and its docstring states the licence: "Reads only the executor's synchronous snapshot API. Its mutating blocks are await-free by invariant, so a heartbeat scheduled between them can never see a torn state." A pump that awaits a sink outside the executor is a heartbeat with a sink instead of a logger, and it needs nothing added to the executor at all.

docs.title: Step 9 — the bridge, which is that pump with a sink
docs.text:
In: a CampaignManager and a CycleSink. Owner: integrations/reporting.Bridge. Out: one CampaignDigest per absorbed cycle, and reports/<sink>.jsonl beside provenance.

run_with_sink(manager, sink) races the campaign against the pump, exactly as cli.run_campaign already races it against the heartbeat. The executor is unchanged: the pump reads observe() between its mutating blocks and awaits the sink outside them, so no await enters a block that writes campaign state.

decision why Triggered on obs.seq advancing the absorption watermark. Not cycle, which is incremented in _dispatch:1036 and so counts submissions — a report fired there carries no results. Not _activity, which pump:1471 clears, so a second consumer would race it. A monotone integer is race-free. period_s is a floor, not the only trigger a cycle of the real chain runs minutes of tasks with nothing absorbed, and a caller's staleness bound has to be satisfiable while that happens One report before the run, one after the first is a liveness anchor before any work exists to describe; the last is the only one guaranteed to be read, because the stores a caller receives these through keep one value per workflow — so no digest may be a delta Every sink call guarded a sink is somebody else's code reaching into a process holding an allocation. A listener that raises costs a log line and a counter, never the run — the rule policy/reasoning.py:175 already applies, and the one _log still does not (finding 3) Digests land in reports/, not provenance/ the executor is the only writer there, and a tenth provenance kind would make a record of what somebody else was told look like a record of what the campaign did

CampaignDigest (core/decision.py) is a projection of observe()'s return value, not a new operation, so ADR 0007 stays out of play for the same reason adding a field to the observation does. It drops the ToolkitView, the Spec and the DesignNode bodies — static for the campaign, and already given to a caller once by impress-a offer — and carries both spending scales under distinct names, because declared and measured are two different numbers and a caller charging its own budget wants the second (finding 8).

Pause is in the same loop, because it is the same cadence. It gates admission: in-flight runs are allowed to finish, since cancellation is advisory, so a paused campaign keeps spending for up to one cycle.

docs.title: What the observation plane does not enforce
docs.text:
Eleven places where the implementation does not do what a reader of the design would reasonably assume, two of them since repaired and marked in place rather than deleted, because the evidence that forced them is the useful part. Each is verified against the source at the anchor given. Read this section before changing any step above.

# the reasonable assumption what the code does anchor item 1 An observation reports what went wrong, and how diverse the population is failures and PopulationStats.diversity are declared and never populated by the only method that builds one core/decision.py:87,71, runtime/executor.py:536-562 G 2 A campaign's own view of itself at cycle N can be read back No observation is ever persisted. Nine provenance kinds, none of them observations; cycle N's view must be re-derived from four other files core/provenance.py:22, runtime/executor.py:484 G 3 A campaign can be watched by more than one listener RESOLVED. It could not: prov_sink was one slot, and control/plane.py:104 and cli/__init__.py:890 both assigned it, so attaching a monitor evicted the log heartbeat silently — and the call was unguarded, so a listener that raised stopped the campaign from inside a provenance write, the most expensive place to raise. It is a guarded list now, with prov_dropped counting failures so a deaf subscriber is discoverable, and prov_sink kept as a property over the first listener. The rule is policy/reasoning.py:175's, arriving late runtime/executor.py:343-365 G18 4 The event stream is a stream _events is an unbounded in-memory list, never persisted, lost on exit; "streaming" is a 50 ms poll of that list with a 100 ms poll on top control/plane.py:94,160-167, control/http.py:151 G 5 An observation says what the campaign tried, not only what it found Chosen parameter values are absent. They reach stages provenance under mappings and no observation field, so a caller sees scores without the knobs that produced them runtime/executor.py:1005,1019 G, and resolution.md finding 7's neighbour 6 The payload carries what its consumers read It embeds every TaskCard and each toolkit's whole SKILL.md, plus the applied Spec and the full front, rebuilt per call with no projection — and ToolkitView.skills is read by nothing at either end tools/view.py:67, runtime/executor.py:533-562 G 7 Watching a campaign is free of consequence observe() refreshes the liveness clock. touch() sets _last_contact, and _control_lost_for is what drains and stops a campaign whose caller vanished. The coupling is deliberate — the Listener polls observe() every cycle, so no heartbeat operation was added — but the consequence is that a purely passive observer keeps drain-and-stop from ever firing, which is exactly the shape of a caller that watches without steering runtime/executor.py:532,491-498,501-525 G 8 Spending reported to a caller is spending RESOLVED. It was not: BudgetLedger.spent is declared cost - _settle settles results.cost, documented "DECLARED, summed - unchanged on purpose" - and declared figures sit multiples above measurement deliberately, because they feed gates that refuse graphs. So an outer manager told our spend was told the headroom too, and its own learned cost could never converge. _settle now also calls charge_measured(results.cost_measured), which was already summed per run and folded into nothing, and CampaignDigest reports both scales under distinct names. The measured figure bounds nothing and gates nothing, deliberately: a measurement arrives after the work it describes is paid for, so an admission gate reading it would refuse tomorrow's work on yesterday's luck runtime/executor.py:1170-1175, core/budget.py:84-91 G20 9 A TaskCard carries the cost terms its spec declares RESOLVED. It did not: tools/view.py:46-48 passed burn_rate= and max_commitment= to a model that declared neither field, and pydantic's default extra is ignore, so both were discarded in silence while core/budget.py:67 documented the rule min(goal.budget[d], card.max_commitment[d]) against a field that could not exist. Both are fields now. The fix is not extra="forbid" — these models cross the HTTP boundary, so forbidding extras would turn a newer peer's observation into a 500 — so the general case is guarded mechanically instead, by tests/test_layering.py::test_every_keyword_passed_to_a_core_model_is_a_field_of_it tools/view.py:46-48, core/toolkit.py:59-89 D1, realised in our own code rather than in a user's YAML 10 A caller can project a burn-down from what it is told There is no rate. BudgetLedger is constructed without walltime=, so burn_rate() returns empty permanently and project() is inert. Limits, spent and holds cross; a rate does not runtime/executor.py:230, core/budget.py:160,172 E 11 The chain that runs is the chain the campaign declared _admit_once composes against the whole Registry and reports available: self.reg.ids(); nothing restricts a submitted Stage to spec.stages. The bound holds by construction for the shipped planners, whose ToolkitView is narrowed — it is not a gate, and anything pricing a campaign from stages is relying on that runtime/executor.py:673-694, tools/view.py:55 G, and resolution.md's "available means three different things"

One asymmetry that is by design and is listed so it is not mistaken for the above. Gate 1 does not check that a required root port was satisfied — the loop is a literal pass commented "roots may be satisfied from campaign inputs" (compose/validate.py:81) — because input data arrives through params: rather than as typed reference data. That is resolution.md finding 1, and it belongs to resolution rather than to observation; it appears here only because a caller reading unsatisfied_root_ports off an offer is reading a computation, not a gate.

docs.title: Seeing it on disk
docs.text:
Every step's output except step 2's is in provenance, which is the only way to check this page rather than trust it. impress-a mock-lab --only arms --stage sweep writes one campaign per arm in about half a minute with no allocation.

step where it landed 1 provenance/results.jsonl — one row per absorbed node 2 nowhere — finding 2 3 provenance/decisions.jsonl — what each half was asked and answered 4, 5 provenance/*.jsonl is the record; the event list is memory only 6 the campaign's control_plane.url, written 0600 under serve 7 the table in step 7 8 the heartbeat +… lines in a run log, which is step 8's third option already working 9 reports/<sink>.jsonl under the campaign root — one line per digest, with the ts it was sent — telemetry/ under the campaign root, when telemetry_checkpoint_s > 0: the engine's own trace, a span per Stage block with its node tasks and tool commands under it, each naming the backend it ran on. Not one of the nine steps — it is the execution layer's record, not the campaign's

A step whose output cannot be pointed at in one of those files is a step this page has described wrongly — step 2 included, and that is finding 2 rather than an exception.

docs.title: Being one workflow of a larger campaign
docs.text:
The two steps above are the whole of what an enclosing campaign manager needs, and integrations/aucam.py is the hundred lines that connect them to one. It is the only module in the package that imports AuCaM, which tests/test_layering.py asserts, so the dependency stays optional and one file wide.

from impress_a.integrations.aucam import launch_bounds, reward_fn, workflow_config

config = workflow_config("campaigns/delta-small-molecule.yaml", model="D")
# -> an AuCaM WorkflowConfig: declared_spending and spending_limit from the offer,
#    resources from its resource shape, supports_pause=True, stale_timeout_s at 4x
#    the report interval the offer declares.
bounds = launch_bounds(offer)          # for the caller's own LaunchRequest.bounds
policy = BanditSchedulingPolicy(reward_fn=reward_fn)

Four things in that adapter are decisions rather than plumbing, and each is a defect avoided:

  • It does not declare flow. AuCaM passes its shared engine to a block that asks for one. Taking it would be wrong twice: WorkflowEngine.__init__ captures the loop it is built on, and the executor must build its own through exec.backend.make_engine_bounded, which also bounds Dragon's synchronous startup. There is no "use this engine instead" seam, and inventing one is how jobs 22328172 and 22328262 spent their allocations on an engine that dispatched nothing. The price is that our tasks are invisible to the caller's per-task telemetry — which is why spending travels in our own reports.
  • The caller's spending limit becomes the campaign's own budget, narrowing it and never loosening it. A limit enforced from outside can only cancel a campaign after it has overspent; the same number as a budget is refused by reserve and gate 5 before a task runs, and the campaign stops itself with a reason naming the dimension.
  • score is a float, not a dict. AuCaM's default bandit reward is 1.0 if returncode == 0 else 0.0 — throughput, and its own comment says science scores belong to the controller — so no shipped policy of theirs can rank a dict. The scalar is progress toward the asked-for front; reward_fn is what ranks arms by it.
  • metrics carries the MEASURED spend under the keys the caller charges from. Without them it prorates our declared cost, and the declared figures are inflated on purpose (finding 8).

The campaign is still ours throughout: it keeps the engine, the outer loop and the decision to stop, and the caller gets no privilege over campaign state that a policy would not have. That is decision 0014, and tests/test_aucam.py runs a real AuCaM campaign over a real IMPRESS-A one to prove the page is describing something that works.

docs.title: Resolution: from caller inputs to a programmed Stage
docs.text:
How a campaign's four inputs — the toolkit, the goal, the budget and the parameters — become the targets the campaign is scored on and the work it actually runs.

This page is the spine. Every step says what it takes, who owns it, what it produces and what refuses it, in the order a campaign executes them. Steps 4 to 6 are the ones a reasoner takes part in, and what each model is shown when it does is control-models.md; architecture.md covers the loop around all of this. If this page and the code disagree, the code is right and this page is a bug.

Two things to read it for. Reconciling the implementation against a theoretical account of what an adaptive campaign ought to do — for which the last section, What the pipeline does not enforce, is the important one. And changing any of this safely, for which the refusal named in each step is the thing to preserve.

toolkits/*/tools/*/spec.yaml ──load, validating──→ Registry.specs           step 0
campaign.yaml ──load_spec──→ CampaignSpec                                   step 1
   ├─ goal, objectives, budget, target_front ──goal_from_spec──→ Goal       step 2
   ├─ stages ──view_of──→ ToolkitView      (narrowed; frozen hidden)        step 3
   └─ params, replicas, loop bounds ───────→ the executor keeps these
Goal ──initial_spec (no toolkit in the room)──→ Spec: Aims + SpecObjectives step 4
Spec × ToolkitView ──reporting()──→ which targets are producible at all     step 5
Spec.ready() × ToolkitView ──_resolve + _knobs──→ Stage[TaskMapping]        step 6
Stage ──compose_stage──→ TaskGraph ──Reviewer + Scrutiny──→ RunRecord       step 7
RunOutcome ──ingest──→ readings ──satisfies──→ targets closed               step 8

docs.title: Step 0 — the toolkit becomes a typed vocabulary
docs.text:
In: toolkits/<toolkit>/tools/<id>/spec.yaml plus the toolkit's SKILL.md. Owner: tools/registry.py. Out: Registry.specs: {tool_id: ToolSpec}.

Discovery walks the search paths, IMPRESS_A_TOOLKITS included, so toolkits are not package data — a tool can be added without touching the package.

Loading is validating (Registry._load_toolkit:52). A malformed spec, a default outside its own declared range, a qc_gates entry naming an unimplemented check, a duplicate tool id, or a SKILL.md missing one of REQUIRED_SKILL_SECTIONS (:19 — Purpose, Canonical sequences, Cost posture, Pitfalls) is a load-time error. And it is all-or-nothing per toolkit: a toolkit that fails anywhere registers nothing, never a partial set, so a campaign can never plan against half a toolkit.

What each ToolSpec carries that a later step reads:

declared read by typed inputs / outputs ports steps 6 and 7 — chain resolution and gate 1 parameters with min/max/default/trades, frozen_parameters, operator_only step 6 (_knobs), gate 3 metrics — the metric names this tool's agent reports step 5, the whole producibility question qc_gates, each role: integrity \| acceptance step 8, and trust (decision 0013) cost_model, resources gates 4 and 5, the interlock's cap

metrics is declared, never inferred (tools/spec.py:127). Inferring it from metric_in_range gate parameters was tried and warned falsely on the mock campaign, whose tools emit ddg/iptm/sc_rmsd and gate on none of them — so a graph that demonstrably produced a four-node front was reported as unable to produce anything. The declaration is held honest at runtime by the metrics_reported gate (tools/gates.py:85): an adapter that could not read a value must omit it rather than report 0.0, and that gate, not the threshold, is what catches it.

docs.title: Step 1 — the campaign YAML becomes a CampaignSpec
docs.text:
In: campaigns/<spec>.yaml. Owner: cli.load_spec:69. Out: CampaignSpec.

The rule this loader is written to, recorded in its own comment: every field is read exhaustively, because a key a spec file sets and the loader ignores does nothing and says nothing. control_liveness_timeout_s: 120 sat in all three Delta specs doing exactly that until the line existed, and sites/*.yaml's tool_delivery switch is the same shape still open (backlog E1).

Three resolutions worth naming:

  • objectives: → core.pareto.Objective(**o). The caller's target schema is the ranking-objective type (core/pareto.py:21): name, direction, and optional min/max. There is no second vocabulary for "what the campaign wants".
  • params: → _resolve_path_params:53. A relative *_path value is resolved against the campaign YAML's directory, not the CWD, because the launcher cds into a per-job directory before loading the spec; an absolute path would tie the spec to one checkout on one machine.
  • replicas: 0 means unset, not one. replicas is a cap (step 6), and defaulting it to 1 would silently narrow every campaign that never mentioned it.

root, trust_root and seed_salt are read from the environment when YAML does not set them, deliberately: the right value is machine-specific or must be shared across several submissions of one spec, and YAML carries no env expansion.

docs.title: Step 2 — the split: what the campaign is for vs how it is driven
docs.text:
In: CampaignSpec. Owner: runtime/roles.goal_from_spec:210. Out: Goal.

The Goal carries text, objectives, budget and target_front — and deliberately nothing about the loop. target_front crosses because it is success criteria ("ten designs over the bar"), while max_cycles, stagnation_limit and concurrency stay on the CampaignSpec for the executor because they are statements about how the engine gets there. That split is what makes Goal → Spec a statement about the science rather than about the engine, and it is why a Specifier can be handed the Goal and nothing else.

Two of the Goal's own fields are inert: reference_data is never populated and never read, and walltime_s is never read. The caller's input data therefore does not travel as typed reference data — it travels in params: as input_spec_path, ligand_smiles and their like (see What the pipeline does not enforce, finding 1).

docs.title: Step 3 — the toolkit is projected, and narrowed to the campaign
docs.text:
In: Registry + CampaignSpec.stages. Owner: tools/view.view_of:55, called once at runtime/executor.py:255. Out: ToolkitView — the only toolkit a reasoner can ever see.

policy may import core only (ADR 0010, asserted by tests/test_layering.py), so a reasoner cannot hold a ToolSpec or a Registry. card_for:14 projects each spec into a TaskCard, and runtime is the one layer that can see both sides.

Narrowing to stages: is a safety property, not economy. A Specifier shown the mock toolkit on a real campaign can map the Goal onto outputs that would then execute mocks on a GPU allocation — the headline bug of the real-toolkit work. Gate 6 refuses such a graph; this keeps it from being proposed. mock_noodle is the reason the floor matters: it completes successfully, reports a confident designability, and produces a structure with no secondary structure.

card_for is also the single seam where a parameter is hidden from a reasoner. Both frozen_parameters and operator_only arrive in TaskCard.frozen with their reason and are absent from TaskCard.parameters, so everything that reads a card — _knobs.tunable, the oracle planner's prompt, its schema check — treats them alike without a flag threaded through four readers. ToolSpec.parameters keeps an operator_only entry, so gate 3 and the campaign's own params: see it exactly as before: the campaign may set difficulty; a reasoner may not propose it.

ToolkitView.skills is filled with each toolkit's SKILL.md text here and reaches no prompt (finding 6).

docs.title: Step 4 — targets: Goal → Spec, with no toolkit in the room
docs.text:
In: Goal. Owner: ThresholdSpecifier.initial_spec:59. Out: a Spec of Aims and SpecObjectives, applied by the executor.

One Aim from the Goal's prose, then one SpecObjective per declared objective, with targets=[name] — names, never sources (decision 0012), so a measurement arriving months later supersedes against the same name.

The satisfaction rule attached here decides everything downstream:

declared objective rule n bounded (min and/or max) metric_in_range target_front, or 1 unbounded (direction only) metric_present always 1

An objective with a direction and no bound is an optimisation target, not a finish line: it ranks and never prunes, so what the campaign owes it is a measurement. Raising n on one would be meaningless — ten readings of a number nobody has to beat say nothing more than one.

And n counts readings, not distinct designs: DataRegistry.satisfies is len(metrics(metric)) >= n, one row per (task, metric) per ingested outcome. The experiment's own endpoint — distinct designs after sequence clustering — is a different and smaller number. This rule is a stopping condition, not a score.

initial_spec takes the Goal alone; the toolkit arrives only with the observation, at step 5. That is deliberate, and it is why models A and B both delegate this call to model D's Specifier: every arm of a comparison must start from the same objectives, and a model asked to restate four objectives it was given can only get it wrong.

docs.title: Step 5 — which targets this toolkit can inform
docs.text:
In: Spec + the observation's ToolkitView. Owner: ToolkitView.reporting(metric) and ThresholdSpecifier.unproducible:104, run per cycle. Out: the open objectives that no enabled tool can measure.

for obj in spec.open_objectives():
    if obj.targets and not any(view.reporting(t) for t in obj.targets):
        out.append(obj.id)

Read off the enabled view, not the registry: a campaign that narrowed its stages has narrowed what it can produce, and saying otherwise is the mock-chain-on-a-GPU failure in another form.

What happens next is the one genuine difference between the control models at this step, and it is pre-registered rather than incidental: model D records unproducible in the statement and leaves the objective OPEN, so its Spec can never complete while one exists; model A retires it by DELETE; model B retires on action: "retire". Both answers are defensible; they are not the same campaign. On the real six-stage chain every declared objective is producible, so the branch does not fire there.

failed() (:190) returns only the unproducible. Everything else is a matter of more draws, and at the one-in-three acceptance rate this project has measured, calling that failure would end most campaigns that were merely unlucky.

docs.title: "Available" means three different things
docs.text:
scope computed by who sees it everything installed Registry.ids() nobody in policy the campaign's chain ToolkitView the Specifier and the Planner this graph _producible_metrics(graph) (executor.py:719) the executor only, as a gate

The executor checks the third scope itself, trusting no reasoner's account:

  • _objectives_without_a_producer:751 — campaign objectives no tool in the admitted graph reports. A refusal on the Stage path (gate="coverage"). Job 22675512 is why: a budget correction truncated boltz_predict off the chain, taking the only producer of complex_plddt and ligand_iptm — two of four objectives. The composer and validator never receive spec.objectives at all, so the graph was type-correct, affordable, admitted, and incapable of informing half of what it was for. The admitted graph recorded rejected: null.
  • _could_reach_the_front:734 — the same comparison restricted to constrained objectives, because unbounded ones rank but never prune, so missing one costs a node nothing.

The gap between scopes two and three is where that campaign was unwinnable from the moment it was admitted.

docs.title: Step 6 — the Stage is programmed
docs.text: In: Spec.ready() — open objectives whose dependencies are SATISFIED (core/spec.py:218) — plus the ToolkitView. Owner: ThresholdPlanner.plan:100, which A, B and C all delegate to. Out: a candidate Stage of TaskMappings.

docs.title: Which tools, and how they wire
docs.text:
_resolve:189 selects by output type, never by chain position:

  1. For each ready objective's targets, _producer_of:240 returns the earliest enabled tool declaring that metric. Earliest rather than best: a metric reported twice in one chain supersedes by name (ADR 0012), so taking the earlier producer never loses the later one, while taking the later could drop the chain that feeds it.
  2. _require:251 adds that tool and recurses through its required input ports, finding each port's producer with _source_for:274 — the nearest tool declared before the consumer whose output unifies_with the port. Restricting to earlier tools is what keeps the result acyclic with no topological pass: the campaign's declared order is the only ordering either side has.
  3. Producers for every declared campaign objective are added even when only one objective is ready, because a node missing one of those can never be feasible and so can never reach the front whatever the science did. Planning the minimal chain for one refinement objective produced a child measured on iptm alone, incomparable with everything already on the front, and unwinnable from the moment it was planned.
  4. The chain is sorted into the campaign's declared order, and a ready objective no enabled tool can measure gets a Deferral naming what it waits on — never a silent drop.

The same unification rule is used by the composer and gate 1, so a Planner, a validator and a composer agree about what satisfies what.

One TaskMapping per tool per lineage, carrying the served objective ids, the typed inputs, and params. Attribution is at lineage granularity and that is a property of the engine: _absorb produces exactly one DesignNode per lineage, with that lineage's whole chain merged into one candidate judged on all the objectives. So tasks are not severally responsible for separate objectives — which is why rfd3_design, reporting no campaign objective at all, is indispensable to every one. The cost is recorded rather than hidden: deleting one objective can no longer orphan a single task, only a whole lineage once every objective the Stage serves is DELETED, which is still decidable and is what TaskMapping.objectives being a list exists for.

docs.title: Which parameters may move, and how far
docs.text:
What a parameter is for is read from the one sentence the spec gives about it — ParamCard.trades — by policy/planners/_knobs.py, shared by every Planner half because what a parameter means is a property of the Toolkit, not of a control model.

kind example raising it may a Planner? quality diffusion_steps, recycles the same draw, harder yes — the refinement axis diversity temperature a different draw, same cost yes, and nearly free breadth num_designs, batch_size, nstruct more draws, more cost no identity seed a different lineage no

kind_of:48 returns None for a sentence that says nothing and for one naming two kinds — ambiguity is refused rather than guessed, because a planner resolving a spec's ambiguity is how a GPU bill doubles. tunable:60 additionally demands a numeric type, declared bounds and a default, and excludes anything in card.frozen (so operator_only lands here). Breadth is excluded on evidence: rfd3_design's own spec records that num_designs stays at 1 because its adapter keeps index 0, and the tools whose adapters do select from an ensemble already carry 8 as their declared default. Identity is excluded because moving seed would break the independence of the replica lineages the arm is credited for.

How far a knob moves is the one thing each model does differently (control-models.md): D steps step_up:91 a quarter of declared headroom per refinement and nothing while exploring, because a rule-driven arm has no business inventing a vector from no evidence; A sets at_fraction:72 from the strategy its model named; B names values itself.

docs.title: Then the campaign's own parameters are merged — underneath
docs.text:
executor._apply_campaign_params:800 (and _apply_campaign_defaults:772 on the intent path) merges CampaignSpec.params into the Stage as defaults under whatever the policy set: the policy always wins on any key it did set. Target identity lives there — boltz_predict.ligand_smiles, rfd3_design.input_spec_path, the contig — so a reasoner never has to learn a tool's parameter names to run a campaign correctly, and difficulty can be a campaign condition no model is shown. A roles-driven Delta campaign once ran boltz_predict with no ligand because this merge was missing on the Stage path; it does not fail, it models no ligand and the front optimises the wrong objective.

replicas is the exception to that order, because it is a cap: min(intent.replicas, spec.replicas). How wide a campaign may go is the campaign's call; how wide to go within that is the policy's, so a policy that shrinks its request after a rejection still shrinks.

The merge order has a consequence worth knowing before you set a knob in params:. A Planner's escalation is computed from the tool spec's declared default, not from the campaign's value — step_up is base = float(param.default) — and the policy wins on any key it set. So a quality knob a campaign raised above that default is lowered by the first refinement. Read off arm-rescued-D's own stages.jsonl:

knob spec default the campaign set cycle 1 (explore) cycle 2 (refine) rfd3_design.diffusion_steps 50 200 200 88 ← 50 + (200−50)/4 packmin.cycles 1 5 5 2 ← 1 + (5−1)/4 boltz_predict.diffusion_samples 8 25 25 25 — breadth, so no planner touches it

Nothing is wrong at any one step: exploring emits no parameters, so the campaign's values stand; refining escalates from the tool's own headroom, which is the only scale a planner can reason about on a chain nobody wrote its numbers for; and the policy must win, or a campaign's defaults would override the decisions being measured. The composition of the three is still that a campaign cannot raise a quality floor that survives its own first refinement — only a breadth or frozen parameter persists. Backlog G17.

docs.title: Step 7 — the Stage becomes a graph, and is admitted
docs.text:
In: Stage. Owner: compose.composer.compose_stage:83, then runtime/reviewer.StageReviewer.review:106, then the interlock. Out: a RunRecord, or a ValidationFailure with the gate that refused it.

Three properties compose_stage preserves, because the rest of the system rests on them:

  • Shape only reaches pattern_signature(). Stage id, generation, attempt, rationale, deferrals — and parameter values — are excluded, so tuning a parameter never resets a pattern's accumulated trust.
  • Lineages stay independent. A replica is a whole chain, never a fan-out that funnels back, and each gets its own seed from _replica_seed:18 over the run label, the lineage index and the campaign's seed_salt.
  • P6 is inlined, never scheduled — a scheduled P6 node is a composer bug (gate 4).

What each node of that graph then executes — the adapter, the command line, its placement — is invocation.md.

A refinement Stage's root tasks are seeded from the parent design's artifacts by declared type (_seed_inputs), not by name: the producer names an artifact for its own output port and the consumer for its own purpose, so matching by name would work only where the two happen to agree.

Then the Reviewer, cheapest refusal first, which is deliberate because only the last step instantiates anything:

layer refuses coverage (:40) a ready objective neither planned nor deferred; a task serving no live objective; a task naming an objective not in the applied Spec gates 1–6 (compose/validate.py) type mismatch · cycles, empty graph, missing QC gates · out-of-range, unknown or frozen parameters · P6 scheduled, resources over the site, unproven GPU portability · estimate over remaining budget · mock tools under tool_delivery: real budget (:88) the Stage-level commitment gate 5 cannot see. Marked transient, because contention is a property of the moment rather than of the graph dry-run (:186) every task agent parameterizes without executing

Coverage reads the executor's applied Spec, never the Stage's claim about what is open. Not trusting that claim is the Reviewer's entire purpose: a Planner that could assert a smaller Spec could widen its own coverage to whatever it had chosen to do. It is also why the Spec has a single writer on the execution side, so a remote Planner cannot smuggle a revision in with a Stage.

Admission then applies the interlock (compose/interlock.Scrutiny.for_pattern:225). An untrusted pattern runs under a cost cap of provisional_budget_fraction (0.10), a mandatory dry-run, an auto-suspect result marking whatever the outcome, and at most one instance in flight — because promotion counts consecutive clean runs, and concurrent instances are one draw sampled N times.

transient matters to what a Planner may do about a refusal: budget and interlock are answerable by asking for less at once, so replan shrinks breadth and never the chain. Truncating the tail is a cost heuristic that knows nothing about what the graph can then measure, and it is what took the only producer of two of four objectives off job 22675512.

docs.title: Step 8 — the loop closes, and the two populations part
docs.text:
In: a RunOutcome. Owner: core/data.DataRegistry and core/pareto. Out: closed targets, a new front, and the next cycle's evidence.

ingest:85 records one RealizedDatum per node, per (task, metric) reading and per output artifact — with no reference to the QC verdict. satisfies:129 then counts those readings against each objective's rule, and BaseSpecifier.satisfied (policy/specifier.py:106) asks the registry. No shipped half overrides it, so the stop condition is computed, never argued: the protocol permits an override and says such a Specifier owes an explanation in provenance, and nothing in policy/ takes it.

Meanwhile pareto.feasible:56 admits a node to the front only if qc.eligible_for_front — a FAIL verdict is never eligible, whatever its scores, because these tools fail silently and an exit code is never sufficient evidence.

So satisfaction and the front read two different populations: readings, and eligible designs. They can disagree completely, and finding 3 below is what that costs.

ThresholdSpecifier.revise:120 is the one place the implementation already compensates. When the front is non-empty it adds at most one refinement objective naming the design to improve on (parent_node), with its threshold bound to new evidence as n = hits + 1 — because satisfaction counts everything realized so far, the parent's own measurement included, so a default n=1 rule would be met the instant the objective existed, and the open-refinement cap would never bind because a satisfied objective is not an open one.

Termination is the executor's, never a reasoner's: budget, stagnation, repeated failure and the abort rule are facts about state a reasoner cannot see. A reasoner may request a stop. An empty Spec is complete (core/spec.py:233), which is what makes a Specifier that declines to specify anything end the campaign through the designed path with no special case anywhere.

docs.title: What the pipeline does not enforce
docs.text:
Seven places where the implementation does not do what a reader of the design would reasonably assume. Each is verified against the source at the anchor given. Read this section first before changing any step above.

# the reasonable assumption what the code does anchor item 1 The caller's input files reach a graph as Goal.reference_data, and gate 1 checks that every required root port was satisfied reference_data is never populated and never read. Gate 1's required-root-port loop is a literal pass commented # roots may be satisfied from campaign inputs. Input data arrives as params: entries, and nothing validates that a root port was satisfied at all core/goal.py:55, compose/validate.py:79-81 H4, and A2's neighbour 2 A budget gate prices what a Stage will actually consume Validator.estimate sums cost_model.cost per node. Raising a breadth parameter buys N draws and costs nothing in any gate compose/validate.py:142 H10 3 A campaign cannot report every target satisfied while producing no usable design Satisfaction counts readings (ingest records metrics whatever the QC verdict); the front counts eligible nodes. Both are reachable at once, and the abort rule is reached by running cycles, so a Specifier that declines to add a refinement objective stops before it core/data.py:85,129 · core/pareto.py:56 G14, H11 4 A reasoner's cycle and front bounds come from the campaign ReasonerOptions.max_cycles and .target_front are read by nothing in policy/. They are forwarded so a model's own bound can never be tighter than the campaign's (X1); the RehearsalOracle literals that consumed them were deleted. target_front reaches a Specifier through Goal instead policy/registry.py:80-81 H4 5 Goal.walltime_s bounds a campaign's wall clock read by nothing. On HPC SLURM's --time is the real backstop core/goal.py:74 H4 6 The guidance written for an agent reaches one Registry.toolkit_skills() has no caller, and ToolkitView.skills is populated by view_of and included in no prompt tools/registry.py:86, tools/view.py:67 H4 7 A knob a campaign sets in params: stays set for the campaign A quality knob raised above the tool spec's default is lowered by the first refinement, because step_up escalates from that default and the policy wins the merge. Only breadth and frozen parameters persist — measured on arm-rescued-D, step 6 policy/planners/_knobs.py:91, runtime/executor.py:800 G17

Two further asymmetries that are by design and are listed so they are not mistaken for the above. An unbounded objective can never be unsatisfied, only unmeasured, because direction ranks and only min/max prune. And only integrity gate failures count against a pattern's trust; an acceptance failure still FAILs the node and keeps it off the front but says nothing about whether the pattern is sound — counting quality thresholds made promotion a function of target difficulty, and job 22702568 ran 30/30 tasks clean and promoted nothing (decision 0013).

docs.title: Seeing it on disk
docs.text:
Every step's output is in provenance, which is the only way to check this page rather than trust it. impress-a mock-lab --only arms --stage sweep writes one campaign per arm in about half a minute with no allocation:

step where it landed 1 specs/<cell>.yaml — the CampaignSpec that cell actually ran 4, 8 runs/<cell>/*/provenance/specs.jsonl — each revision as the executor applied it 6, 7 .../stages.jsonl — deployed carries mappings, the full per-task parameter vector; a refusal carries its gate and reason 7 .../graphs.jsonl, jobs/ledger.jsonl — the admitted graph and its outcome — .../decisions.jsonl — what a reasoner was asked and answered, when one was asked

A step whose output cannot be pointed at in one of those files is a step this page has described wrongly.

docs.title: Academy for Task Agents — Standing Notes
docs.text:
Status: roadmap note, not a decision.

LangGraph owns the main loop and campaign state. Academy was deliberately left open for the task-agent layer. This records the evidence relevant to that future evaluation so it is not re-derived, and the three properties of the current design that keep the option available.

docs.title: 1. What was decided, and what was not
docs.text:
Layer Decision Status Outer loop and campaign state LangGraph Decided Control model A's four-node loop LangGraph StateGraph Implemented — src/impress_a/policy/specifiers/agentic.py + planners/agentic.py Task agents (per-tool: pre-process → parameterize → execute → post-process) Open Currently plain Python classes (src/impress_a/tools/agent.py)

The task-agent layer is where Academy would attach, if anywhere. It is deliberately the part of the design with the least framework commitment: TaskAgent is an ordinary class with four overridable phases and no dependency on LangGraph, asyncflow, or anything else.

docs.title: 2. What Academy is
docs.text: Argonne's actor-based framework for distributed multi-agent systems — persistent logical agents that communicate peer-to-peer, as opposed to LangGraph's graph-of-nodes-over-shared- state model. The two solve different problems and are not substitutes.

docs.title: ChemGraph — the strongest working reference
docs.text:
A survey of adjacent projects found ChemGraph's src/chemgraph/academy/ to be a complete actor-based runtime layered above its LangGraph agent: academy/core/agent.py defines a ChemGraphLogicalAgent using from academy.agent import Agent, action, loop, which internally calls ChemGraph's LangGraph single-agent turn logic (run_academy_turn) while communicating peer-to-peer via academy/peer_protocol.py, with its own event log, observability and dashboard. ChemGraph declares both academy-py and parsl as extras.

The transferable point: ChemGraph does not choose between LangGraph and Academy. It uses LangGraph for reasoning within an agent and Academy for distribution across agents — precisely the split this project has left open.

docs.title: flowgentic — imports it, but the path does not work
docs.text: flowgentic depends on academy-py and imports academy.agent (6 occurrences), but its Academy path is broken or dead: examples do not run and the module is effectively unimported. Its src/flowgentic/academy.py nonetheless shows a workable, if unpolished, direct pattern for Academy-agent-action-as-asyncflow- task that could be adapted without depending on the package.

docs.title: No prior art drives real work with Academy
docs.text: No reviewed codebase on this stack demonstrates Academy driving real work. Adopting it would be pathfinding.

docs.title: 4. What would make Academy worth adopting
docs.text:
Concrete triggers, in rough order of likelihood:

  1. Task agents need to be long-lived and stateful. Today they are constructed per invocation and discarded. A task agent that holds an expensive resource across invocations — a loaded model checkpoint, a warm MSA cache, a persistent tool session — is an actor, and Academy models actors natively.
  2. Task agents need to talk to each other. The current design routes everything through the manager. If, say, a ligand-parameterization agent needed to negotiate directly with an MD-setup agent, peer-to-peer messaging becomes the natural shape.
  3. Campaigns need to span allocations or sites. Academy's distribution story is its reason for existing. A campaign coordinating agents across Polaris and an ACCESS machine is the case LangGraph does not address at all.
  4. Many concurrent campaigns need supervision. A fleet-level supervisor over many CampaignManager instances is an actor-system problem, not a graph problem.

docs.title: 5. What would argue against it
docs.text:
• The current layer is not complex enough to need it. Four phases, no inter-agent communication, no persistence between invocations. Academy would add a runtime for capability we do not use.
  • No working precedent on our stack (§3). ChemGraph's is the only real one, and it is computational chemistry on Parsl, not asyncflow.
  • It is a second concurrency model. We already have asyncio + asyncflow's scheduler + rhapsody's backends. Adding an actor runtime is a third, and the boundaries between the existing three are already where the integration friction lives.
  • The import contract (policy ↛ tools, compose ↛ exec) exists to keep layers swappable. An actor runtime that spans layers would erode it.

docs.title: 6. How the current design keeps the door open
docs.text:
Three properties, all deliberate and all currently true:

  1. TaskAgent has no framework dependency. It is a plain class; execute() dispatch lives in the execution layer, not in the adapter.
  2. ToolSpec.agent already declares the agent kind (deterministic | llm). Adding academy is a third value, not a new mechanism.
  3. ToolSpec.entry resolves a dotted path at runtime, so an Academy-backed agent is registered exactly like any other — no composer, validator or manager change.

docs.title: 7. Recommended evaluation, when the time comes
docs.text:
1. Install academy-py and establish whether flowgentic's Academy bridge can be revived or must be rewritten. Static analysis suggests rewritten; confirm by running it.
  2. Read ChemGraph/src/chemgraph/academy/ in full. It is the only working reference.
  3. Prototype one long-lived task agent — a model-serving agent holding a checkpoint across invocations is the clearest candidate — and measure against the current construct-per-invocation approach.
  4. Decide on evidence from that prototype, not on architectural preference.
